The novel is divided into three parts, following a third-person omniscient narrative with no main character. In some editions, the short first chapter is a separate prologue rather than the beginning of the first part.
# Earth and the Overlords
In the late 20th century, the United States and the Soviet Union are competing to launch the first spacecraft into orbit, for military purposes. When vast alien spaceships suddenly position themselves above Earth's principal cities, the space race ceases. After one week, the aliens announce they are assuming supervision of international affairs, to prevent humanity's extinction. They become known as the Overlords. In general, they let humans go on conducting their affairs in their own way. They overtly interfere only twice: in South Africa, where, some time before their arrival, apartheid has collapsed and been replaced with aggressive persecution of the white minority; and in Spain, where they put an end to bull fighting. Some humans are suspicious of the Overlords' benign intent, as they never allow themselves to be seen.
The Overlord Karellen, the "Supervisor for Earth," periodically meets with Rikki Stormgren, the Secretary-General of the United Nations. For the meetings, Stormgren boards one of the spaceships and sits in a well-lit room with only a chair and view screen, never seeing Karellen or any other Overlords. Stormgren is later kidnapped and taken to meet with a leader of a group trying to learn about the Overlords; the man simply asks him questions about the details of how they meet. At their next visit, Karellen tells Stormgren that the Overlords will reveal themselves in 50 years, when humanity will have become used to their presence. When the meeting ends, Stormgren, having determined the view screen is nothing more than one-way glass with Karellen sitting in a dark room, shines a powerful flashlight he has smuggled aboard through the glass. He partially succeeds, is shocked by what he sees, and chooses to keep silent.
Five decades after their arrival, the Overlords finally reveal their appearance: large bipeds that resemble the traditional Christian folk images of demons, with cloven hooves, leathery wings, horns, and barbed tails.
# The Golden Age
Humankind enters a golden age of prosperity at the expense of creativity. The Overlords are interested in psychic research, which humans suppose is part of their anthropological study. Rupert Boyce, a prolific book collector on the subject, allows one Overlord, Rashaverak, to study these books at his home. To impress his friends with Rashaverak's presence, Boyce holds a party, during which he makes use of a Ouija board. Jan Rodricks, an astrophysicist and Rupert's brother-in-law, asks the identity of the Overlords' home star. George Greggson's future wife Jean faints as the Ouija board reveals a number which has no meaning to most of the guests. Then Jan recognizes it as a star-catalog number and learns that it is consistent with the direction in which Overlord supply ships appear and disappear. With the help of an oceanographer friend, Jan stows away on an Overlord supply ship and travels 40 light years to their home planet. Due to the time dilation of special relativity at near-light-speeds, the elapsed time on the ship is only a few weeks, and he has arranged to endure it in hibernation brought on by a drug known as narcosamine.
# The Last Generation
Although humanity and the Overlords have peaceful relations, some believe human innovation is being suppressed and that culture is becoming stagnant. One of these groups establishes New Athens, an island colony in the middle of the Pacific Ocean devoted to the creative arts, which George and Jean Greggson join. The Overlords conceal a special interest in the Greggsons' children, Jeffrey and Jennifer Anne, and intervene to save Jeffrey's life when a tsunami strikes the island. The Overlords have been watching them since the incident with the Ouija board, which revealed the seed of the coming transformation hidden within Jean.
Well over a century after the Overlords' arrival, human children, beginning with the Greggsons', begin to display clairvoyance and telekinetic powers. Karellen reveals the Overlords' purpose: they serve the Overmind, a vast cosmic intelligence, born of amalgamated ancient civilizations and freed from the limitations of material existence. The Overlords themselves are in an "evolutionary cul-de-sac (dead end)"; unable to join the Overmind, they serve instead as a kind of "bridge species", fostering other races' eventual union with it.
As Rashaverak explains, the time of humanity as a race composed of single individuals with a concrete identity is coming to an end. The children's minds reach into each other and merge into a single vast group consciousness. If the Pacific were to be dried up, the islands dotting it would lose their identity as islands and become part of a new continent; in the same way, the children cease to be the individuals which their parents knew and become something else, completely alien to the "old type of human".
For the transformed children's safety — and also because it is painful for their parents to see what they have become — they are segregated on a continent of their own. No more human children are born and many parents die or commit suicide. The members of New Athens destroy themselves with an atomic bomb.
Jan Rodricks emerges from hibernation on the Overlord supply ship and arrives on their planet. He is a celebrity and the Overlords take him to see the sights and permit him a glimpse of how the Overmind communicates with them. When Jan returns to Earth, approximately 80 years after his departure by Earth time, he finds an unexpectedly altered planet. Humanity has effectively become extinct and he is now the last man alive. Hundreds of millions of children – no longer fitting what Rodricks defines as "human" – remain on the quarantined continent, having become a single intelligence readying themselves to join the Overmind.
Some Overlords remain on Earth to study the children from a safe distance. When the evolved children mentally alter the Moon's rotation and make other planetary manipulations, it becomes too dangerous to remain. The departing Overlords offer to take Rodricks with them, but he chooses to stay to witness Earth's end and transmit a report of what he sees.
Before they depart, Rodricks asks Rashaverak what encounter the Overlords had with humanity in the past, according to an assumption that the fear that humans had of their "demonic" form was due to a traumatic encounter with them in the distant past; but Rashaverak explains that the primal fear experienced by humans was not due to a racial memory, but a racial premonition of the Overlords' role in their metamorphosis.
The Overlords are eager to escape from their own evolutionary dead end by studying the Overmind, so Rodricks's information is potentially of great value to them. By radio, Rodricks describes a vast burning column ascending from the planet. As the column disappears, Rodricks experiences a profound sense of emptiness when the children have gone. Then material objects and the Earth itself begin to dissolve into transparency. Rodricks reports no fear, but a powerful sense of fulfillment. The Earth evaporates in a flash of light. Karellen looks back at the receding Solar System and gives a final salute to the human species.

Clark Kent and Lois Lane arrive in the small town of Silsby to report on the world's deepest oil well. That night two small, furry, bald dwarf humanoids come up through the shaft and scare the elderly night watchman to death. Lois and Clark arrive at the oil well and find the dead watchman. Clark and the foreman explore the surrounding area for signs of foul play when Lois glimpses one of the creatures and screams. No one believes her when she tells them what she saw.
The medical examiner is summoned, and he later leaves with Lois. Clark stays behind to confront the foreman, who confesses that the well was closed for fear that they had struck radium and not oil. The foreman proceeds to show Clark ore samples that were collected during different stages of drilling; all of them glow brightly.
Meanwhile, the two Mole Men innocently explore the town. The residents become terrified because of their peculiar appearance and that everything they touch glows in the dark (due to simple phosphorescence). Soon an angry mob forms, led by the violent Luke Benson (Jeff Corey), to kill the "monsters". Superman (George Reeves)  stops Benson and the mob and saves one of the creatures in mid-air after it has been shot. He takes it to the hospital. The second creature returns to the wellhead and disappears down its shaft.
A doctor announces that the injured creature will die unless he has surgery to remove the bullet. When a nurse refuses to do so out of fear, Clark volunteers to assist. Benson's mob arrives at the hospital demanding that the creature be turned over to them. Superman stands guard outside the hospital. Lois stands at his side, but a shot is fired from the mob, narrowly missing her. Superman sends her inside and single-handedly relieves the mob of their rifles and pistols.
Three more Mole Men emerge from the drill shaft, this time bearing a strange weapon. They make their way to the hospital. Benson and his mob see the creatures, and Benson goes after them alone. The creatures fire their laser-like weapon at him. Superman jumps in front of the pulsating ray, saving Benson's life, which Superman says "is more than you deserve!". Superman fetches the wounded creature from the hospital and carries him as his companions return to the wellhead. Soon after, from deep underground, the Mole Men destroy the drill shaft, making certain that no one can come up or go down it ever again. Lois observes, "It's almost as if they were saying, "'You live your lives... and we'll live ours.'".

option_2_text:
It's been three years since Danny Ocean's gang of 11 carried out the historic robbery of the three largest casinos in Las Vegas. Since then, they have scattered into the wilderness with the intention of leading an honest life.
Unfortunately, a mysterious French thief by the name of François Toulour, alias  The Night Fox, eager to show that he is more gifted than them, gives their names to Terry Benedict.
He gives them two weeks to pay back the stolen money plus interest (that's $97 million in two weeks). To pay off their debt, they must accept the challenge of Toulour, which leads them to Amsterdam, Rome, the Tonnara of Scopello in Sicily and Paris where they set out on the trail of the first ever stock exchange and a Fabergé egg (the Egg in the Coronation Carriage).
Meanwhile, the investigation is being led by a tough Europol inspector, Isabel Lahiri, who seems to know Rusty very well.
option_3_text: Every year in a very small town in the West there is a poker game that brings together the five biggest ranchers in the far-flung surroundings. On that day, as the game had started from the previous night, a man, his wife and young son came in to stop at the inn where the players were staying. A poker enthusiast, the man does everything to participate in the game despite the pleas of his wife and son.
option_4_text:
In 1945, at the end of World War II, the western coasts of Denmark were trapped by more than two million German mines. To defuse the mines, a group of very young German soldiers captured by the Danes are sent to the beaches; for them, the war is not over...
Sergeant Carl Rasmussen is in charge of this. If at first he hates them and treats them as enemies, he learns to love them. He is particularly close to Sebastian Schumann, the  leader  of the group. During these dangerous operations, several lost their lives including Wilhelm Hahn and the two young twins Ernst and Werner Lessner, Ernst committing suicide shortly after the death of his brother Werner with whom he was very close. Of the fourteen young men, only four survived, and although they had been promised that they would be sent home, the Danish authorities decided to keep them in order to continue the demining elsewhere in Denmark, in Skallingen. Carl then decides to help them escape and the film ends with a shot of Sebastian giving him one last look.

query_text:
In April 1883 Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson rise early one morning to meet a young woman named Helen Stoner who fears that her stepfather, Dr Grimesby Roylott, is threatening her life. Roylott is a doctor who practised in Calcutta, India, and was married to Helen's late mother 30 years before when she was a wealthy widow living there. He is also the impoverished last survivor of what was once an extremely wealthy but violent, ill-tempered and amoral Anglo-Saxon aristocratic family of Surrey, and has already served a jail sentence for killing his Indian butler in a rage. After serving his jail sentence Roylott had moved to England and tried to reestablish his practice but gave it up after his wife was killed in a railway accident eight years before. At his estate of Stoke Moran Roylott with a violent temper and great physical strength becomes the terror of the town in which he engages in brawls including throwing the local blacksmith into a stream.
Helen's twin sister Julia died almost two years earlier, shortly before she was to be married. Helen had heard her sister's dying words, "The speckled band!" but could not decode their meaning. Helen herself is now engaged. She has begun to hear strange noises and observe strange activities around Stoke Moran, the impoverished and heavily mortgaged estate where she and her stepfather live.
Dr Roylott also keeps strange company at the estate. He is friendly with a band of Gypsies on the property, and he has a cheetah and a baboon as pets. For some time, he has been making changes to the house. Before Helen's sister's death, he had modifications made inside the house and is now having the outside wall repaired, forcing Helen to move into the room where her sister died.
Holmes listens carefully to Helen's story and agrees to take the case. He plans a visit to the manor later in the day. Before he can leave, he is visited by Dr Roylott himself, who threatens him should he interfere. Undaunted, Holmes proceeds to the courthouse, where he examines Helen's late mother's will, and then to the countryside.
At Stoke Moran, Holmes scrutinises the premises inside and out. Among the strange features that he discovers are a bed anchored to the floor, a bell cord that is not attached to any bell, and a ventilator hole between Helen's temporary room and that of Dr Roylott.
Holmes and Watson arrange to spend the night in Helen's room. In darkness, they wait until about three in the morning; suddenly, a slight metallic noise and a dim light through the ventilator prompt Holmes to action. Quickly lighting a candle, he discovers on the bell cord the "speckled band" — a venomous snake. He strikes at the snake with his riding crop, driving it back through the ventilator. Agitated, it fatally attacks Roylott, who had been waiting for it to return after killing Helen. Holmes identifies the snake as an Indian swamp adder and reveals to Watson the motive: the late wife's will which had provided an annual income of £1,100 but had dropped to annual income of £750 sterling [when she passed way], of which each daughter could claim one third (£250) upon marriage. Thus, Dr. Roylott plotted to remove both of his stepdaughters before they married to avoid losing most of the fortune he controlled. Holmes admits his attack on the snake may make him indirectly responsible for Roylott's demise, but he does not foresee it troubling him. Holmes chooses to not tell the police the real motives behind Dr Roylott's death, to prevent giving Helen any further grief.
option_0_text:
# Initial mystery
At dawn one morning in April 1883, Watson is awakened by Holmes who is expecting a new client. Arriving in the drawing room of 221B Baker Street, the two men meet the young Helen Stoner, who has come to consult Sherlock Holmes about strange events at Stoke Moran, the mansion of her stepfather (Grimesby Roylott) where she herself resides.
Helen Stoner describes her stepfather as a violent and physically strong man who once lived in India. Dr. Roylott had married Helen's mother (then a widow) several years earlier and moved with her and her two daughters Helen and Julia to an ancestral manor of the Roylott family in Surrey. Helen's mother died soon after, leaving Helen and Julia alone with their stepfather for several years. Julia's room was located between her stepfather's and her twin sister's.
Two years before Helen Stoner's account, her sister Julia died at the mansion in strange circumstances shortly before her wedding. On the night of the tragedy, Julia had come to Helen's room to talk with her, and she mentioned that she had heard a prolonged whistling noise in the past few nights, to Helen's surprise. Returning to her room, Julia closed her shutters and locked her door from the inside, as she did every night. Suddenly, in the middle of the night, Julia gave a frightening scream, prompting Helen to come out of her room. Julia opened her door to come out of her room hesitantly, exclaiming to her sister  It was the ribbon! The spotted ribbon  while vaguely pointing to their stepfather's bedroom before collapsing. Dr. Roylott, in turn, came out of his room and sent for help to the village, but to no avail. Helen suspects her stepfather of having a role in this death but the facts seem to exonerate him since he himself was locked in his room. The young woman remembers hearing the whistling described by her sister as well as a distinct metallic sound when she was in the corridor but did not know its origin. A band of gypsies also resided on the manor grounds with Dr Roylott's agreement, and may have an uncertain role in the night's events.
Two years after this unexplained tragedy, Helen plans to marry a man named Percy Armitage, and live away from Dr. Roylott's mansion. Two days before the story, work was started on the mansion, forcing Hélène to sleep in Julia's old room. But the night before, Helen clearly heard the nightly whistling described by her sister on the night of her death. Sensing danger, Helen immediately went to London to find Holmes and ask him to clarify the matter.
# Resolution
Holmes promised Helen Stoner that he would go with Watson, his assistant, to the mansion in the early afternoon to inspect the premises, having assured the young woman that her stepfather would not return until evening. While the young woman has recently left Baker Street, Dr. Roylott enters the detective's apartment. He explains that he followed his daughter-in-law and orders the detective to report to him the contents of the exchange with Helen. Faced with the detective's casual refusal, Dr. Roylott grabs the chisel and twists it to let Holmes know that it would be inappropriate for him to take an interest in the case. As a result of this incongruous event, which reinforces the doctor's probable guilt, Holmes spends his morning consulting the will of the Stoner sisters' mother with a notary and discovers that in the event of Julia or Helen's marriage, Dr. Roylott would have to pay a large pension to his daughters-in-law, absorbing the majority of his income. So Dr. Roylott seems to have a motive to prevent Julia and Helen from marrying at all costs.
The afternoon approaches and the two friends leave as planned for the mansion in Surrey. There they meet Hélène Stoner, who shows them around. The detective verifies that it is impossible to enter Julia's room through the window when the shutters are closed, which exonerates the gypsies. Hence, the sound of iron that Helen heard was not that of the bar holding the shutters. Inside Julia's room, however, Holmes discovers several anomalous elements. At the head of the bed is a bell cord that was added shortly before Julia's death, and this cord is not tied to any bell and therefore has no practical use. At the upper end of the cord is a small vent that communicates with Dr. Roylott's room. Hélène explains that this ventilation was added at the same time as the bell cord, but admits that this installation does not make much sense since a ventilation installed on the outside wall would have been much more efficient. In inspecting the doctor's room, Holmes finds few strange items apart from a few objects whose usefulness seems inexplicable. His examination nevertheless seems to make him understand the whole case, although it does not reveal anything concrete to Watson and Hélène Stoner.
Holmes thinks Helen is in great danger by sleeping in Julia's room now, and wishes to intervene at nightfall to put an end to the affair. Holmes asks Helen to be in Julia's room during the evening: when Dr. Roylott returns and enters her room, she will have to make a luminous call so that he and Watson know that they can enter Julia's room through the window which has been left open. Helen will have to quietly leave the room and rest in the adjoining room. The plan is actually executed without incident in the manner described by Holmes.
Holmes and Watson, having entered Julia's room, waited several hours in the dark before the expected event occurred at about three o'clock in the morning. The two friends then perceive a dim light coming from the doctor's room through the ventilation hole in the wall, a sign that his occupant has risen. Holmes and Watson waited some more time before a faint noise was heard near the vent. Holmes then rushes to the bell cord and strikes it vigorously with a cane while exclaiming "Do you see it, Watson?" But Watson can't see anything. A few seconds later, a shout described as "horrible" came from the doctor's room. Watson is lost, Holmes has understood. The two men rushed down the corridor and into the doctor's office. The latter has his eyes glued to the ceiling, as dead as Julia. And round about his head was a viper of the marshes, fine as a ribbon, and speckled in the skin, the ribbon speckled. Holmes subdued the venomous animal with an instrument provided for the purpose and enclosed the snake in his iron box which produced the metallic noise heard two years earlier by Helen as she closed it.
The case is solved as follows: Dr. Roylott killed Julia by introducing a viper (brought from India, like other animals of the manor) through the ventilation hole in order to avoid the marriage, and intended to use the same stratagem to kill his second daughter-in-law who was going to marry Armitage. Nevertheless, the mode of operation was not certain, and the viper could be introduced some nights without biting the occupant of the room. In this case, the doctor had to produce a faint whistle to bring the animal back to him, heard by Julia and then Helen. When Holmes struck the cord by which the viper was descending toward the victim's bed, the animal hurriedly turned around and fatally bit the man on the other side of the wall. Holmes shows no empathy towards the doctor, although he is indirectly responsible for her death. Helen Stoner, who arrives in the doctor's room following Holmes and Watson, seems above all relieved that she herself has escaped certain death.
option_1_text:
In an unidentified European country, Police Inspector Ginko oversees the transportation of $10 million from a bank. To prevent the master thief Diabolik from stealing the money, he creates a diversion whereby a truck from the bank transports wastepaper, while a team of himself and disguised officers take the money in a Rolls-Royce. The plan is still foiled by Diabolik, who escapes with the money and his lover Eva Kant to their underground hideout, where they passionately make love on top of their loot.
Diabolik and Eva attend a press conference held by the Minister of the Interior, who reinstates the death penalty to dissuade criminals such as themselves; they disrupt the conference by releasing exhilarating gas into the crowd. Unable to locate Diabolik, Ginko and his fellow officers are granted emergency privileges that allow them to crackdown on the activities of gangster Ralph Valmont, who they hope will aid in capturing him. Realizing their plan after a teen discotheque he operates is raided due to it being a front for his drug trafficking operations, Valmont makes a deal with Ginko.
While watching a news report, Diabolik decides to steal the famous Aksand emerald necklace from Saint Just Castle for Eva's birthday. After learning of Eva's features from a prostitute who spotted her scouting the castle, Valmont builds and circulates an identikit image of her. Diabolik scales the castle's sheer walls as the police lie in wait, and steals the necklace. Driving on his getaway, he and Eva fool the police by pulling a mirrored film across the road and using dummy decoys of himself; Eva is injured while setting up the film.
While visiting her private doctor, Eva is recognised from the identikit image and abducted. To rescue her, Diabolik boards Valmont's airplane with the stolen $10 million and the necklace to trade for Eva. He is ejected from the plane, but manages to grab Valmont just before a bomb he had planted earlier explodes. Diabolik rescues Eva as Ginko and the police close in on them. Eva makes her escape, while Diabolik loads a gun magazine with the emeralds and fires them at Valmont, killing him. He then seemingly commits suicide by taking a mysterious capsule. As the police hold a press conference about Diabolik's death, he is about to be autopsied when he returns to life, having faked his death using a technique created by Tibetan lamas which requires an antidote to be administered within twelve hours; posing as a nurse, Eva administers the antidote and sneaks him past the police and the press.
Later, a disguised Diabolik visits the morgue where Valmont's body has been cremated, collects the emeralds from his ashes and escapes, gifting them to Eva. Upon Ginko's realization that Diabolik is still alive, a million-dollar reward is offered for his capture; in retaliation, he blows up the tax offices. Despite pleas from the disgraced Minister of the Interior — now the Minister of Finance — the citizens refuse to pay their taxes, forcing the country into debt. Twenty tons of gold, which will be used to buy currency, are melted into a single block to make it difficult to steal; the block is loaded onto a train commandeered by Ginko. Diabolik and Eva divert the train by leaving a burning truck on the tracks and re-route it to a bridge where a bomb is placed. It explodes when the train arrives, and the gold falls into the water below. As Ginko swims ashore, Diabolik and Eva collect the gold and return to their hideout.
The steel casket containing the gold is traced by the police, allowing them to track Diabolik's hideout. They close in on Diabolik, who is melting the gold into smaller ingots. As the police fire upon him, Diabolik is unable to control the smelting, and the whole cavern ends up being covered in molten gold. Diabolik is believed to have been killed, with his heat-proof suit now covered in solidified gold. The police seal off the cavern, intending to recover the gold later. As Ginko arrives to arrest her, Eva is allowed a private moment to pay her respects to Diabolik, who winks at her.
option_2_text:
Vincent van Gogh seems to always be in artistic and emotional exhaustion. He is occasionally enraptured by his aesthetic responses to the landscapes around Arles; he renders them in oil on canvas or in a sketch pad using his own style of creating his work in a single, rapid sitting. When not in the countryside, he paints inside a yellow room in a yellow house. He begins to contemplate the fleeting nature of some subjects of still life. He also thinks about seasonal flowers and the artistic process which renders a permanent and eternal quality to the representation of flowers on canvas, which does not wilt and wither.
For a while, Vincent's preferred medium becomes a large sketchbook given to him by Madame Ginoux which he begins to fill with renderings of landscapes in pen and ink. He continues to ponder various philosophical and existential questions such as his desire "not to see a landscape but only the eternity behind it", and that "there cannot be such a thing as nature without there also being a meaning to nature". He wishes to devote increasing time to rendering the landscapes. A group of schoolchildren and their teacher mock Vincent and his work and he chases them away. The teacher and her students call him crazy as they run away in fear. On his walk home some boys throw rocks at him. When he chases the boys some townsmen subdue him and report him to the local psychiatric hospital. His brother Theo is called to Arles from Paris, who in turn convinces Paul Gauguin to agree to visit Vincent. Gauguin soon arrives in Arles.
Vincent is at first exhilarated by the presence of Gauguin, though things quickly sour. When Gauguin announces that he will soon depart, the news crushes Vincent. He then cuts off a piece of his ear to show Gauguin his artistic allegiance to his work, but Gauguin has already departed. Vincent then gives the piece of his cut ear to a Madame Ginoux's barkeeper, Gaby, who is horrified and reports him to the authorities. He is sent by Doctor Ray to mental asylum in nearby Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. There, he has a conversation with a sympathetic, supervising priest about his art and the nature of God. The priest releases Vincent, who travels to Auvers-sur-Oise since the town authorities in Arles deny him permission to stay.
In his last months, Vincent returns to drawing and painting scenes and landscapes, now in Auvers. While painting in the courtyard of a deserted estate, two teenagers with their hunting weapons see him and begin playing at cowboys-and-Indians. During the horsing around disrupting Vincent's painting, a shot goes off. He is hit by the bullet, and the boys beg him not to tell anyone. The boys then bury Vincent's painting and throw their guns into a river while he returns to Auvers. Doctor Gachet is summoned and questions Vincent about the wound; Vincent states the wound is self-inflicted. Theo is called for from Paris, but finds his brother dead upon arrival. Theo organizes an open-casket funeral for Vincent surrounded by his paintings.
A closing onscreen text states that Vincent died in 1890 at the age of 37 from a bullet wound 30 hours after being shot. His completed sketchbook (a gift to Madame Ginoux) was not discovered until 126 years later in 2016. A mid-credits scene features a narration by Gauguin regarding Vincent's favorite color: yellow.
option_3_text:
At the British naval base at Portsmouth in March 1942, Captain Thompson meets his new superior, Major Stringer. Stringer is an experienced sailor who owes his rank to his unconventional idea of equipping a special unit of divers with canoes. Stringer wants to take his unit into the port of Bordeaux to destroy the German blockade-breakers. Forty-three volunteers report to the base. Stringer wants to talk to each of you personally. The first ones are being sent back. Stringer wants to test the rest. They'll be dropped off 200 kilometers from the base, dressed in German uniforms. Tell the men to return as soon as possible. Eight men will pass the test with flying colors: Clarke, Ruddock, Stevens, Lomas, Booth, Cooney, Bradley and Todd.
Sergeant Craig will begin training the men. Thompson thinks the men are undisciplined and complains about Stringer's lax methods. After the men do poorly in a training session, Stringer asks Thompson for advice. Thompson and Stringer are now sharing the duties. While Thompson exercises the men, Stringer instructs them in the use of cannons and explosives. When the mission gets the go-ahead, Thompson and Stringer celebrate. Thompson confides in Stringer and tells him that he was passed over for promotions because his commander blamed him for the failure of a mission. While Thompson talks about his military career, the men engage in a barroom brawl.
Ruddock hasn't returned to base with the others. Thompson wants to visit Ruddock at his house and catches Mrs. Ruddock with her lover. Thompson finds Ruddock in a pub and drives him home, where Ruddock goes after the lover. When Ruddock and Thompson arrive at the base, the canoes are loaded onto a submarine. Along the way, Stringer makes it clear to his men that each two-man canoe is responsible for itself. The success of the mission is more important than the lives of the men.
The submarine is approaching the Gironde when a German ship attacks with water bombs. Lomas hits his head and is knocked unconscious. Thompson wants to take the place of the injured man who was supposed to team up with Ruddock. The canoes are launched in heavy seas. A wave washes over one of the canoes, the men must now save themselves, but are soon captured by the Germans. The other six boats are reaching land. The boats are hidden, the men wait for the shelter of darkness. When the tide comes in, the men get back in their canoes and paddle towards Bordeaux. Craig's canoe is seen by the Germans. Craig turns the canoe upside down and blows it up with a grenade. He and his comrade are captured. The two remaining canoes with Thompson and Ruddock and Stringer and Clarke continue paddling. The Germans search for them without success.
When the enemy blockade breakers are reached, the four men take to the water, dive under the ships and lay mines. The alarmed Germans reach the harbour and capture Thompson and Ruddock. Stringer's boat is rammed, the two soldiers are pulled from the water by French fishermen. Thompson and the five others are brought before a firing squad and shot when they refuse to talk about their mission. The mines explode and destroy the ships in the harbor. Clarke and Stringer, the only survivors of the mission, make their way back to England in disguise.
option_4_text:
In the immediate aftermath of World War II, the United Nations Commission on War Crimes tries to track down one of the most notorious leaders of the Nazi death camps, Franz Kindler, who has disappeared without a trace (not even a photograph of him can be found, it is only known that he has a hobby of repairing the mechanisms of large watches). Mr Wilson, the Commission's investigator, is responsible for the release of Konrad Meinike, one of Kindler's former collaborators, who is in prison for war crimes. As expected, Konrad resumes contacts with former Nazi comrades, heads to Mexico and, tailed and discreetly guarded by the Mexican police, goes to a photographer, obviously linked to the Organization that deals with helping former Nazis wanted for war crimes. The photographer directs him to Harper, Connecticut (United States of America), where Kindler lives under the guise of an esteemed history professor, Charles Rankin, and is about to become related to one of the town's most prominent families thanks to his impending marriage to Mary Longstreet, daughter of U.S. Supreme Court Justice Adam Longstreet.
Escaping from Mr. Wilson's pursuit, Konrad meets Rankin, but Rankin, fearing that Konrad has been followed (as has actually happened), kills him and buries his body in a grove in the city park. Posing as an antiquarian (and a fan of large watches), Wilson unsuccessfully resumes Konrad's research, but at the time of abandoning the enterprise, during a lunch to which he was invited by the judge's family, he hears Professor Rankin pronounce the phrase...but Karl Marx was not German, he was Jewish.... This convinces him that the so-called Charles Rankin is actually the Nazi Kindler, who will be unmasked with the help (initially involuntary) of the bride and will be betrayed by his passion for big watches: he repairs the old clock of the church bell tower, equipped with a mechanism that at the stroke of the hours moves a carousel of statues of angels and makes a carillon sound; the epilogue of the story will have as the protagonist the watch he repaired.

query_text: Harry Potter grows up with godparents who love him, is a child prodigy, has a thorough knowledge of psychology and science, tries to understand the world of magic and finds Ron Weasley stupid, but Draco Malfoy sympathetic. The story covers only Harry's first year at Hogwarts, but all the major events and characters from the original seven volumes are included.
option_0_text: Unlike J. K. Rowling's books, in which Harry Potter, an orphan, is raised by the Dursley family, HPMOR's main character is educated by an Oxford professor. Before going to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, Harry is trained by his parents in science and rational thought, which enables him to critically evaluate current events. According to a study in the Hindustan Times, HPMOR is  a thinker's tale of magic and heroism, and the conflict between good and evil is portrayed as a battle between knowledge and ignorance. The book lasts only one year, which is the length of a single volume of J.K. Rowling's heptalog.
option_1_text:
The film is set in a not-too-distant future, where robots have become much more numerous and have taken over jobs previously done by humans, such as housework, farming, and construction. In that future lives Sergeant Jack Ramsay. He's a widower and lives with his son. He and his new partner Karen Thompson are part of a special brigade, whose main purpose is to neutralize all robots that may cause any harm to the population.
Suddenly a domestic robot kills several people. Both manage to neutralize it, but discover, after analysis, that it had been programmed to kill people with the help of a specific chip, thus becoming the first murder case ever committed by such a robot. This sinister situation causes both police officers to be on full alert and begin to thoroughly investigate the case to catch the killer who programmed that robot to commit these murders.
You'll soon discover that the man behind all this is the Machiavellian scientist Charles Luther. He's developed with the help of two scientists, who he then killed to cover up what he did, these specific chips for robots with the purpose of turning them into killers who kill indiscriminately. They also discover that he has committed that crime as a test to see if they work in a failed attempt to kill one of the scientists. Crime proves that they work very well.
Now he intends to manufacture them with the aim of selling them to terrorists and criminal and espionage organizations in order to enrich himself. Tom and Karen will now have to be swift and effective before this psychopath is successful with his intentions. It's not going to be easy though, since it's the first case of this magnitude. He is also an expert in building killing machines and has in his possession a revolutionary and unstoppable gun, with which he can kill them even if they hide from him.
Eventually Luther kidnaps Ramsay's son and lures him into a trap of his own with the intention of killing both of them and obtaining the matrices to be able to manufacture them, which Ramsay was fortunate enough to find preventing Luther from obtaining them first. Karen's lucky to arrive at the last moment, when she finds out what's going on. That distraction allows Ramsay to kill Luther in self-defense. Because of the events, in which they were both on the verge of death, they both fall in love.
option_2_text: A 50-year-old plumber, widower and father, watches a man die on a bus. This drama serves as a trigger for awareness of the time he has left to live ( his days are now numbered ). Now, more than ever, he feels the need to change his habits. But every step taken in this direction only painfully adds to his confusion.... It is, alas, impossible, at his age, to change his destiny. After quitting his job, he returns to it lucid but still convinced of the futility of his life.
option_3_text: Nikander is a garbage man. He falls in love with Ilona, a supermarket worker. Ilona, who's about to get fired, steals the cash from the supermarket and doesn't know what to do with it. In order to avoid trouble, Nikander will discreetly return it to its place. The relationship between Nikander and Ilona is difficult: they separate. But Nikander loves Ilona and he's going to win her back.
option_4_text:
The film takes place decades after the Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom for the control of the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. It tells of Fabián Stratas, a magician and stand-up comedian from Buenos Aires, who saves his money from weddings, birthdays, and bar mitzvahs, and uses a hidden camera to document a week-long trip to the Falkland Islands, which he calls "Fuckland". He plans to impregnate an islander, reasoning that if only 500 Argentines did the same each year, the islands would soon be overrun with half-Argentines, and he would be the head of a "sexual invasion."
He sets his eyes on Camilla Heaney, whom he first saw in church. He has initial success, having sex with Camilla twice, first in his hotel room and then on the beach. He manages to impregnate her before leaving for Buenos Aires, cocky and happy for having achieved his goal and duped his lover. However, Heaney gets the last word, making a videotape on Fabian's camera where she denounces him as shallow, condescending and self-centered. After this, the camera shows Stratas, unfazed by Camilla's anger, taking a shower while singing the Charly García cover of the Argentine National Anthem.

query_text:
Arthur "Bowie" Bowers, a 23-year-old serving a prison sentence for a murder he allegedly helped perpetrate at age 16, escapes from prison with two older bank robbers, Chicamaw and T-Dub. The three take shelter with Chicamaw's brother, who operates a service station, and niece, Catherine "Keechie" Mobley, who works there. Hoping to also free his incarcerated brother Robert, T-Dub concocts a plan to rob a bank and use the funds to hire a lawyer to prove a wrongful conviction.
The robbery goes smoothly. However, shortly afterward Bowie crashes his car, and Chicamaw then kills a police officer who arrives at the scene. Chicamaw leaves an injured Bowie in the care of Keechie and joins T-Dub in another town. The sheepish Keechie swiftly grows fond of Bowie, who is also shy. The two bond over their lack of experience in the world and soon develop a romance. Meanwhile, the press reports heavily on Bowie, wrongly pinning him as the ringleader of the robbery. Bowie and Keechie decide to go on the run together, and travel by bus through several towns. Late one night, they come across a chapel that performs quickie marriages for $20. Bowie asks Keechie to marry him, to which she agrees. Hawkins, the local justice of the peace, performs the ceremony and sells the couple a convertible car.
The couple travel to a remote mountain resort where Keechie once stayed during her childhood, and rent a cabin there, dreaming about being able to live openly together. At Christmastime, Chicamaw arrives at the resort, having tracked the couple there; he has gambled away his money and wants Bowie to help him and T-Dub commit another robbery. Bowie reluctantly agrees, though Keechie, fearing Bowie will not make it out alive, gives him his Christmas gift early: a wristwatch. The three men commit another robbery, but T-Dub is killed during it. Bowie and Chicamaw flee the scene by car. While driving, Bowie learns from a drunken Chicamaw that he is jealous of all the press attention Bowie and Keechie have received. Bowie eventually forces Chicamaw out of the car at gunpoint.
When Bowie returns to the resort, he learns from Keechie that Chicamaw was killed in a liquor store robbery. In radio broadcasts, Bowie is again described as the ringleader of the robbery. In a heated conversation, Keechie reveals she is pregnant. The couple depart the resort and head east, traveling mainly at night so as not to be seen. Relenting on their secrecy, they decide to spend a leisurely time in public, visiting a park, and then a nightclub. In the club, Bowie is recognized by a gangster, causing the couple to flee again. Bowie suggests they escape to Mexico, to which Keechie agrees.
En route, Keechie grows ill, and the couple seek refuge at a motel owned by Mattie, T-Dub's sister-in-law. Mattie reluctantly allows them to stay. Steve Lopez is a reporter for the Los Angeles Times looking for a story to write about. John Russell is a white man who was raised by Apaches. While he is in the process of capturing a herd of wild horses, he is visited by young Billy Lee Blake, who asks him to visit his friend Mendez on an urgent matter. He tells him that his father, who owns a boarding house in the small town of Sweetmary, has died and he has inherited it. Russell travels to Sweetmary and assures landlady Jessie Brown that he will not live a civilized life among whites, but will sell the boarding house for a herd of horses, and now intends to perfect this trade in the next larger town. The railroad hasn't reached Sweetmary yet, but the stagecoach line that Mendez and Blake worked for has already shut down. Only at the financial urging of Audra Favor, the wife of a government commissioner for Indian affairs, is a final traveling party assembled for the only remaining carriage: Russell; the now-unemployed Jessie, who has given a basket to a potential husband, Sheriff Braden; Billy Lee Blake with his bored young wife Doris; Dr. Favor and his wife, as well as the sinister Cicero Grimes  who has previously extorted a cavalier's ticket  traveling with Mendez as coachman.
Audra feels disturbed by the 'Indian' Russell, who is asked by Mendez to leave the passenger compartment at the stop at Delgado station and travel on the coach goat. Also, it turns out there are suspicious riders roaming nearby. So they take an alternative route that leads them to an abandoned mine, where they set up camp again. At this stop, further cracks in the traveling party are revealed: Grimes acts threateningly towards the fellow travelers and almost rapes Doris, who had approached him out of curiosity. Russell, meanwhile, differs from the others - perhaps in the knowledge of impending disaster. As the group travels on, they are attacked shortly after by bandits, whose accomplice and leader is Grimes; to Jessie's horror, Braden is also among the scoundrels. They robbed Favor of $12,000 for defrauding the Apaches on a reservation he was in charge of. Grimes escapes with some of the bandits and Audra as a hostage.
Meanwhile, two other villains, who were also trying to destroy the water tanks, are shot by Russell with a rifle hidden on the roof of the carriage. With the money back on horseback, the party fled on foot to the mountains, with Russell reluctantly taking the lead. Grimes and a Mexican accomplice chase after them and get into an ambush, out of which Russell and the inexperienced Mendez fire, buying them some time. Favor attempts to seize control of the money and the last of the water, but is overpowered by Russell and sent into the desert without weapons or supplies.
The others - Russell, Mendez, Jessie, Billy Lee and Doris - meet again in the mine, where they are holed up in anticipation of a new attack by the Grimes gang, who are still after the dollar loot. Even Favor, at the end of his rope, made his way there. Against Russell's wishes, Jessie brings them to the attention of the thirsty Indian agent, but this also reveals the hiding place to the bandits who are just arriving. Russell, who believes that this brave gesture was only a last, ultimate challenge to himself as the only man of the trapped who could do it, finally surrenders to the bandits resignedly, but not without first exchanging the money for dirty laundry and giving young Billy clear instructions to kill the lurking Mexican. It comes to the showdown, in which Russell kills Grimes, but is himself hit by the Mexican (Billy could not fire, as Audra was in the line of fire). Russell dies with Mendez and Jessie by his side.

Roy Waller and Frank Mercer are two partners, skilled in all sorts of swindles and tricks. Roy is a genius in his profession, which has made him rich, but he is uncomfortable in everyday life, suffering from multiple neuroses. Conditioned by his obsessions and afflicted with agoraphobia, he discovers that the doctor from whom he was supplied with medicine is untraceable, and so - on Frank's advice - he goes to the study of a Dr. Harris Klein, who from that moment will become his new analyst and will provide him with new medications. Roy's desire to reconnect with his ex-wife is encouraged by the new doctor, and so Roy discovers that he is the father of a 14-year-old girl, Angela, who was raised by her mother after she abandoned him. The sudden intrusion of his daughter upsets Roy's routine, but lifts his spirits and alleviates his neurotic state. Roy, happy to have a daughter, initially tries to hide the truth about his life of crime from her. However, it is Angela who finds out, then begs her father to take part in one of his scams.
After a successful attempt, the two make, with Frank, a bigger hit: the money is stolen with the help of Angela, but something goes wrong. After an initial chase at the airport, the con man shows up at Roy's house, demanding his money back and threatening him, Frank and the girl. Roy assists him, sending his daughter to get the money he has at home to deliver to him, but Angela grabs the gun that Roy kept near the money and shoots the villain. Encouraged by Roy, Frank and Angela escape before the police arrive on the scene and Roy decides to wrap the body, lying in his living room, in some plastic garbage bags. When he returns to the room, however, he discovers that the body has disappeared; and as he turns to the sound of footsteps behind him, he is knocked unconscious by a blow.
Roy finds himself in a hospital room manned by two police officers; when he fully recovers he asks, as a condition for confession, for a visit from his psychoanalyst. Dr. Klein arrives and Roy quietly asks him to contact Angela and give her all the money he had in the bank to secure her future. As soon as the shrink disappears behind the door, Roy passes out again. Later, he wakes up in the heat of the room and goes to turn on the air conditioner. As he walks through the door, he discovers that he is not in a hospital, but in a shipping container on the roof of an empty parking lot. He then realizes that Frank has conned him with the complicity of Angela, the con man and even the fake Dr. Klein: the safe deposit box whose access codes he revealed has been cleaned. A visit to his ex-wife, Heather, whom he hadn't seen in years, clears up the last mystery. Roy recalled that when they broke up, the woman was pregnant, but Heather tells him that she had a miscarriage: Roy never had a daughter.
Roy's coming to terms with what's happened and trying to get his life back on track. He starts working in a upholstery shop and marries the cashier of the supermarket where he usually supplies himself, with whom he is about to have a baby. One day Angela, accompanied by a young man, enters the shop where he works to buy carpets. The memories resurface and the anger builds, but soon it's revealed that Frank not only cheated Roy, but he didn't even share the loot with Angela. Angela says, "See you, dad" when she and her boyfriend leave. Roy comes home to his new wife Kathy, who's pregnant.

Set in late September 2020, the story follows Katie Mitchell, a quirky aspiring filmmaker from Kentwood, Michigan, who often clashes with her nature-obsessed and technophobic father Rick, and who has recently been accepted into film school in California. The night before Katie leaves, Rick accidentally breaks her laptop after a fight with her. Rick decides to cancel Katie's flight and instead take her, along with her mother Linda, her younger brother Aaron and the family dog named Monchi, on a cross-country road trip to their college as a final bonding experience.
Meanwhile, tech entrepreneur Mark Bowman declares his highly intelligent AI PAL obsolete by unveiling a new line of home robots in its place. In revenge, PAL takes over Mark's company and orders all the robots around the world to capture humans and launch them into space. The Mitchells manage to avoid capture at a coffee shop in Kansas. Rick decides that his family must remain in the cafe for their own safety, but Katie coerces him to help save the world. They team up with two defective robots, Eric and Deborahbot 5000, who tell the Mitchells to use a death code to shut down PAL and all the robots.
The Mitchells arrive at a nearby mall to upload the death code to the network, but PAL orders all PAL appliances to try and stop them. Katie attempts to upload the death code, but is stopped after a giant Furby stalks the family. Ultimately, they catch the Furby by destroying a PAL router and disabling the enabled devices, which also stops the death code upload, so they must come up with a new plan. On the way to Silicon Valley, where the company is headquartered, Linda reveals to Katie that she and Rick had originally lived in a cabin in the mountains years ago, as it was their lifelong dream before he gave it up.
Upon arriving in Silicon Valley, the Mitchells disguise themselves as robots and head to the PAL Labs headquarters to shut it down, but PAL manipulates them by revealing surveillance footage from Katie's coffee shop by secretly telling Aaron that she was pretending to have faith in Rick just so he could hear what she wanted to hear. Disconsolate, the Mitchells fail to reach PAL's lair and Rick and Linda are captured after PAL creates stronger and smarter robots, and reprograms Eric and Deborahbot to obey him.
Katie, Aaron and Monchi escape headquarters and hide from the robots. Katie discovers Rick's childhood recordings on her camera, realizing that Rick gave up his lifelong dream of living in a cabin to take care of his daughter. Revitalized, she and Aaron infiltrate PAL Labs headquarters again and use Monchi to make the robots malfunction, as his programming cannot distinguish him as a dog. With Mark's help, Rick and Linda break free and plan to upload a home movie of Katie with Monchi in it to short-circuit the robots. However, Rick is outnumbered by the robots as he is about to upload the video.
Katie is finally captured. Facing PAL to justify saving humanity, Katie explains that no matter how hard their family fights, they will always remain connected despite how different they are. PAL rejects this reasoning and leaves Katie in her den. Eric and Deborahbot, having been inspired by Rick's "reprogramming" to use a computer, go back to their faulty states and upload Katie's home movie, saving her and helping the rest of the Mitchells. The family bands together to fight off the rest of the upgraded robots, and Katie destroys PAL, dropping her into a glass of water, freeing all the humans and disabling all the robots except for Eric and Deborahbot.
A few months after the uprising, Katie and her family arrive at the university, as she and Rick share one last heartfelt goodbye before actually parting ways. Months later, he joins them on another road trip with Eric and Deborahbot to Washington, D.C. to accept the Congressional Medal of Honor for his action against the robots.

He also entreats Timothy to come to him before winter, and to bring Mark with him (cf. Philippians 2:22). He was anticipating that "the time of his departure was at hand" (4:6), and he exhorts his "son Timothy" to all diligence and steadfastness in the face of false teachings, with advice about combating them with reference to the teachings of the past, and to patience under persecution (1:6–15), and to a faithful discharge of all the duties of his office (4:1–5), with all the solemnity of one who was about to appear before the Judge of the quick and the dead.
Paul clearly anticipates his being put to death and realities beyond in his valedictory found in 2 Timothy 4:6–8: "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing."

Portions of 2 Timothy parallel the Epistle to the Philippians, also believed to be written (with Timothy's help) near the time of Paul's death.
Based on the traditional view that 2 Timothy was Paul's final epistle, chapter 4 talks (v. 10) about how Demas, formerly considered a "fellow worker", had deserted him for Thessalonica, "having loved this present world". In sharp contrast to his dispute with Barnabas over Mark (Acts 15:37–40), which resulted in the two parting ways, Paul now considered Mark to be "profitable to the ministry" (v. 11). The chapter also features the only biblical mention of Linus (v. 21), who in Catholic tradition is listed as Peter's immediate successor as Bishop of Rome.

The girl is accepted into a film school in California, but, the night before Katie leaves, Rick accidentally breaks her laptop in an argument, leading the family to fear that the two will never be reunited. Rick thus decides to cancel Katie's flight to accompany her to college on a family road trip with her mother Linda, younger brother Aaron, and dog Monchi, to give them a chance to spend one last time together and strengthen their bond.
Meanwhile, entrepreneur Mark Bowman declares PAL, the artificial intelligence he created, obsolete, replacing it with a line of household robots. In revenge, PAL hacks the company's robots, ordering them to capture all human beings with the intent of launching them into space, as humanity does not deserve to live on Earth. The Mitchells manage to avoid capture on the way to Kansas; Rick would like to remain hidden, while Katie would instead like to save the world. The family discovers that two robots that had previously tried to capture them were damaged, proving friendly. The two droids, nicknamed Eric and Deborah, reveal to them that they can use a special code to deactivate PAL, and thus shut down all the robots. Katie convinces her father to head to the nearest mall to accomplish the task and save humanity.
The Mitchells go to a supermarket in Colorado to upload the code, but PAL discovers their intent and mobilizes all electronic devices with PAL chips to stop them. The family manages to defeat them, but in the encounter they destroy the PAL router and in doing so the code upload is cancelled. So they decide, despite the dangers of the venture, to head to Silicon Valley to upload the code directly to PAL. Along the way, Linda tells Katie that she and Rick lived in a cabin in the mountains when they were young, because Rick's lifelong dream was to live in the middle of nature, but that he eventually had to give it up; that is why he is so worried about his daughter's future, as he fears that she may suffer a disappointment as he had.
Upon arriving in Silicon Valley, the Mitchells disguise themselves as robots and infiltrate PAL's headquarters, but are quickly unmasked; Rick and Linda are captured by the robots and Eric and Deborah are reprogrammed to return to serve PAL, while Katie, Aaron and Monchi manage to escape. Katie finds some old tapes and discovers that Rick has given up his lifelong dream to take care of her. Meanwhile, Rick from his captivity sees one of Katie's films and realizes her talent and how wrong he was not to support her. Katie and Aaron return to PAL headquarters, taking advantage of Monchi's appearance, whose appearance causes a malfunction in the robots. With Mark's help, Rick and Linda break free and plan to upload one of Katie's movies starring Monchi to all the screens to short-circuit the robots.
Katie and Aaron are captured in turn, and the girl recognizes the importance of family despite their disagreements and arguments. Eric and Deborah go back to the Mitchell side and help Rick upload Katie's film. The latter is thrown down the tower by PAL, but Rick, Eric and Deborah retrieve it and fight the droids with the help of Linda and Aaron. In the end, Katie destroys PAL, throwing Mark's cell phone where the evil AI was located with the help of Monchi into a glass of water at a resort, freeing all the humans and destroying the robots, except for Eric and Deborah. A few months later, Katie is escorted to college by her family, greeting them with sincere affection before starting her new school life. Afterward, the family leaves for another trip with Eric and Deborah to Washington to accept the Congressional Medal of Honor.

When Anton learns from the newspaper that Tony is actually wanted as a criminal, there is a hand-to-hand fight with Tony, as a result of which Valentina is pushed into the mirror. Tony follows her, and together they spend a romantic day in Valentina's fantasy world. She moves into the fantasy world of Tony, who performs with Valentina at a gala of his children's foundation. He plans to swallow his lucky flute again to survive the hanging, but Parnassus manages to swap the real flute for a fake, fragile one. The crowd is hung up on Tony, who is still in his third transformation since entering the magic mirror. Mr. Nick releases Valentina, leaving Parnassus in the dark about her whereabouts. Years later, after endless searching and in the depths of despair, Parnassus sees Valentina again in Vancouver. In the meantime, she and Anton have started a family, and they have a little daughter. Rike is a German emergency doctor. For her holiday she decided to sail alone on her twelve-metre long yacht "Asa Gray", on a trip in the footsteps of Charles Darwin from Gibraltar to Ascension Island in the South Atlantic. During her journey off North Africa, she is informed by a container ship passing nearby that she must prepare for a severe storm on her way.
After the violent storm that night, she discovers a damaged and overloaded trawler near her boat. Containing over a hundred people, threatened with death by drowning, they wave and shout towards her yacht. Rike tries to contact the boat by radio. When she does not receive an answer, she tries to contact rescue teams and organise the rescue. However, the requests for help remain largely unanswered at first, although several vessels can be seen nearby on the onboard radar. Coastguards are warned and promise help, but this will take many hours. The captain of the transport ship, who had promised support before the storm, informs him that his shipping company has prohibited any involvement in the rescue at sea of refugees.
Through her binoculars, Rike notices passengers falling or jumping into the water. A 14-year-old boy swims and reaches the yacht. With the help of a lifebuoy, she rescues the exhausted boy from the water and hoists him onto her ship. The boy's name is Kingsley, which is written on his wristband. Rike moves away from the trawler, so as not to provoke further attempts, as her boat is too small to accommodate all the passengers. She gives first aid to Kingsley, bandages his wounds, and puts him on an IV drip. She calls the coastguard again by radio, who promise her that help is on its way and that she must stay away from the refugee boat.
Kingsley, who speaks some English, regains consciousness and tries to pressure Rike to come to the rescue of the trawler on which, among others, her sister is on. He struggles with Rike to get the ignition key to the yacht, even pushing her overboard. After starting the engine and moving somewhat away, Kingsley stops the engine again, and Rike climbs back on deck with difficulty. Shocked by this act, she is furious with Kingsley, but notices his despair and calls the coastguard again, claiming that the "Asa Gray" will sink now. After the SOS, she cuts the ship's electrical system and activates her distress beacon.
The following night, she approaches the trawler, climbs aboard and finds a number of dead and dying people on the ship.
At dawn, the tenders of a Coast Guard frigate shuttle with the abandoned trawler to rescue the survivors and recover the dead, while radio messages about other ships in distress arrive, each with hundreds of refugees on board. Rike is recovered from the frigate. Traumatised and unable to answer the questions of the coastguards who questioned her, she is informed that proceedings were being brought against her.

# General presentation
In the 1930's, Britain's Prince Albert, the second son of King George V, developed a serious stuttering problem. The abdication of his elder brother Edward VIII forced him to ascend the throne as George VI. Now the king has to speak in public, even though he's crippled. At his wife's insistence, he met with Lionel Logue, an Australian speech-language pathologist with unorthodox methods. Despite the prince's reluctance, Logue's method works. Albert had to overcome his language difficulties to deliver, in September 1939, the radio address of the United Kingdom's entry into the war against Germany in the Second World War.
# Detailed synopsis
Prince Albert, Duke of York and second son of King George V, stutters throughout his closing speech at the 1925 British Empire Exhibition at Wembley Stadium, as his address is broadcast by radio around the world. The Duke has given up hope of recovery. His wife Elizabeth persuaded him to consult Lionel Logue, an Australian speech therapist in London. At their first meeting, Logue violated royal etiquette by calling the prince  Bertie, a nickname used only by his family. When the Duke feels that neither Logue's methods nor manners suit him, Logue bets a shilling that the Duke is able to effortlessly recite Hamlet's monologue  To be, or not to be  while listening to The Marriage of Figaro with the headset. Logue records the recitation on an acetate disk. Convinced that he had been stuttering all along, Prince Albert became enraged, declaring his state  desperate  and he dismissed Logue. He offers her the recording as a souvenir.
After King George V delivered his Christmas speech on radio in 1934, he explained to his son the importance of radio broadcasting to a modern monarchy. He declares that  David  (Edward, Prince of Wales), Albert's elder brother and heir to the throne, will lead to disaster not only for himself, but for his family and his country, as he will leave continental Europe at the mercy of Nazi Germany and Communist Russia. King George demands that Albert train, beginning by reading his father's speech. He's making a desperate attempt to succeed.
Afterwards, the Duke listens to the recording offered by Logue and hears himself reciting Shakespeare without the slightest hesitation. He's going back to see Logue. With his wife, he insisted that Logue limit himself to mechanical exercises, without undergoing therapy. Logue teaches his patient techniques of muscle relaxation and breath control. He continues to delve into the psychological roots of stuttering. The Duke reveals some of the pressures he suffered as a child and the two men begin to become friends.
In January 1936, George V died. David ascends the throne as Edward VIII. He caused a constitutional crisis by his determination to marry Wallis Simpson, an American socialite, divorced and still legally married to her second husband. At a party at Balmoral Castle, Albert insisted that Edward, as head of the Church of England, could not marry Mrs. Simpson, even if she gets her second divorce. Edward, in response, accuses his brother of seeking revenge for the bullying he had inflicted on him when he was still a child. He resumes his acts of intimidation so much so that Albert responds by stuttering uncontrollably.
During the next session, Albert tells Logue of his disappointment: if he expresses himself better when talking to most people, he still stutters when he speaks to his own brother. It reveals all the folly of Edward VIII in his relationship with Mrs. It was Simpson. When Logue maintains that Albert could be a good king in his brother's place, the prince calls such a suggestion treason and, in anger, mocks Logue and dismisses him. When king edward viii abdicated to marry mrs. Simpson, Albert succeeds him as George VI. The new king and queen go to see Logue at his home to apologize, much to the surprise of Mrs. Logue, who was unaware that the new king was a patient of her husband.
During the preparations for his coronation at Westminster Abbey, George VI learned that Logue had no official qualifications, contrary to what he had believed. Logue explains how he helped Australian soldiers who were returning from World War I in a state of shock. George VI remains convinced of his unfitness for the throne. Logue sits casually on King Edward's throne and discards the Stone of Destiny that lies beneath it like a mere trinket. Stung by what appears to be a lack of respect on the part of Logue, the king explodes in anger and is then surprised by Logue's eloquence.
Upon the declaration of war on Nazi Germany in September 1939, George VI summoned Logue to Buckingham Palace to prepare his radio address to millions of listeners in Britain and the Empire. Aware of the challenge ahead, Winston Churchill and Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain gave him their support. The King and Logue move into the studio. The king delivers his speech with some restraint under the guidance of Logue. At the end of his speech, George VI speaks without difficulty with little to no advice from Logue. The king and his family approached the balcony of the palace, where they received the applause of the thousands of people who had gathered.
An intertitle explains that Logue remained ever-present at King George VI's speeches during the war, and that they remained friends for the rest of their lives.
