The film's prologue is introduced with an animated sequence in which director Otto Preminger as a bald-headed comic figure in striped prison clothes sails down and dances with a hippie flower, while the name tag Skidoo appears.
Tough Tony Banks, a retired mob killer, lives happily ever after with his belligerent wife Flo, as seen in the film's opening sequences. He worries about his well-built and extraordinarily attractive blonde daughter Darlene, who has met her new boyfriend, the long-haired Stash, in a hippie environment and is carelessly going about her day with him and his like-minded friends. Then one day, Angie and Hechy burst in, two minions of the big gangster boss, who everyone just calls "God". God has one last assignment for Banks: to assassinate Blue Chip Packard before he can testify before the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Crime. After an old buddy of his, the career genius Harry, is found dead with a hole in his head, the initially unenthusiastic Tony decides not to contradict the Big Boss and gets himself imprisoned in Alcatraz.
That's where Packard is being held in maximum-security custody. While Banks, with the help of the schemer and establishment adversary Fred, nicknamed "The Professor", tries to get to Packard, Tony's wife has invited Flo Stash and his friends to move in with her during Tony's absence, as they are homeless. Flo himself goes to 'God's' yacht, which is anchored in international waters, as the gangster boss no longer feels safe anywhere. She's trying to convince the mobster to take back the hit order that got her husband sent to Alcatraz. But instead of thinking about it, Darlene, who is over half a century younger than Darlene, joins her mother on the yacht a short time later. Also, the Stash that accompanies her is being groomed by God's black lover.
After Tony realizes that he can't kill Packard, he writes a letter to his wife saying that he may never get out of here again. Although Fred "the Professor" warns him not to wet the envelope with his tongue to close it, Banks does just that. The adhesive tape is coated with LSD, and soon Banks will have the most extraordinary trip of his life. He's about to get so high, he's going to hallucinate. Shortly thereafter, all the other inmates began taking LSD. Now somewhat sober, Tony and Fred plan their escape from Alcatraz. They use freezer bags and trash cans to make a makeshift balloon to escape from prison.
With her hippie friends at her back, Flo Banks now storms into the hiding place of "God", and the "Balloon" with Fred and Tony on board floats in as well. Under such pressure, he disguises himself as Groucho Marx with his typical insignia and first hides in a wall cabinet of the yacht. Flo and Tony fall into each other's arms and first test the bed in one of the various yacht cabins. Meanwhile, the skipper of "God's" yacht, Captain Garbaldo, is trusting the petty thief Angie and "God's" black mistress, holding the famous book "The Death of God" by Gabriel Vahanian.
option_4_text:
Lorenzo Carcaterra (nicknamed "Shakes"), Michael Sullivan, John Reilly and Tommy Cohen Marcano are four teenage friends who live in Hell's Kitchen, a rather notorious neighborhood in Manhattan. The children live in a social reality with codes of behaviour dictated by the criminal underworld and endure difficult family situations, finding comfort only in the unity of their friendship and in the environment that protects them and does not tolerate harassment towards the inhabitants of the area. The only people interacting with them are Carol Martinez, a girl of Puerto Rican and Irish descent, and Father Roberto Carrillo, a priest with a criminal past for whom three of the young people serve Mass and who acts as a father figure to them, keeping an eye on their behavior. Despite this, the four of them, in order to earn some easy money, start doing small jobs for the old local boss, King Benny.
On a scorching day in the summer of 1967, the four accidentally injure a passenger who was leaving the subway station, with a heavy cart of hot dogs that they had tried to steal almost as a joke or as a prank: the boys are sentenced to the Wilkinson male reformatory in New York State; Tommy, Michael and John have to serve 12-18 months, while Shakes, not directly involved, 6-12 months. The group is housed in the arm guarded by four guards, of which Sean Nokes serves as the head guard. After a fight in the cafeteria with another inmate, the boys are targeted by the four guards and are subjected to physical and sexual abuse for the duration of their imprisonment; the experience forever changes the members of the group and their friendship.
While the boys are in the facility, they attend Wilkinson's annual guards-inmates football game. Michael convinces Rizzo, a young black inmate, that they should play as hard as possible to show the guards that they can react to their abuse. Rizzo, initially reluctant, accepts and helps his team win the game. As a result, all four boys are beaten and thrown into solitary confinement for several weeks, while Rizzo is beaten to death by the guards covering up the murder by informing his family that he died of pneumonia.
By the spring of 1968, shortly before Shakes' release from Wilkinson, the boy insists with his friends that they should publicly denounce the abuse. The others refuse, and Michael sums up their point of view by saying that they wouldn't be believed or that no one would really care about them even after they were released. The night before the boys' collective release, Nokes informs them that he and the other guards have organized a "farewell party" for them, during which they inflict particularly brutal abuse on the boys.
Fourteen years later, on the night of November 1, 1981, John and Tommy, by now professional killers and drug addicts, walk into a diner. On his way to the bathroom, John recognizes Nokes, who has become a private security guard; after returning to the counter, he invites his friend to observe the guy sitting in the corner on the far left and Tommy also recognizes him. They confront him, who, accused by them as the author of the abuses, claims to have "made them stronger", to which the two take revenge by shooting him repeatedly in front of witnesses. Michael, now a deputy district attorney, manages to get the case assigned to him and informs Shakes, a newspaper columnist, that he has been tracking the overseers who abused them over the years: one of them, Adam Styler, has become a corrupt cop; another, Henry Addison, works for the mayor and still cultivates the practice of pedophilia; the last, Ralph Ferguson, is now a respectable citizen working in social services. Michael's intention is to secretly sabotage the prosecution and expose Wilkinson's crimes. The attorney assigned to John and Tommy is Danny Snyder, a broken, drugged-out, alcoholic man who wants to plea bargain, but is convinced by King Benny to plead not guilty; he will be briefed by Shakes, on Michael's instructions, on the questions and objections to be made during the debate. They're helped in the plan by Carol, now a social worker, and King Benny.
Michael's plan will only work if he can damage Nokes' reputation and place John and Tommy in another location at the time of the shooting. Ferguson, when called to testify in court on Nokes' behalf, comes under pressure and admits that he, Nokes and other guards abused boys in custody. To close the case, however, we need a key witness who can provide John and Tommy with an alibi. Shakes has a long conversation with Father Bobby, who at first refuses to testify falsely but - after Shakes tells him of the abuse he suffered - reluctantly agrees. At the trial, Father Bobby testifies that John and Tommy were with him at a New York Knicks game at the time of the shooting and shows the three ticket plates to prove it. As a result, John and Tommy are acquitted.
The remaining guards are also punished for their crimes: Addison is killed by "Little Caesar" (i.e. Eddie "Little Caesar" Robinson, local drug boss and Rizzo's older brother): the former guard is handed over to him in exchange for a share of the money by King Benny, who reveals the truth about his brother's death; Styler is arrested for taking bribes and killing a drug dealer; following his admission to court, Ferguson loses his job and family.
Michael, Shakes, John, Tommy, and Carol meet in a bar to celebrate the event, while Shakes' voiceover explains that it would be the last time they would all be seen together, what would happen to them, and how the reformatory experience marked them: Shakes will remain a journalist and live in Hell's Kitchen; Michael will leave the district attorney's office, move to the English countryside to be a carpenter and never marry; Carol will remain in the city as a social worker and have a son, whom she will name after her four friends; both John and Tommy will die before the age of thirty: John, who as a boy would have become a priest like his father Bobby but was indicted at the time of death for five unsolved homicides, will be dismissed for poisoning a gin bottle, and both will be unlawfully immobilized with a crucifix, and Tommy will be murdered with a crucifix in his pocket.

During the Second World War, Georg Droste served as an officer in the German Wehrmacht, where he gained extensive experience in espionage. Well, in 1950, he lives as a harmless wine merchant in Vienna and meets, allegedly by chance, at the station an old acquaintance, Baron Ferdi of Dust. You have a drink in the station bar, and then the baron invites his old pal to his house. There, in a castle in Baden near Vienna, located in the Austrian Soviet zone, Georg Droste meets Staub's sister, Countess Carla Cosimano. This one, after some small talk, asks Droste for a small favor. Tell him to take a package to Vienna and deliver it to a certain address. The parcel is said to contain a rare book. Droste has no idea that he will become a courier for the Soviet intelligence service at this moment, because in the package there is, as expected, much more, namely, hidden in the book, intelligence-important information material.
Returning to Vienna, Droste is intercepted by the U.S. military police before the package is handed over and is sent to the representative of the U.S. intelligence service there, a certain Mr. Smith, brought in. He explains to him that the Countess's castle was nothing but a Soviet spy nest and that he, Droste, had become a Soviet agent in her eyes with the parcel transport. They've got Droste now, and they're forcing him to work for the Americans as a double agent. First, they send Droste with a new assignment behind the Iron Curtain, to Budapest. There he meets the pretty and basic Nora Gülden, who desperately wants to leave the country that has become communist. Droste helps her escape to Austria, and during this dramatic time, the two fall in love. While the Americans now have him on the hook, the Soviet side is also pressing for more from Droste.
There follows a brief period of harmony with sufficient money and personal happiness. On a fishing trip, Droste's son Johnny and Nora also get to know each other better. For some time, Droste conceals his true professional activities from his new girlfriend. However, this fresh happiness does not last long, because Nora eventually learns of Droste's double agent activity and cannot live with it. Eventually, she leaves him. Then Smith reluctantly re-employs the agent and requires Droste to contact former Wehrmacht General Greenhahn, who is obviously pursuing sinister plans. Greenhahn, in turn, bribes Droste to obtain information about his two employers. Soon Georg Droste has become so entangled in the traps of the two secret services that he can hardly escape this whirlwind. After his last highly dramatic mission, Georg Droste wants to leave the life-threatening trade again, but now they won't let him go. One day, he gets murdered in the street.

In this case they help the son of Santa's dog Zampa Natale Junior, who had escaped from the North Pole because he was tired of his monotonous life and angry with his father, to escape from a kennel and make him understand the importance of Christmas.

American comedian Dave Chappelle hosts a concert, a so-called Block Party, at the intersection of Quincy Street/Downing Street in Bed Stuy, Brooklyn on September 18, 2004.
In addition to the concert part, the film also documents part of the organizational processes, such as the choice of the street, the use of the Daycare Center as a backstage area or the provision of rental furniture by the Salvation Army.
The dilapidated but also extraordinary Broken Angel House with its unusual owners and the adverse weather conditions, a storm with heavy rains, are also part of the cinematic narrative.
Before the concert begins, Chapelle personally invites people from his small-town hometown of Yellow Springs, Ohio, and from New York City. The people and their own story become part of the film. In Ohio, he also encounters the Central State University (CSU) Marching Band with their Invincible Marching Marauders, which he invites. Buses have to be organized on short notice. In New York, Chappelle drives through the streets with a megaphone and the party is posted on the Internet.
The block party kicks off with the arrival of Kanye West at the helm of the Invincible Marching Marauders, followed by hip-hop artists such as Mos Def, Common, Erykah Badu, Talib Kweli and Jill Scott. It is held together by a main band consisting of professional musicians, led by Ahmir? Thompson will take over. The end of the concert is the unique reunion of the Fugees.
The concert was documented by several cameramen acting independently of each other under the direction of Ellen Kuras.

option_1_text:
Nine-year-old Patricia McFarland, nicknamed "Trisha", suffers from the separation of her parents and the endless arguments between her brother Pete and her mother. On a hike into the New England wilderness, she moves away from the two to pee unnoticed between bushes and trees. She tries to cut back and gets lost. With increasing anxiety and despair, she searches for a way back, only to find herself deeper and deeper into the forest. In her backpack, she has two Twinkies, a hard-boiled egg, a tuna sandwich, a bottle of lemonade, a bottle of water, a bag of potato chips, a rain poncho, a Game Boy, and her battery-operated Walkman with radio reception.
As she wanders through the forest, she remembers helpful things that her mother has told her or that she has read in books, such as that rivers never flow in a circle but always lead to people. On the way to a stream, she slips against a tree with a wasp nest and is stung by dozens of wasps. The path taken along the stream ends in a swamp. Their food supplies are running low. She has now moved far away and is outside the area being searched by search parties.
Again and again, she has to fight against her own inner voice, not being able to find her way back from the wilderness. She feels watched and pursued by a "special thing" who introduces himself in a dream as the "god of the lost". Especially at night, she feels it near her.
Meanwhile, a lot is happening in the outside world, too: her quarrelsome brother is withdrawing into himself, mother and father are sleeping in the same bed again. Meanwhile, the police are misled, arrest a suspect, and then narrow the search.
Trisha drinks river water and feeds on strawberries, buckwheat, raw fish, and tadpoles. First, she vomits what she's eaten and has diarrhea. She's slowly getting sick, but she's dragging herself along feverishly. She finds hope in conversations with her idol, Tom Gordon. This is a pitcher for the Boston Red Sox baseball team. She listens to his team's games every night on her radio walkman as long as its battery lasts. Later, when reality and imagination are mixed by the loss of strength, Tom Gordon appears again and again as her strengthening companion. He motivates the dirty, weak, sick and frightened Trisha to make more and more effort until she finally finds a road.
With the target within reach, her pursuer emerges from the undergrowth and enters the street opposite her. It's going to be a decisive battle.
In the aftermath of the novel, father, mother, and brother gather around Trisha's hospital bed. She spent nine days in the wilderness. She concludes her victory with Tom Gordon's winningest: with her index finger outstretched to the sky. Then she falls into a deep sleep.

American comedian Dave Chappelle wants to host a block party at the corner of Quincy Street and Downing Street in the Clinton Hill neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. So he goes to the neighborhood to look around and talk to the people, especially at the Broken Angel House.

The architect Walter Craig opens up to several seemingly complete strangers in a country house (Pilgrim farm) that he had already dreamed of meeting. A recurring dream that begins harmlessly, but then after a certain event (the breaking of the glasses of the psychiatrist Dr. van Straaten, who takes the role of the skeptic in the round) turns into a nightmare, the end of which he can not remember.
Each of them has a creepy story to tell, and one after another contributes an episode to the sequel. The most famous is the ventriloquist episode with Michael Redgrave, in which a ventriloquist puppet slowly gains control over his master and completely dominates him after he shoots a colleague who he believes was trying to steal his puppet from him.
Further episodes deal with the ghost of a murdered little boy at a children's Christmas party, the premonitions of racing driver Hugh Grainger (as in his dream the bus driver shares him with Just room for one inside, whereupon he does not get on and escapes an accident), a golf game about a woman, an old mirror, which becomes the origin of an almost murderous marriage dispute of the Cortlands. The film has a surprising ending, which Craig fears as part of his recurring nightmare.
option_4_text:
One night while staying at a hotel, a man named Gant Hoxey (Stephen McHattie) rambles in bed about his family, stating that his wife gets worried whenever he doesn’t call her, and stresses the importance of family matters. When Gant addresses his female companion Sara Jean, it’s revealed that she’s already deceased with lacerations all over her body and nails ripped off from her fingertips. In remorse, Gant mentions that Sara Jean’s father would kill him for doing this heinous act to her, so people are “nothing without their family”.
One day, a wandering young woman named Summer Mathews (Ashley Greene) is hitchhiking along the side of the road when a man named Cliff pulls over. He asks her where she's going, and she tells him she’s heading to a small town called Massey; Cliff says he's going through that town and that it was no trouble. Maybe, for this favor, she would do a favor for him. Cliff expects Summer to pay him back by giving him oral sex. However, Summer pulls out a revolver and tells him to keep his eyes on the road. Summer is next seen in a gas station. Summer shoplifts food and accessories at the gas station convenience store in Massey. The local sheriff (Paul Whitney), who just walked out of the restroom, watches Summer from a distance. He approaches Summer, informing her that "people around here pay for their items." Summer throws down a rack of bottled water as a diversion. As she flees, the sheriff falls over the rack.
Summer runs outside, hiding behind a dumpster. A handsome young man named Tom Hoxey (Peter Mooney), who witnesses the incident, directs the sheriff to a different direction, and tells Summer to hide inside his truck. Summer is reluctant to accept Tom's offer, but he urges her to hurry up or else the sheriff will find her. Tom drives off with Summer. She asks Tom the reason he helps her to escape the sheriff. He claims the sheriff previously busted him for a drinking charge.
At a local bar, the two of them have a few drinks. They chat about Summer's travels. Summer is obviously a confident girl who can take care of herself. Although Summer asks to stay at a motel, smooth-talking Tom charms her into staying at his house for the night. Outside, they come across the town mechanic Jessie (Cinthia Burke). Summer asks how many times he slept with Jessie, but Tom states she’s “not his type”.
Tom takes Summer back to his house. Summer discovers that Tom lives with his security-conscious mother, Gaia (Barbara Niven), and that there are bolts on the windows. When Summer teases him about living with his mother, Tom confesses that he originally planned to move out, but misses his mother’s cooking. Tom is direct with Summer, so the two agree to go upstairs and have sex. As they are having sex, the audience then sees Gaia outside Tom's door, listening to him and Summer having sex.
In the morning, Summer wakes up and puts her clothes on. She scavenges the kitchen, taking money from a jar. Just as she was about to leave, Tom catches her in the kitchen. He tells Summer she can stay. Summer is not interested. She tells Tom he was good last night, and that she wanted to avoid the awkward morning goodbye. Tom refuses to let Summer leave, continually telling Summer she can't leave. Summer pulls out her revolver, threatening Tom to let her go or else she'll take action. Tom's mother Gaia smacks Summer on the back of her head with a blunt object. Tom shows his mother that in his hand are the bullets to Summer's revolver, reassuring her that he had it under control.
Meanwhile, an ex-convict named Darwin returns home, as he is released from jail. Upon entering the house, he calls out to his daughter, but there was no response and he doesn’t see her anywhere. Investigating, Darwin finds his house a mess, his pet bird is lifeless in its cage, and that there's rotten food in the fridge and on the table.
Later, Summer regains consciousness, and finds herself stored in the basement and chained to a dirtbed. A frail, battered, and barely conscious young woman named Amber (Danielle Kind), tied to a chair, is also held hostage (as well as the daughter of Darwin from the previous scene); the lack of sun is what's hurting Amber, not Tom. When Tom appears, Summer shouts and curses at him, but he tells her to calm down as not to upset Amber.
When Summer inquires how long Amber was kept in the basement, Tom states that she was kept there since the death of another woman named Clarissa. Tom then shows Summer the skull of the deceased Clarissa. Summer shouts that he’s a serial killer, and that he will never kill her. Tom, defends that he didn’t kill Clarissa, and he would never kill Summer because he doesn’t hurt and kill women. Instead, Tom states that she died from a spider bite. When Summer refuses to believe his claim, Tom angrily pins her down, and stresses that he didn’t kill Clarissa and he would never kill his girls.
The next day, Tom is at a clothing store where his mother works. When they notice Darwin outside, Gaia panics, knowing that he’ll inquire about Amber. Tom is nonchalant however, clarifying to his mother that Amber is known to be a runaway.
Back at Tom’s basement garden, Summer begs to be released, but Tom refuses, insisting that he needs her for his garden. Getting nowhere, Summer confesses to Tom that she’s searching for her long-estranged father in Massey. In response, Tom teases her that her father was there with him and his mother. Horrified and confused, Summer watches as Tom opens a large bin, and waves off a nonexistent odor. When Tom pours out the contents of the bin, only a garden hose slips out. Much to Summer’s relief, Tom suggests he’s just joking, and he doesn’t know her father. Summer tries to survive in the basement by antagonizing Tom when he offers her food cooked by his mother. She is defiant toward Tom and his mother.
Meanwhile, Darwin asks about Amber at the bar where Tom and Summer stopped by. The bar tender mentions that she hasn’t been there in a long while, but she used to go out with strangers back then.
The following day, Gaia tells Tom to get rid of the women in the basement and scolds him for taking Amber, someone who lives in their town. In response, Tom slams the counter and stresses to his mother that he’s not getting rid of his garden. Afterward, Tom assists Summer in drinking water and tells her he’ll be gone for a few hours to work. Before leaving, he plays music for them, making the crazed, delirious Amber laugh.
Later, Darwin asks the sheriff (who’s having lunch) whether he has heard from Amber, saying that he heard around town that Amber was hanging around Tom. The sheriff is biased toward Darwin, telling him that she probably just ran away, especially when Darwin mentions that her car and purse are gone. However, Darwin still pushes for the sheriff to look in case Amber is missing. Dismissively, the sheriff says he’ll look into her case when he’s finished eating.
Meanwhile, Summer talks to the weakened Amber, asking if she wants to die in the basement, though Amber can’t seem to speak anymore. During a supply run at Jessie’s shop, Tom gets a call from Darwin, asking him to stop by to check his oven (as it’s not working) since Tom is also a handyman. Playing it cool, Tom agrees he’ll be there.
When Tom returns home, Summer asks him how long he had the garden in the basement. Tom tells her that he’s been growing plants in his spare time since childhood because his father locked him in the basement as a punishment for misbehavior. In which Summer comments that his garden can still be beautiful without her and Amber. Tom disagrees with the comment, stating that women are the “most beautiful thing”, so they can bring life and beauty to his garden.
Tom then inquires about her mother, which Summer states that she and her mother don’t get along. Summer then recounts that she found a letter from her father, revealing that her mother Twila lied about losing her due to a miscarriage. Thus, her father doesn’t acknowledge her existence, that was when Summer left home. When Tom stresses that family is the most important value, Summer points out that he’s keeping her from her father just as her mother did. Tom then asks her father’s name, but Summer doesn’t know. Instead, she has an old photo of her father and hopes to find him through that. Summer then attempts to manipulate Tom, hinting that she can be the “special garden angel” he lets go, but he just walks away dismissively.
The next day, the sheriff visits Gaia at the clothing shop to make a purchase and starts flirting with her, stating that her husband has been gone for a long time. However, she brushes off his advances. When the sheriff mentions to Gaia that Darwin is worried about Amber's whereabouts. Feigning innocence, she tells the sheriff she hasn't seen Amber.
Back at home, Gaia drinks in stress, afraid of getting caught. Gaia feels that keeping the garden is too dangerous since Darwin is snooping around town. Tom, however, remains unbothered since he’s coming over to Darwin’s house to fix his stove, so he’ll set him straight. Gaia then slaps Tom, and demands that he get rid of the girls. In anger, Tom pins his mother onto the table, forcing her to give in and say that he is right, before kissing her. Gaia pushes him off, but touches herself while in tears after Tom leaves the kitchen.
While Tom is fixing Darwin’s stove, Darwin asks him about Amber. Tom tells him it’s been a couple months since he saw her. Tom then claims that Amber had mentioned wanting to see a music band, so he assumes that’s where she went.
Back in the garden, Summer attempts to communicate with Amber again. This time Amber regains some consciousness, and asks for her "Daddy.” Promising Amber to return her to her father, Summer pleads with her to grab the tools hanging on the wall. Amber, at first, is delirious, not understanding what Summer means. When she mentions her father, Summer uses this to make Amber get up and limp toward the tools, despite her feet being shackled. Amber manages to walk a few steps, trying to reach for one of the tools on the wall shelf. However, due to her weakened condition and her shackles, Amber trips and falls to the ground, hits her head on a concrete block, and dies upon impact.
When Tom returns home, he is pissed off that Amber died, as he takes any casualty seriously. While Tom buries Amber, Gaia expresses her dislike for Summer. Summer begs her to release her so she can be out of their lives, but Gaia notes that Tom’s garden is important to him.
After burying Amber’s body, Tom cries in grief. He then goes searching through Summer’s belongings in his bedroom, finding an old picture and her diary with the aforementioned letter inside, which forces Tom to realize that he only has one "garden angel" left. Tom then unlocks Summer from the chains, gives her a bath upstairs, and lets her sleep on his bed again.
The next morning, Summer tries to leave again. After that, Tom and his mother search Summer's purse and find an old letter. Whatever it is, upsets Gaia, and she goes downstairs, pulling Summer's chin back and forth before giving Summer permission to work upstairs while Tom is home. She must stay in the basement when Tom and Gaia are gone.
Tom's father Gant is on his way home, after calling that night that after she found the letter in Summer's purse. She sounds upset, he said, and he wants to know why. He realizes he has a surprise at home. Tom and Summer have sex again. Summer is obviously manipulating Tom, telling him she loved him when he told her to. The two talk about their future plans to leave. Tom wants to stay in the property, but Summer has other plans.
Jessie, who is a witness to Tom’s association with Amber, tells him that Darwin had stopped her auto shop by asking about his daughter and she mentioned seeing Amber with Tom. Tom decides to take Jessie hostage to prevent her from speaking to Darwin again. Tom is injured in the basement after Jessie, who he tied up, manages to get the ropes off her wrist and getting a knife from her ankle and stabs him on his leg. Tom asks Summer to give Jessie water. Jessie thinks Summer and the rest of the bunch are expecting her to become a sex slave. She agrees to do anything sexual, if only to survive. Summer begs Jessie to stay quiet, obviously scared for her. Jessie begs Summer not to leave her alone, but she's scared of Tom and goes back upstairs.
The next day, after Darwin goes to Jessie's auto shop and finds Tom's handyman cards on the ground after Jessie ripped his pocket, he drives to Tom's house. Summer attempts to escape as Darwin drives up to the front of the house. Summer enters Darwin's car, anxious to leave the property right away. Darwin asks Summer if his daughter is in the house, which Summer ignores as she’s in a rush to leave the Hoxey property. Tom shoots a perfect shot, blowing apart Darwin's head. Summer runs out of the car. She tries to escape on foot, but Tom shoots a shot next to her foot, and she pauses as Gaia pulls up, seeing the blood all over Summer and Darwin's car.
Summer is restrained again in the basement, to Jessie. Gant arrives home asking his wife where his daughter is. He visits downstairs to meet Summer for the very first time. Gant tells Summer that her mother, Twila, never told him about her existence, telling her that Twila told him she miscarried her. Summer connects the dots and realizes that Gant is her father. She came looking for her father; however, she finds a sadistic, femicidal wolf in sheep’s clothing. Gant guts and murders Jessie, forcing Summer to watch, after which he lets her go upstairs. The family have a cake celebrating Gant’s return. Tom defies his father, informing him he is not going to take Summer. Gant makes a joke that Tom is in love with his sister saying that "has a hard-on" for her. The next morning, as they're all sitting down for breakfast, Gant informs them that he's going to take Summer with him. Tom insists that he isn't, that Summer is going to stay with him. They fight, and Gant belittles him, calling him a "pussy" and throwing him into the next room.
Tom walks out with a shot gun and threatens his father, asking if he's a man now. Gant takes the gun from Tom, shooting him to death. Summer is shocked. Tom's mother is saddened to see her son dead. Gant also shoots Gaia dead after she realizes, and says that it was Gant's plan all along - to get rid of his old family to make a new one. He tells her that she's right, and forces Summer to leave with him. Gant and Summer leave the house. They drive to a nearby park. Gant approaches a woman who is having a picnic. Summer walks up to her father and stabs him to death. The mortified woman screams, pleading Summer to not to kill her too. Summer tells the woman he was going to "kill you, and then me eventually."

query_text: Blake Thorn (Hulk Hogan) is a conceited self-made millionaire who sells bodybuilding supplements and equipment that have his picture on them. One day, while recklessly playing paintball, he is targeted by police. He is chased to a shopping mall, where he hides by putting on a Santa costume. He slides down a garbage chute to escape the police and bangs his head, resulting in amnesia. Mistaken by Lenny (Don Stark) as the mall Santa, Blake begins to think he really is Santa Claus. Meanwhile, the evil scientist Ebner Frost (Ed Begley Jr.) tries to take over an orphanage in order to gain access to the magical crystals underneath it and dispatches his henchmen to destroy it. However, Blake after discovering that being Santa has made him a better person and that Frost wants to destroy the very same orphanage he grew up in, manages to rescue the children. Frost and his henchmen are arrested, but the orphanage is destroyed due to the overload of the crystals. Frost's compound is now the new orphanage founded and helped run by Blake. Many more orphans have joined since then. They all watch though a telescope at Frost and his henchman doing hard labor in the prison yard.

This time the opponents of the famous Belgian detective Hercule Poirot are not ordinary murderers or common criminals, but even an organization headed by the four greatest criminal minds in the world. Led by a diabolical and enigmatic Chinese mandarin, they want to take over the world using powerful means of destruction. Helping the investigator is not only his loyal friend and companion Captain Arthur Hastings, but also a twin brother unknown to all. The novel consists of a series of episodes that see Poirot facing and solving from time to time different criminal puzzles, until the final clash against the four bosses.
The conclusion of the novel is set in the "Labyrinth", at the foot of the Latemar Dolomite group in Trentino-Alto Adige.
option_1_text:
The plot of the film takes place in Glasgow and revolves around 50-year-old Barney Thomson, who has been living a boring life for 20 years and works as a barber at Henderson's Barbers. Meanwhile, Detective Inspector Holdall is inspecting a series of body parts being shipped across town. Due to the lack of progress, the case has been assigned to Detective Inspector June Robertson.
Manager Wullie Henderson, son of Barney's friend James Henderson, is preparing to fire Barney because of his pessimistic outbursts, which are having a negative impact on the business. Barney desperately pleads with Wullie not to fire him, leading to an altercation in which Barney accidentally stabs his boss with a small pair of scissors. In a panic, Barney wraps the body in a sack and puts it in the trunk of his car, which his friend Charlie notices. Holdall interrogates Thomson, who denies any knowledge of Wullie's habits or whereabouts. Holdall then attaches himself to Barney's heels. He asks his mother Cemolina for help and hides the body with her. Later, Barney is horrified to discover that his mother chopped up the body, wrapped it in foil, labeled it, and stored the parts in the freezer.
Through a mistake by Charlie, Barney's younger colleague Chris Roberts begins to suspect him, whereupon Barney confesses that there was an accident. When Chris then attempts to attack him, a frightened Barney hits him in the chest with a broomstick, accidentally killing him as well. Which means Barney's taking Chris' body to Cemolina, too. However, when he retrieves Woolley's remains from the freezer, he notices an extra hand in it, along with a notebook with addresses of the various places where the killer's body parts were shipped. He also finds out that his mother has been prostituting herself for younger men. Later, he breaks into Chris's apartment to plant Wullie's remains and incriminate him. However, Barney must realize that the freezer is too small for the body. When Holdall and his partner show up, Barney is forced to flee, leaving the body parts behind.
When he confronts his mother, he realizes that she is the killer and that she killed her dates and sent her remains. She reveals that Barney's father abandoned her, but didn't go far and never contacted Barney. After cruelly mocking Barney, she dies from over-exertion from a heart attack (or possibly a stroke). Barney dumps Chris' body in Lubnaig's hole and angrily attacks Charlie when he suspects that he knows something about Chris. In the end, however, Barney leaves in disgrace. The next day, James Henderson is doing Barney's hair when he gets a phone call in the middle of the woods. That's where both cop duos show up, and in a subsequent shootout, all but Barney are killed. Holdall blames Barney, but Barney reveals what really happened. Holdall will die before he hears everything. With his reputation restored, Barney will become a local legend.
option_2_text: This is Sanville, California. A peaceful, picturesque little town, where life was good until violence and crime took over. Only a miracle could save her. This miracle comes in the form of a mysterious stranger who claims to be... Santa Claus! Things are starting to change, but the bad guys haven't said their last word.
option_3_text:
In 15th-century Dijon, the Duke of Burgundy, Charles the Bold, hosts a knightly tournament. This is in honor of his cousin, King Louis XI of France, whose throne Charles would like to take over. He also wants to marry Louis' goddaughter, the Countess Jeanne de Beauvais. After initially Charles' knights are victorious in duels, Louis' best paladin Robert de Neuville enters the field and can easily defeat his opponents. Karl wants to win the tournament and impress Jeanne, which is why he personally competes against Robert. After Robert falls from his horse and suffers such a defeat, he is hospitalized in a tent, where he is visited by Jeanne, who is in love with him, which in turn angers Karl. It also turns out that Robert's saddle was secretly manipulated by Count Jean de Sénac before the fight. When Jeanne finds out, she refuses to dance with Charles on the night of his victory, and with the permission of her uncle, the Count of Hesselin, leaves the party early. The next day, Louis returns to Paris and presents Charles with pigeons raised by Jeanne as a peace offering.
Despite the agreement, Karl still plans to depose both Louis and marry Jeanne. He introduces de Sénac to his project, captain of Ludwig's bodyguard, who was smuggled there by Charles. A few days later, Louis is at the castle of the Count of Hesselin in Clermont-en-Beauvaisis to participate in a traditional hunt. Jeanne asks Louis to marry her to Robert, who refuses. Although he regards Robert as a loyal knight, he believes that after marrying Jeanne, he would not be able to maintain peace with Burgundy.
Shortly afterwards, Charles has Jeanne kidnapped and, with the help of de Sénac, makes Robert responsible for it. Louis is deeply affected by Robert's alleged betrayal and publicly declares him a serious criminal. After this, Robert is ambushed by Charles' followers, attacked, and thrown from a bridge into a river. However, unbeknownst to Karl, he has survived with serious injuries and is being nursed by Jeanne's maid, Catherine du Tillais. Meanwhile, Karl blackmails Jeanne, who is imprisoned in Mailly-le-Château. He threatens to marry her to the sister of Britain's King Edward IV if she does not marry him, whom he would then help to conquer France. Jeanne finally manages to tell Catherine where she is. Robert immediately sets out and spontaneously recruits peasants who have been looted by Charles, in the evening they reach his castle.
Robert disguises himself as a masked, mute wrestler to gain entrance to the castle. Before he does, he orders the peasants to disguise themselves as servants and take out Charles' bodyguards. Robert manages to inform Jeanne of his plan, which is why she encourages Karl to challenge the wrestler to a fight. After Robert defeats Charles, he flees with Jeanne and his men. The next evening, Robert and Jeanne arrive at the castle from the Count, who explains to them the latest developments. He was asked by Louis to go to Liège. The Count is to deliver a message from Louis to the inhabitants who want to rebel against their vassal Charles, in which he asks them to refrain from doing so. Louis thus hopes to gain advantages in a negotiation with Charles for the domination of Picardy in Péronne.
The next day d'Hesselin and Jeanne travel to Liège, Robert to Péronne. In the latter place, Louis and de Sénac are received by Charles, who is convinced that Jeanne has been freed on Louis's orders. Ludwig informs Karl of his action in Liège and offers Karl all the cities on the Somme as a kind of peace pledge. Shortly after, a false messenger arrives and announces an uprising in Liège. That's why Louis de Sénac sent for the Count. Robert, in turn, pursues de Sénac, whose treachery he knows. In Liège, de Sénac murders the Count, who has passed on the royal message to Jeanne. She escapes into the forest, where de Sénac is attacked by wolves. He leaves, believing Jeanne to be lost, but she prays to the Virgin Mary, whereupon the animals become tame and even protect them from the cold until Robert finds them.
In Peronne, de Sénac hands Louis a forged letter in which the inhabitants of Liège are called to rebel against Charles. Although the king sees through the intrigue, Charles brings him before a church court for high treason. At first, things look bad for Ludwig when Robert and Jeanne arrive. After the latter presents the real letter to the court, de Sénac claims that she is possessed by the devil because she has controlled the wolves in the forest with witchcraft. Therefore, Robert challenges Karl to a sword fight, the outcome of which God wants to decide the verdict. Charles is replaced by de Sénac, whom Robert eventually defeats and kills. The protagonist is a man named Keola living on the island of Molokai, Hawaii. Keola and his wife live with her father Kalamake, a notorious sorcerer who appears to have an inexhaustible supply of money despite never doing any work.
One day, Kalamake uses a magic spell to transport Keola to an unfamiliar island where the two of them are invisible to the inhabitants. There he reveals that by burning the leaves of a certain tree, the island's sea-shells can be transformed into coins and the pair transported home.
Keola attempts to blackmail Kalamake for a share of his riches, but Kalamake retaliates by abandoning Keola at sea. He is rescued by a passing ship heading for the Tuamotus islands, but does not get along with the first mate, so jumps overboard when they sight land. To his amazement he discovers he is on the very same island he had earlier visited supernaturally.
Getting to know the inhabitants (who turn out to be cannibals intending to eat him), Keola discovers that not only Kalamake but also a huge variety of other invisible visitors from all parts of the earth are regularly heard there harvesting its shells. He tells the islanders that these unwelcome manifestations could be banished by destroying the tree necessary for their spells. Eventually they attempt to do so, and in the confusion of a huge battle between the invisible wizards and the islanders, Keola is rescued by his wife, who has used her father's incantations to come to the island herself. They are magically transported home to Hawaii, stranding Kalamake on the island, and hope that without his magical supplies he will never be able to return.

The novel opens in the German bathing resort of Baden-Baden (or simply Baden) in the summer of 1862, where the young Russian Grigory Litvinov has arrived en route home to Russia to meet his fiancée Tatiana Shestov, who will soon be arriving with her aunt and guardian, Kapitolina Markovna Shestov, from Dresden. In Baden Litvinov soon encounters Rostislav Bambaev, an acquaintance from Moscow. Later that evening at a social gathering Bambaev introduces Litvinov to the political activist Stepan Nikolaevitch Gubaryov. Litvinov is not overly impressed by the gathering nor especially by the nondescript looking Gubaryov. After this Litvinov returns to a local restaurant where he is approached by Sozont Ivanitch Potugin, who introduces himself to Litvinov as a fellow Russian. Litvinov had noted Potugin at the earlier get-together at Gubaryov’s where Potugin had not spoken a word. Potugin now opens up to Litvinov and Litvinov in turn is captivated by Potugin’s way with words. In a rather one-sided conversation Potugin vents his frustrations regarding the Russian character – its tendency towards servitude and flights of idealism that lead nowhere. Later back in his rooms, Litvinov finds a letter from his father and also a gift of heliotrope flowers on his windowsill brought by a mysterious woman who, according to the servant, did not leave her name. The letter from his father reveals the superstition of the rural Russian. The flowers, though they come without a note, seem to strike a deep and powerful resonance with Litvinov. Later that night, unable to sleep, he suddenly realizes who might have brought them.
The story now reverts to about a decade earlier to relate the background story of the young Grigory Litvinov and Irina Osinin. Acquaintances in Moscow, the two fall in love when barely out of childhood and promise themselves to one another. Unlike Litvinov, Irina comes from an ennobled family of long pedigree, though in recent times fallen into near penury. One day the Osinin family, in view of their nobility, are invited to a ball being thrown by the emperor on his visit to Moscow. Irina agrees to go though she pleads with Litvinov not to go himself and Litvinov acquiesces to her wishes, though he does bring her a bouquet of heliotrope. Irina’s beauty makes quite an impression at the court ball and the very next day the court chamberlain Count Reisenbach, a relation of the Osinins and a wealthy man with high connections, decides he will adopt his niece Irina and bring her to live with him in St. Petersburg. Irina is heartbroken but bends to her parents’ wishes to become his adopted niece and heiress. It means leaving Litvinov and she writes to him breaking off their relationship. Soon thereafter she is whisked away to St. Petersburg and her new home.
The story moves back to Baden. Litvinov wonders excitedly whether it wasn’t Irina who left him the flowers. The next morning Litvinov decides to escape Baden and the Russian crowd by hiking alone up in the hills around the town's old castle. Stopping later at the old castle for refreshment, he encounters the arrival of a large Russian entourage, clearly composed of Russian nobility of the highest rank, many in military uniforms. Among them, a young woman calls to Litvinov and he soon recognizes her as Irina, his former love. The ten years since their last meeting in Moscow has brought her to her full bloom and he is struck by her mature beauty. Litvinov is introduced to her husband, the general Valerian Vladimirovitch Ratmirov, an affable man who it soon becomes clear holds very conservative opinions, wishing to turn back the clock on all the reforms that have taken place in Russia. As the “son of a plebeian”, Litvinov feels out of place among these aristocrats and put off by their manners and opinions. He bids farewell to Irina and she urges him to come see her while in Baden.
Though affected by his meeting with Irina, Litvinov does not go to see her. Several days pass. A letter from Tatiana telling him that she will be delayed arriving in Baden due to the illness of her aunt puts Litvinov in a petulant mood. One day Potugin comes to see Litvinov. Litvinov is glad for the company but soon learns that Potugin knows Irina quite well and that he has in fact come to bring a message from her urging Litvinov to come see her that very day. He agrees. Irina is staying in one of the finest hotels in the city and her husband is away on personal business. Irina and Litvinov have a long talk catching up on the past decade. Irina pleads with Litvinov to forgive her for what she did to him and Litvinov seems to dismiss the notion of forgiveness, as those events were long ago in their childhood. When Litvinov touches upon the flowers left in his room, Irina claims to know nothing about them. The return of Irina’s husband seems to break up the meeting. Later Litvinov passes Irina again while out walking but feigns not to recognize her. Irina later accosts him on his walk, asking why he ignores her and pleading with him not to do so, for she is desperate and alone and misses their simple relationship. Litvinov tells her what is in his heart, that she meant much to him and was the cause of great anguish and now that their paths and situations are so different he sees no point in renewing an acquaintance has only the potential to hurt again and to reveal to Irina how much power she still holds over him. She urges him again warmly that they might be, if not friends, at least friendly, “as if nothing had happened.” Litvinov promises her not to treat her as a stranger, though he still does not understand her intentions. Irina is then called off by the approach of an aristocratic friend. Litvinov, walking on, again encounters Potugin, now sitting and reading on a bench. They have another lengthy conversation about Russia that Potugin dominates, ridiculing those Slavophiles who are constantly heralding the native Russian genius but who refuse to see that the mastery of things comes with training and education and not through any internal nature or instinct. Litvinov is still unable to learn of just how Potugin knows Irina, only that he has known her for some time. Returning to his rooms, Litvinov later finds an invitation from Irina to attend a soiree in her rooms, where he will be able to meet many from her circle and better understand “the air she breathes.”
Litvinov later attends this soiree and returning to his rooms comes to realize with exhilaration and horror that he loves Irina and that his marriage with Tatiana is threatened by this looming passion. Litvinov decides he must leave Baden and Irina forever and makes arrangements for the omnibus to Heidelberg. He visits Irina’s hotel rooms to reveal both his love and his determination to leave rather than ruin himself. Irina is moved by this confession and though she initially supports his decision, she later comes to him to confess her love and tells him her destiny is in his hands.
Meanwhile, Tatiana and her aunt arrive from Dresden. Litvinov’s rather distant attitude towards Tatiana has his fiancée suspicious that something is not right. When the couple pass Irina on the street and Irina throws them a glance, Tatiana’s suspicions are further aroused. That evening, rather than staying with his fiancée and her aunt, Litvinov goes to see Irina who has summoned him. Irina tells him that he is in no way obligated to her and that he should feel completely free. On the way back to Tatiana’s rooms Litvinov encounter Potugin, who is forward enough to warn Litvinov to beware of his love for Irina and to not cause Tatiana pain. Litvinov feels insulted by this presumption on the part of Potugin, but the latter assures him he speaks from experience, for he too has been ruined by his love of Irina, albeit a love that has never been and never will be requited.
The story then reverts to eight years previous to relate Potugin’s history with Irina. At that time he was still working as a government official and would visit the country estate of the Count Reisenbach, the guardian of the young Irina, near St. Petersburg. Later, Irina, realizing that the older Potugin had fallen in love with her, uses this leverage to seek a great favour of Potugin. Irina’s close friend Eliza Byelsky, an orphan but the heir of a wealthy estate, was facing ruin (though left unsaid in the novel, this is understood to be pregnancy out of wedlock). For a large sum of money, but primarily because Irina desired it, Potugin agreed to secretly marry Eliza. Eliza later had her child, a daughter whom Potugin then adopted, before poisoning herself. Since that time Potugin has followed in the train of the Ratmirovs, utterly devoted to Irina.
Back at his hotel, Litvinov spends the evening with Tatiana and her aunt. He now tells Tatiana that he has something important he must tell her the next day. Tatiana has a foreboding of what this might be. The next morning a distraught Litvinov attempts to inform Tatiana of the situation but it is Tatiana, rather, who guesses he has fallen in love with that other woman they saw on the street. Soon thereafter, Tatiana leaves unceremoniously back to Dresden with her aunt without leaving any farewell note for Litvinov. Meanwhile, Litvinov writes a letter to Irina telling her of his break and urging her to run away with him only if her will is strong enough to stand such a life. If not, he will go away. Irina arranges for him to come see her again when her husband is out, and she reaffirms her commitment to follow him, though all her finances are in her husband’s hands. Eventually, however, Irina writes to Litvinov telling him that despite her love she is not strong enough to abandon her current life and declaring sorrowfully that she is unable to elope with him. Litvinov is heart-broken and leaves Baden on the train back for Russia. Along the way he muses over the mutability and seeming meaninglessness of all things, which have all the permanence of the smoke being blown forth by the train.
Back in Russia Litvinov returns to his estate in time to see his elderly father pass away. On his land Litvinov slowly recovers and even begins gradually to implement some of the land management and agricultural techniques he had learned in Europe. One day he hears through a visiting relative that Tatiana is living not too far away on her own estate with Kapitolina. He writes to Tatiana asking if he might visit her one-day and she responds in the affirmative, signaling to Litvinov that she has forgiven him. Litvinov wastes little time and sets out for her village. At a way station en route he encounters none other than Gubaryov and his brother. They reveal their true colors by their derision of the peasantry and their base treatment of Bambaev who, his finances wiped out, has been forced to become a servant to the Gubaryovs. Arriving at Tatiana's, Litvinov falls at her feet and kisses the hem of her dress. Here the narrator leaves the story, with the note that readers can guess the end by themselves.
As he does with almost all his novels, Turgenev then briefly relates what became of some of the other characters. Irina is related to be older but still lovely, with young men still falling in love with her "ironical intellect." Her husband is steadily rising in the world. As for Potugin, the little girl he had adopted has died but he still follows in the train of Irina.

However, at the climax of the challenge, both Mariah and Wolf end up disappearing into the sewer, never to be seen again; as a result, the game ends on a lose-lose draw.
# Mrs. Parker's plot
Mrs. Parker's plot revolves around attempting to start a collection of celebrity dishes, one per each dish night, at the Orpheum Theatre run by Leopold Doppler. She acquires the first dish, a Ronald Colman gravy boat, though she accumulates more as Doppler announces the other dishes are unavailable due to 'misshipment'. The frustration of accumulating the gravy boats combined with the events throughout the movie get Mrs. Parker over the edge, resulting her in throwing the gravy boat she won at the theater in Doppler's head. All other housewives, encouraged by Mrs. Parker's act, also start raining down the surplus gravy boats towards Doppler, enraged at the frustration and the apparent fraudulent scheme. Mrs. Parker is arrested for the act, though with a relieved smile on her face.
# Mr. Parker's plot
Mr. Parker's plot revolves around his odds with the Parker's hillbilly neighbors, the Bumpuses (or Bumpi, as the Parkers tend to refer them in plural), especially due to their loud overplaying of hillbilly music, obnoxious behavior and the constant harassment on Mr. Parker by the Bumpuses' forty-three Bloodhounds named Big Red. The escalation turns into war when the Bumpuses inaugurate an outhouse bathroom, which Parker clearly perceives as a health code violation. When Mr. Parker attempts forcing the Bumpuses to demolish the outhouse, they respond by having Big Dickie, the largest of the Bumpus family, destroy their house's porch as a show of force. Parker attempts unsuccessfully to torment the Bumpuses with music, which they mistake for Parker calling a night party, prompting him to hurriedly escape to the fishing trip with Ralphie. Mr. Parker does a second attempt, this time with a sound effects record disk simulating a federal bust, but by the time he unleashes the sound disk, the Bumpuses have long moved away. Mr. Parker interprets this as a defeat, and the act earns the ire of the woken-up neighborhood, who strongly suggest to bring the Bumpuses back and be rid of Parker.

Inspector Japp leads the investigation, assisted by Poirot and Hastings, but they discover the body of the impersonator Carlotta Adams when they went to her home to ask her to testify in the case. On the distant planet Eternia, the sorceress of Castle Grayskull has a dream in which the newborn girl Adora is abducted into another dimension by the villain Hordak. When the sorceress awakens, she sees a sword floating in front of her that closely resembles the magic sword of He-Man, the leader of Eternia's defenders against Skeletor and his evil warriors. The sword shows her the way to a hidden dimensional portal.
The sorceress then summons Adam and Cringer - the true identities of He-Man, the leader of Eternia's Defenders, and his battle-hardened Battle-Cat - and sends them both through the portal with the sword. It turns out that in the world behind the dimensional portal, the planet Etheria, the people are being oppressed by Hordak and his horde. Only a small rebellion stands against the Horde. Adam joins the Rebellion as He-Man and realizes in a battle between the Rebellion and the Horde that Force Commander Adora, Hordak's right-hand man, must be the one he needs to bring the sword to.
He-Man can convince Adora that the Horde is actually evil and not the Rebellion, as Hordak claims. It turns out Adora is Adam's twin sister. Adam was also to be kidnapped, but he could still be rescued in time. Skeletor, Hordak's protégé, remained on Eternia for fear of Hordak, having failed to abduct He-Man.
With the help of the sword He-Man brought to Adora, Adora is transformed into She-Ra. She frees He-Man and joins the rebellion. However, Skeletor betrays Hordak and sends him back to Etheria through another dimensional portal. Adora herself, however, is able to overpower her guardian Beast-Man and transform into She-Ra.
Back in the royal palace, She-Ra makes the difficult decision to return to Etheria to help the people there who are oppressed by the Horde.
On Etheria, meanwhile, the Rebellion plans to liberate Bright Moon Castle, which is occupied by the Horde. When She-Ra and He-Man, who has once again accompanied her, arrive, a huge army of animals suddenly appears to support the Rebellion in the Battle of Bright Moon.
The Battle of Bright Moon ends in a rebel victory, but before Hordak flees with Shadow Weaver, he warns She-Ra that a victorious battle does not mean a victorious war. After the battle, during the victory celebrations of the liberated people, He-Man asks She-Ra if she is happy. In 1976, priest John Geoghan was arrested for raping a minor in Boston. During the night, a high-ranking priest went to the police station to negotiate with the child's mother and allowed Geoghan to go free while the attorney general asked the officers present not to publicize the case.
In 2001, the Boston Globe saw a slight decline in sales. The new editor, Martin  Marty  Baron, decided to relaunch the newspaper with a major case: several priests in their town were accused of sexually abusing children and got away with it without being prosecuted. After getting wind of the story through an article about the fight by Mitchell  Mitch  Garabedian, a lawyer who had tried several times to reveal the truth about this scandal, Baron tasked the Spotlight team  a team specializing in investigative journalism  to investigate these priests and prove not only their guilt but also that their superior, Cardinal Bernard Law, and the highest levels of the Catholic Church were aware of and suppressed the case each time.
With the enlightened help of Mitchell Garabedian, the Spotlight team, led by Walter Robinson, will investigate the case for months and discover that not only did the Church cover up each of these cases using the services of crooked lawyers who negotiated large settlements with the parents of the abused children, but more importantly, the pedophile priests turn out to be far more numerous than previously thought. Phil Saviano, a victim who has since founded a support group, says there are 13 priests in Boston, but Richard Sipe, a former priest who has studied the issue for a long time, estimates that the number is closer to 90, or 6 percent of Boston's Catholic priests. By cross-referencing information provided by Sipe about the church's cover-up, the Spotlight team compiled a list of 87 priests. Robinson and Baron are approached by several people who participated in the negotiations and are all advised not to press.
As the team planned to publish, the attacks of September 11, 2001 led them to change their priorities and postpone the writing of the article. Journalist Michael Rezendes obtained valuable information from Garabedian: the lawyer had managed to attach to a publicly defended file letters addressed to Cardinal Law proving that he had ignored the victims' appeals for help. Rezendes manages to get them, however Robinson wants to stall in order to be sure to expose the entire system and that Law can't get rid of himself, which puts Rezendes out of his mind. The Boston Globe also won a case to get the seals lifted for several files on bargaining arrangements between lawyers. Baron agreed to publish the article after New Year's Day 2002.
Shortly before publication, Robinson realised that the newspaper had already received a list of 20 priests accused of paedophilia in 1993 from the victims' lawyer Eric MacLeish but had never acted on it. Baron pushes him to publish, with a web link to the documents and a phone number to file the testimonies. The next morning, the Spotlight team is overwhelmed with calls from victims who want to testify.
The film concludes with a text revealing that Cardinal Law eventually resigned in December 2002 before being appointed if not promoted to archpriest of the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, and then a list of cities where similar scandals have erupted around the world.

In the finale Lucille and Benoît escape to Paris to join the resistance with a pass provided by Bruno, who helps them even after the two are stopped at a checkpoint and kill the German soldiers who presided over it. A final embrace between Lucille and Bruno enshrines the impossibility of a love divided by the events of war.

After the United States enters World War I in 1917, the limousine carrying Daisy Heath (Margaret Sullavan), a sophisticated Broadway musical theatre star, knocks down Bill Pettigrew (James Stewart), a naive young soldier from Texas. A policeman orders the chauffeur to take Bill back to camp. During the ride, he becomes slightly acquainted with the cynical, but not cold-hearted Daisy.
Upon their arrival at the army camp, Bill lets his buddies assume that Daisy is the date he had lied about. In fact, he has no one. When they find out the truth, they decide to get even. On their next leave, they take Bill to Daisy's show, so he can introduce them. However, Daisy pretends that she is Bill's girl. When Sam opens the letter, Bill's ID tag falls out. Orphaned at an early age, orphan brothers Stephen and Bloom begin to develop self-confidence as young children. While Stephen comes up with sophisticated scenarios and the first infidelities of his childhood spring from his pen, Bloom, on the other hand, is the calmer one, living in his brother's shadow.
Twenty-five years later, the brothers have turned out to be real con men. Also joining the team now is Bang Bang, a Japanese explosives expert who rarely speaks. However, Bloom is dissatisfied with being nothing more than an actor in Stephen's fraud schemes. He's tired of not being more than the characters his brother made up, and he wants a "unwritten life". He's giving up and moving to Montenegro. Three months later, Stephen finds Bloom and convinces him to do one last job. Bloom reluctantly agrees. The plan targets Penelope Stamp, a wealthy, socially isolated heiress who lives alone in a New Jersey mansion. After
Bloom fakes a car accident and the two of them meet in the hospital, the first trust is gained. After Penelope invites Bloom to her mansion, the two become closer. Penelope reveals to him that she has been alone most of her life and that she is increasingly bored day after day. Bloom senses Penelope's sense of adventure and hints that he will sail to Europe the next day. As planned by the brothers, Penelope appears the next day, just before the anchor is lifted.
On the ship, Melville, a Belgian hired by Stephen, starts the scam and tells Penelope that the Bloom brothers are actually antique smugglers and he wants her help with a smuggling job in Prague. Penelope is enthusiastic about the idea of becoming a smuggler and convinces the brothers to take the job, unaware that this is part of the scam. Meanwhile, Bloom and Penelope become increasingly attracted to each other, despite Stephen's warning that the scam will fail if he actually falls in love with Penelope.
In the hotel bar in Prague, Bloom is visited by the brothers' former mentor and current enemy, Diamond Dog. He warns Bloom that Stephen won't be around forever, and offers him cooperation. Stephen, who then surprises Diamond Dog with a broken glass bottle, stabs him in the hand.
In Prague, Melville swindles Penelope of a million dollars and flees as planned. Penelope still wants to become an antique smuggler and steal the rare book Melville told her about. As a distraction, the team then plans to fire a small explosive at Prague Castle, which triggers the fire alarm and allows Penelope to sneak into the museum and steal the book. As Penelope mistakenly exchanges the backpacks with the explosives, and to the horror of the brothers, the entire tower is blown up, a large-scale police operation takes place. Despite all the panic, Penelope enters the museum and steals the book. She gets caught, but convinces the police chief to let her go. The team then flies to Mexico to complete the con. Bloom, who has since fallen in love with Penelope, confesses to her the night before the finale that they are impostors and that the whole adventure was planned as a hoax. Stephen, however, foresaw his brother's change of heart and worked his way into the plan. After the brothers struggle with each other and a gunshot is fired, it seems Stephen's time has come. Penelope examines the wound, but discovers that it is fake blood, and leaves Mexico with a broken heart. The equally depressed Bloom now wants to go his own way, and so the team falls apart.
Three months later, Penelope meets up with Bloom. She confesses that she wants to be with him. Unable to deny his love for her, but not wanting her to be like him, Bloom meets with Stephen to forge a final con in which they fake their own deaths. The team travels to St. Petersburg to sell the rare book to Diamond Dog. They'll be ambushed by Diamond Dog's gang on their way to the exchange. Stephen is subsequently kidnapped and held for $1.75 million. Bloom suspects that this is just another one of Stephen's tricks. Penelope transfers the money from her bank account to the gangsters for all cases. Bang Bang takes this opportunity to give up working for the Bloom brothers. As she leaves, her car explodes, with Penelope and Bloom unsure whether she was involved in the explosion or faking her death. At the subsequent exchange in an abandoned theater, Bloom finds Stephen helplessly tied to a chair. When Stephen is finally shot, but it's unclear how much of the whole thing is a hoax and how much is real, the brothers finally break up.
Bloom and Penelope are leaving to start a new life. After a while, Bloom discovers that Stephen's blood stain on his shirt has turned from red to brown, indicating that it is not fake blood. When he realizes that Stephen is definitely dead, Bloom collapses on the side of the road while Penelope tries to comfort him. As they leave, Bloom recalls what Stephen had said earlier: "The perfect scam is one in which everyone involved gets exactly what they want".

By his daily evening visits, first in military clothes, then in civilian clothes, to reduce the impression of occupation in the eyes of his guests, he shared, under various pretexts, with his uncle and niece, his love of France, literature, music, its nature, and his hope of seeing a great Europe born of the rapprochement between France and Germany. The film follows five young women from five different cultures who rebel against the repression of female sexuality in their cultural and religious communities. It shows her struggle for a self-determined female sexuality. Patriarchal structures and today's porn culture are discussed.
In 2014, Doris Wagner published a biography about her experiences, including sexual abuse, in the Catholic community Clergy Family Das Werk.
3sat describes the film as a plea for the right to self-determination and against the demonization of female lust by religion and social restrictions.
According to the press release of the distributor, the film is based on the idea of exploring the theme of sexuality and women in relation to the five world religions and cultures. The protagonists and their backgrounds could hardly be more different:
Leyla Hussein was born in Mogadishu into a strict Muslim family and was allowed to attend school in Somalia. She shares her story of female circumcision in fundamentalist Islam, which happened to her when she was seven years old.
Deborah Feldman grew up in an ultra-Orthodox Jewish family in New York. The devotion to God, obedience, guilt marked her childhood. She was forced to marry at the age of 17. After the birth of her son, she ventured away from the Orthodox community and published the book Unorthodox, which caused an earthquake in the Jewish community.
Rokudenashiko was born into a traditional Japanese family and grew up as the daughter of devout Buddhists in the greater Tokyo area. Rokudenashiko, who had studied art, developed into an action artist who made prints of her vulva and made plastic figures in the shape of her vulva. Women's sexuality, as opposed to men's sexuality, is a highly taboo subject in Japan. At a rally in Tokyo, the artist was arrested for "causing public outrage", facing several years in prison.
For Doris Wagner, God was the most important person in her life from her earliest childhood. At the age of 19, she entered the monastery of Thalbach in Bregenz. While continuing her monastic training, she was raped by a priest 20 years her senior during a stay in Rome. After a long history of suffering, she found the strength to leave the convent. Her book "Not Me Anymore" elaborates on what happened and warns against the dependencies and chasms in ecclesial communities.
Vithika grew up as a girl in a traditional Hindu family in Rajasthan, northern India. At the age of 12, she experienced sexual harassment for the first time. Vithika founded Love Matters, the first online sex education project in English and Hindi, in Delhi with the support of Radio Netherlands Worldwide.
