Gary Hamilton is released from prison after ten years and sets out to take revenge on Acombar, the man who took his money, his mansion, his wife Maria and his freedom. On his way to meet him, he meets in the horse-drawn carriage the returning, ignorant Dick Acombar, the son of his enemy, and announces his arrival at the villa for the evening.
Dick passes on Hamilton's announcement and is surprised by his father's violent reaction. This one's got a $10,000 bounty on Hamilton. A tornado is coming. The city is taking precautions. Acombar's men try to lure Hamilton into an ambush on the outskirts of the city, but the approaching storm allows him to enter the city unnoticed. Hamilton uses the tornado, the darkness, and the caverns beneath the city to appear and disappear like a ghost, gradually taking out Acombar's men.
Meanwhile, at a dinner party, Acombar and Maria celebrate Dick's return. Suspicious of the shooting in the city, he leaves the villa. From the old doctor and the saloon owner Rosie, he learns the whole story: that Acombar cheated on his former friend Hamilton with his wife, robbed a money train and killed several men in the process, and blamed Hamilton for it.
Gary Hamilton breaks into the mansion of Acombar. Confused and nervous, the father accidentally shoots his son and then, in a rage of grief, kills Maria as well. After the final duel, Acombar, shot by Hamilton, plunges into the treasure chamber of the burning villa. The next morning, the storm has subsided and Hamilton is riding on.

Ivan, a tractor driver, lives in a Siberian village in the far north of the country. He can leave his collective farm and go to the sea for a cure. Actually, he wants to take his two children with him, but his mother has reservations. That's how he ends up leaving with his wife Njura. In the sequel, they first meet an unfriendly gentleman, who ironically meets them because of their origin and with whom the impetuous Ivan almost starts a fight. Finally, the conductor takes the man to another compartment. Ivan and Njura now share their compartment with Viktor, who carries a large suitcase that he opens with a knife. He pretends to have left the keys to the suitcase at home. In reality, however, he stole the suitcase. Inside is cash, a bottle of vodka that Viktor immediately opens, and an expensive blouse that he gives Njura. All three now drink vodka until the unfriendly passenger at the next station reports Ivan to a policeman. However, he only warns the naive Ivan about Viktor, who gives them alcohol on an empty stomach in broad daylight  Ivan should be careful. Viktor soon disappears with his suitcase and jumps off the moving train. The police are looking for him and Ivan and Njura learn that they were dealing with a thief. They are questioned by the police about Wiktor and Njura secretly makes the gifted blouse disappear.

Only the conductor can correct Ivan and explain to both that Stepanow is a linguist. Stepanov has even appeared on television and is recognized by other travelers. They invite him to another compartment, and Ivan is allowed to come with them. They sing and Ivan drinks a little too much alcohol, after which he becomes talkative, much to Njura's chagrin. They go shopping with Stepanow's daughter in the big city and Ivan tells an episode from the peasant life in the end in Stepanow's TV show.

Mike Reilly (Stephen Dorff) is a New York City police detective who is called to the scene of a mysterious death in the subway system. The victim, Polidori (Udo Kier), has bleeding in his eyes and other holes and, by the frozen look on his face, seems to have been a death scare.
At the Department of Health researcher, Terry Huston (Natascha McElhone) is intrigued by the find and especially when several more victims turn up with identical symptoms.
When a contagious virus is ruled out, team two tries to figure out what could be killing these people. After some digging for clues, they order forensic specialist Denise Stone (Amelia Curtis) to check the hard drives of the victims' computers.
Denise ends up discovering that they had visited a website called Feardotcom that features voyeurism, torture, and murder. Looking at the same page, Denise is subjected to various sights and sounds of torture that ultimately result in her madness and death from her apartment window.
Mike feels guilty, thinking that Denise should never have gotten involved in the case. Terry realizes that people who visit the website end up dying within the next 48 hours. Despite knowing it's dangerous, both she and Mike end up visiting the site in order to find out what's going on.
As they begin to experience paranoia and hallucinations (like the dead one), including that of a young girl, they race against time to find out if there is any connection to a very vicious serial killer, Alistair "The Doctor" Pratt (Stephen Rea), who has eluded Mike for years.
It is revealed that Feardotcom is in fact a ghost site of one of Pratt's first victims, Jeannie-Jean Marie (Gesine Cukrowski) who seeks revenge, because people saw her being tortured and killed. Tortured by Pratt for 48 hours before she begged him to kill her, which explains why the victims have 48 hours to live. Mike and Terry locate Pratt and release the spirit of the murdered girl on the website, which kills Pratt. However, Mike is also killed.
The final scene shows Terry lying in her bed with her cat, staring at the ceiling when the phone rings; Terry answers, but no one on the line answers, so Terry hangs up again.

The Five Golden Dragons are an international criminal gold trafficking secret society syndicate based in Hong Kong.  They plan to break up after selling their criminal enterprise to the Mafia for US$50 million. However the members of the group fear the greed of each other in receiving their share of the profits. Visiting American playboy Bob Mitchell, as well as sisters Ingrid and Margret, become targets of killer Gert and his murderous accomplices, while Shakespeare-quoting police commissioner Sanders and his subordinate, Inspector Chiao investigate the matter. Sanders quotes Hamlet, act 1, scene 4, but Chiao corrects him, "Scene 5", and leaves. Sanders then quotes Merchant of Venice, act 1, scene 2.
Margret sneaks into Mitchell's hotel suite, looks through his papers and, when he returns, tells him she knows he is really "Doctor Mitchell, graduate of Stanford". She then confesses that, as a stewardess, she was working for the Dragons, but now fears for her life. In the morning, as Chiao knocks on the door of Mitchell's suite to take him for questioning by Sanders, the door to the bedroom, where Margret spent the night, is locked and, when opened, reveals her in bed, covered with a Dragons cape, dead as a result of a broken neck.
Mitchell sneaks out and, upon learning from his friend and helper Ah Sing about The Blue World nightclub, goes there to watch the club's star singer, Magda, perform "Time of Our Lives" while being observed by the club's shady manager Peterson. He tells Peterson, "I sell chewing gum... confections...
Magda spots Mitchell, sings to him, kisses him in front of Peterson and leads him to her dressing room where she asks him to help her change outfits. She then locks the room and goes out to perform another song, "Five Golden Dragons". When she finishes, the emcee introduces "one of Japan's most popular singing stars, Miss Yukari Ito", who performs a song in Japanese.
Meanwhile, in his office, Sanders struggles to remember a quote which Chiao finishes for him and adds that it is from "Henry Five". Sanders then adds, "Act 2, scene 1". Trapped in Magda's room, Mitchell discovers a secret passage to Peterson's office and escapes with Peterson's briefcase, but is intercepted by Chiao and his men and brought to Sanders' office. Exiting, he sees Ingrid outside and they leave together as Sanders closes the door and quotes Macbeth, act 4, scene 3.
One by one, four of the Dragons arrive in Hong Kong. When the second Dragon arrives, it is Chiao who provides the quote which Sanders recognizes as Othello. The Dragons are members of a secret society, each with a key to a cabinet. Each member wears a golden dragon head. When this scene is first used one of the dragons is revealed as Christopher Lee. The earlier scenes only have four dragons. Learning that Ingrid has been kidnapped, Mitchell argues with Sanders about rescuing her and storms out as Sanders, alone, quotes Othello, act 3, scene 2. Having captured Ah Sing and Ingrid, Gert menaces her, but Ah Sing manages to free himself and strangles Gert.
The climax of the film results from the arrival of Mitchell, disguised as the fifth dragon but, owing to a double-cross by Magda, Peterson switches places with Mitchell and, while still wearing his mask, is fatally shot by the gun concealed inside the cabinet he opens, thus inadvertently saving Mitchell's life. Immediately thereafter, Sanders and Chiao arrive in the Dragons' meeting room and arrest them as well as Magda.
When asked by Sanders about his plans, Mitchell replies, "Well, uh... I... I think that's... uh... more or less up to Ingrid... right? As Sanders and Chiao watch a plane take off from the airport, Sanders quotes, "That is the true beginning of our end" from Midsummer Night's Dream, act 4, scene 1.

He is full of concern for Mina, provides her with a new home and helps her win a lawsuit against her father-in-law who wanted to take away her custody of his daughter, but he does not tell the whole truth about him to Mina because he knows that she will not forgive him.

Street musician James lives on the streets of London. He's a drug addict on a methadone replacement program. With the junkie Baz, he occasionally meets, he actually wants nothing to do with, but is still seduced by him to a shot, after which he ends up in the hospital. His caregiver, Val, manages to get James a place to live. There he is surprised by a red-tipped cat that has climbed in through the open window. He feeds it and tries to find its owner. Failing to do so, he throws her out in the park again, but she returns to James with an injury. Betty, a neighborhood animal friend, arranges for him to receive free veterinary treatment, but he has to sacrifice the last of his money for the expensive medication. Betty also names the cat Bob and arranges for it to be castrated. James is very fond of Bob and talks to him a lot. The animal follows him around town to play music, and James finds that the passersby are giving him a lot more money since he joined. He now always performs with Bob, who usually sits on his shoulder. One day, James finds Baz dead from an overdose. Although James takes immediate care of him and the paramedics are quickly called, he does not survive.
James develops a friendly relationship with Betty, though he does not tell her about his drug use. Betty's brother, in whose apartment she lives, died of an overdose, which gives her an aversion to drug addicts. James tells her that his parents separated when he was a child and his mother now lives in Australia while his father rejects him. One day, he meets his father by chance with his father's new life partner and expresses his desire to come for Christmas dinner. To discourage him, the father suggests a possible visit on New Year's Day. James actually visits him unannounced that day, which ends in disaster as Bob knocks over a vase and the Christmas tree.
One day, during a street performance by James, there is a brawl. Even though James didn't do anything wrong, he's banned from performing in the city. Instead, he gets a job as a salesman for the homeless newspaper The Big Issue. Here, too, Bob is making himself very successful. When he sells a newspaper in a colleague's "district", he is slandered and James is banned from selling for a month, which puts him back in financial and mental distress. Betty overhears James taking his methadone at the pharmacy and turns away from him. When he's allowed to sell again, a local reporter writes a story about James and his cat.
James is doing so well now that he can do the methadone withdrawal. Betty offers to help, but it's Bob's presence that gets him through this difficult week. Although Betty moves out of the apartment next door and back to her parents, she gives James her new address and telephone number. James visits his father again, and they apologize to each other. Literary agent Mary, who has frequently gifted James and Bob at their performances, stumbles upon the newspaper report and comes up with the idea of publishing a book about James' story. Although it's not easy for him, James actually writes this book, which he presents at a reading, where he thanks everyone who has helped him. Most of all, Bob showed him that he could live a different life.

query_text:
Every Day is about the story of A, a genderless person who wakes up occupying a different body each day of a sixteen-year-old living in the East Coast. As described by Frank Bruni of The New York Times, "A. doesn't have a real name, presumably because they don't have a real existence: they're not a person, at least not in any conventional sense, but they have a spirit, switching without choice from one host to the next and, for just 24 hours, replacing its consciousness with their own." A has their own memories, but they are also able to tap into the memories of the person whose body they are occupying. A calls this "accessing."
The story begins with A waking up in the body of a teenage boy named Justin. Upon arriving to school, A meets Justin's girlfriend, Rhiannon, and feels an instant connection to her. Based on Justin's memories, A can tell that Justin and Rhiannon are having a rough time in their relationship, so in order to learn more about her, A invites her to the beach. The pair open up to one another, though A's sharing is limited and very carefully worded. A had never felt such a connection with anyone before, and so attempts to discover a way by which to stay in Rhiannon's proximity in days to come. A then does their best to convince Rhiannon that the day shared at the beach was not between her and Justin, but rather between her and A.
A spends almost every day following this event trying to figure out the best way to approach Rhiannon, since they are luckily never more than just a car ride away. After going through some trouble, A is finally able to convince Rhiannon of who they are, and the phenomenon they experience every day. While she does believe A, and understands how hard it must be, she also realizes that a relationship with A would be impossible, even if she wished to be in one. As the story progresses, we follow A as they wake up in body after body, still chasing Rhiannon. Meanwhile, they are forced to contend with a boy whose body A inhabited early, and who tracks them down in order to gain answers as to who A is and how they were able to take over their body and mind, as well as a preacher working with that boy, who gathers a following of people who inhabit the bodies of others.
option_0_text: The early years of the donkey Baltasar were happy, in the company of Marie (Anne Wiazemsky), a shy peasant, and Jacques (Walter Green), his Parisian vacation companion. Since there is no legal way to maintain his company, Stoner considers burning down his warehouse to pay for the insurance. Mike Roark is the head of the Los Angeles County Office of Emergency Management, which is responsible for disaster management in Los Angeles. He's on vacation with his daughter Kelly when a small earthquake shakes the city. So Roark cancels his vacation and drives to his workplace. Shortly thereafter, an accident occurs in a storm drain beneath MacArthur Park, killing seven of the city's sewer workers and narrowly saving another. Roark then unsuccessfully attempted to have the subway section under MacArthur Park closed.
At first, an accidentally drilled steam pipe is suspected as the cause of the accident, but it soon becomes clear that the workers were not killed by steam, but by a flame, prompting Roark and his colleague, Gator Harris, to climb into the storm drain themselves. There, they discover a crack in the ground, from which a burning jet of gas suddenly flows and almost kills them both. Roark then consults geologist Dr. Amy Barnes and her colleague, Rachel. Because the temperature of a lake in the park has also risen unusually sharply in just a few hours, the two geologists warn Roark that it is possible that plate tectonic activity is causing magma to rise to the surface just below the city, forming a new volcano. But with no hard evidence, Roark's hands are tied.
At night, Barnes and Rachel climb into the storm drain to investigate the crack. Without warning, the city is rocked by a violent earthquake that knocks out power. Rachel, standing right next to the crack, loses her balance, plunges into the crack, and is killed by a sudden burst of hot gas. The earthquake derails a subway train with several passengers on board. Roark, awakened by the earthquake, is trying to drive his daughter to safety when suddenly steam rises from the sewer. From the La Brea tar pits, a plume of black smoke and lava bombs are rising simultaneously. When one of the lava bombs hits and overturns a fire truck, Roark and Dr. Jaye Calder attend to the injured.
A few minutes later, the volcano erupts near the tar pits and the lava slowly flows onto Wilshire Boulevard. Two of the firefighters trapped in the overturned car are burning in the lava. Kelly is wounded in the leg by a lava bomb and taken by Calder to Cedars Sinai Hospital. The lava, accompanied by immense media coverage, spreads several hundred meters over Wilshire Boulevard.
Meanwhile, a rescue team led by Stan Olber, the head of the Los Angeles Metro, discovers the derailed subway being hit by a lava flow. Since the doors cannot be opened, the passengers are still trapped in the carriages, fainting from the heat. The rescue team can save the passengers before the lava reaches the carriages. Olber notices that the subway driver is still missing and climbs back into the already burning cars. He manages to find the unconscious driver and carry him through the carriages. By now, the lava flow has washed away the entire subway. Olber's attempt to jump from the carriage onto safe ground fails. He falls into the lava flow, but before he dies, he is able to throw the subway driver towards the rescue team.
On Wilshire Boulevard, Roark and Barnes are working with firefighters and emergency responders to stop the lava flow. They erect a barrier of concrete blocks, which initially blocks the lava flow. Firefighters and helicopters pour tons of water over the lava, causing it to crust and solidify.
However, Barnes calculates that the eruption is not over yet and there is still a significant amount of lava flowing underground, which will erupt again at the next obstacle. Calculations indicate that this outbreak will occur at Cedars-Sinai Hospital, the exact location where Roark had earlier transported his daughter and several other wounded.
Since there is not enough time to evacuate all the people, Roark makes the decision to blow up an uninhabited skyscraper so that the debris acts as a barrier and diverts the lava flow into Ballona Creek - a rainwater channel. Just as they begin to explode, Roark notices that his daughter and a small boy are standing right next to the skyscraper. Since the blast sequence can no longer be aborted, Roark immediately rushes to their aid. The skyscraper collapses and all three are washed away. Thanks to a cavity in the adjacent building, they can only be retrieved with minor injuries a short time later. Roark's plan has worked: the lava flow is blocked, diverted into Ballona Creek, and finally empties into the Pacific Ocean. In the end, Roark takes Barnes and his daughter on a well-deserved vacation.
The film ends with a view of the Los Angeles skyline and the still-smoking volcano in the background. The displayed text mentions Mount Wilshire and its status as an active volcano.

Poonam lost her parents when she was very young. Her uncle Krishnakant and her aunt Rama have taken her into their home. But Rama is jealous of Poonam because she is prettier than her own daughter Rajni. But Poonam and Rajni (Chothi) have been getting along very well since childhood.
One day Bhagat-ji, a jeweler and good friend of Krishnakant, visits the family. Immediately he is enchanted by Poonam's manner and decides to find a suitable husband for her. He's already got a young man in his sights, Prem, the son of industrialist Harichandra, who is also a friend of Bhagat-ji.
They send a picture of Poonam to Harichandra, who immediately falls in love with Poonam. When he tells Prem about Poonam, Prem is skeptical at first. But his brother tries to calm him down and tells him about his own experience and marriage to his current wife Bhavna. This calms Prem down a bit and he agrees to meet Poonam.
When Prem and his family travel from Delhi to Madhupur to meet Poonam's family, the two become closer. The two shyly agree to the marriage and become engaged. Since everything has worked so well, Poonam's uncle decides to take a vacation with Prem's family at his holiday home Som Sarovar.
In Som Sarovar, Prem and Poonam, thanks to Bhavna's arranged meetings, are able to be alone and fall head over heels in love with each other. When Prem and the family have to leave the holiday home early for business reasons, the two keep in touch via the Internet, phone and mail. It is only because of the great distance that they reveal their feelings for each other, which they were too ashamed to show.
Two days before the official wedding, a fire breaks out in Krishnakant's house. When Poonam tries to rescue Chothi from the burning house, she suffers severe burns that decorate her entire body except for her face.
After Prem hears about Poonam's accident, he immediately visits her in the hospital. Poonam is very unhappy and insecure as she doesn't know if Prem still wants to marry her. For Prem, however, it's a matter of course to take Poonam home as a bride. And as a sign of this, he wears her scar on his forehead.
The doctor informs the families that there is still hope. Poonam can be operated on, but the procedure can be very risky and the injuries take a long time to heal completely. However, the operation is successful and Prem nurses Poonam in the hospital for some time until he takes her home for the wedding.
option_4_text:
Ultimately, the universe doesn't care about us tells the story of A, a person who wakes up every day in a different body. A does not have a real name, he is not a person in the conventional sense, but has a mind that switches from one host to another without choice, replacing their consciousness with his own for only 24 hours. A has memories of his own, but is also able to tap into the memories of the person whose body he's occupying.
The story begins when "A" wakes up in the body of a teenager named Justin. After arriving at the school, A meets Justin's girlfriend Rhiannon and immediately feels connected to her. Based on Justin's memories, A can tell that Justin and Rhiannon are having a tough time in their relationship, so A invites her to the beach to learn more about them. The two open up to each other, even though A says less and phrases it very carefully. "A" has never felt such a connection to anyone before, so she's trying to find a way to stay close to Rhiannon for the next few days. "A" is doing her best to convince Rhiannon that the day at the beach wasn't between her and Justin, but between her and "A".
A spends almost every day after this event trying to figure out how best to get close to Rhiannon, since luckily they're never more than a car ride away from each other. After some difficulty, A is finally able to convince Rhiannon of who he is and what phenomena he experiences on a daily basis. Although she believes A and understands how difficult it must be, she also realizes that a relationship with A would be impossible, even if she wanted to have one. As the story progresses, we follow "A" as he wakes up again and again in different bodies and continues to pursue Rhiannon. Meanwhile, he is forced to contend with a boy whose body formerly inhabited A, who is tracking him down for answers as to who A is and how he was able to take over his body and mind, as well as a priest who works with this boy, who is gathering a following of people who live in the bodies of others.

query_text:
# In the beginning
The Cloade family live under the protective wing of the Gordon patriarch, resident at Furrowbank, a mansion in the village of Warmsley Vale, not far from London. But when he dies in the bombing of London during World War II, everything changes for the family. First of all, their breadwinner died, but most of all, he left everything to a young widow, Rosaleen, who they say defrauded them of their inheritance. Then a man named Enoch Arden appears on the scene, who turns out to be the young Rosaleen's first husband, presumed dead. Then the widow Cloade would be a bigamist and not entitled to the inheritance. The family hopes so, but Arden is killed.
While at the Coronation Club during an air raid in 1944, Hercule Poirot overhears Major Porter talk about Gordon Cloade, who was killed in an air raid with his entire household. The only survivors are the young widow, Rosaleen, and her brother, but there's an oddity. Porter met Robert Underhay, the young woman's first husband, in Africa, and recalls suggesting that he disappear in order to free her from the marriage without the shame of a divorce. Before his disappearance, Underhay jokingly stated that he would henceforth adopt the name Enoch Arden. In addition to Poirot, another man also heard Porter's anecdote, Gordon Cloade's brother Jeremy, running out of the club with an angry look.
Two years later, in 1946, Poirot receives a visit from Katherine Cloade, who asks him to find out something about Robert Underhay, hoping to annul Gordon's will. He refuses, but soon afterwards he reads in the newspaper the announcement of the death of a man named Enoch Arden, and he becomes curious about the matter again.
# I weave
After the prelude, the story goes back in time, from late spring to early spring, when Lynn Marchmont, recently discharged from the Royal Navy, has difficulty adjusting to everyday life in Warmsley Vale. The girl is engaged to Rowley, one of the members of the Cloade family who live in the area. All of them are financially dependent on Gordon Cloade, an old, unmarried gentleman who will leave everything to his relatives when he dies. Shortly before his death, however, the man married Rosaleen, and his old will is no longer valid. As a result, Rosaleen has inherited all of the old man's fortune, and the Cloade family is going through a time of crisis, aggravated by the post-war economic problems. Rosaleen's fortune is jealously guarded by David Hunter, her brother, and although some people, such as Lynn's mother, Adela, try to squeeze the young woman out of small sums of money, David flatly refuses to help Frances Cloade, whose husband Jeremy is about to be ruined financially.
The arrival in town of a man named Enoch Arden changes everything. Arden tries to blackmail David by telling him he knows where to find Rosaleen's first husband, Robert. Their conversation at the pub is overheard by the club's owner, Beatrice Lippincott, who immediately tells Rowley Cloade. Later, Arden's body is found in his room with his skull cracked open.
Rowley Cloade calls in Poirot to find proof that the dead man was Robert Underhay and, remembering Major Porter, the detective is pleased to have already found a witness. At the inquest, despite Rosaleen's protests that the man killed was not Robert, Major Porter confirms that a gentleman by the name of Enoch Arden was the woman's first husband, Underhay. The Cloades are therefore entitled to the inheritance.
Rosaleen has an alibi for the night of the murder: she was in her flat in London. David, however, has a very shaky one: on his way back from London that day, he met Lynn as she was racing to catch the last train to the city at 9 p.m., and then called her from her London apartment shortly after 11 p.m. Since the murder appears to have been committed shortly before 9:00 p.m., he had plenty of time to commit the crime and provide a fake story to tell the cops.
David's alibi, however, becomes stronger after it is discovered that a woman in heavy makeup and an orange scarf was seen leaving Arden's room after 10 p.m. The police's attention then focuses on the women of the Cloade family, but Poirot points out that Arden's death was caused by an accident, and that the scene afterwards was transformed into that of a murder.
Suspects are starting to behave strangely. Lynn, although engaged to Rowley, seems to be falling in love with David. It also appears that Rowley is attracted to Rosaleen, who, for some reason, seems consumed by guilt and fear. Major Porter commits suicide, but leaves no note to explain his act. After his death, it is revealed that Enoch Arden was actually Charles Trenton, second cousin of Frances Cloade. The woman decided to blackmail Rosaleen after Jeremy told her about Major Porter. Despite this clarification of Arden's true identity, we still don't know who killed him and convinced the major to give a false identification of the body.
Rosaleen also dies of an overdose in her sleep. Superintendent Spence suggests that she may have been murdered as well; the police have been so focused on David's alibi that they haven't checked her sister's at all.
Lynn then goes to Rowley and informs him of her intention to break off the engagement, because she wants to marry David Hunter. Rowley reacts violently, and tries to strangle the girl until Poirot arrives to stop him. That's when David shows up, and the detective tells him everything that happened that night. Rowley goes to see Arden and, seeing his resemblance to Frances, realizes the deception and becomes angry. Arden, pushed by Rowley, falls and breaks his head, and the boy then decides to blame David, leaving Hunter's lighter at the crime scene. Later, Rowley convinces Porter to provide the deceased's false identification, and cleverly turns to Poirot, knowing that the investigator would immediately go looking for the major, given the scene he had witnessed at the club, which Jeremy also knew. Porter's guilt takes over, however, and the major commits suicide, leaving a note which Rowley then destroys.
David was very clever in his actions on the night of the murder, according to Poirot. Discovering Arden's body, he ran to the station to catch the 9:20 train, but missed it; Lynn actually saw the smoke from the departing train, but he convinced her that it was still early and that he had time to meet her. David then returned to the pub, disguised himself as a woman, and created the false clue of the woman who had been visiting Arden to establish the time of death. Then he went back to the station, called Rosaleen and told her to call Lynn but to hang up. Right after, David called Lynn from the station, making her believe he'd picked up the call from London. The next morning the man goes to the capital on the milk train, unseen.
Rowley was involved in an accidental death and a suicide; the only real murder is that of Rosaleen. Murdered with sleeping pills poisoned with arsenic. David had no apparent motive for killing his sister, especially since doing so would have cost the Cloades their entire fortune. But the woman who pretended to be Rosaleen wasn't really her sister, the real Rosaleen had died in the bombing two years earlier. The woman who pretended to be her was actually a waitress, who had become David's mistress, and later, his accomplice in amassing the Cloade fortune. After Arden's appearance, however, David decided to kill the maid so that he could marry Lynn and thus get the amount that the girl would get from the division of the inheritance.
The novel thus has three different conspiracies: that between David and the maid; that between Frances and Charles; and that between Rowley and Major Porter. Poirot ensures that Rowley will not be prosecuted for what he has done, but will instead succeed in marrying Lynn, who has always been in love with him, even if she did not realize it.

option_1_text:
Harry McKee is a successful TV chef at a regional network. Although he has been in the newspapers more often due to his alcoholism, he is very popular with the audience. In his personal life, however, things are different. His wife, Ruth, whom he has cheated on several times, wants a divorce. Emotionally agitated, he embarrasses local politician Walter Adair in his cooking show by mocking his sexual preferences. In the ensuing court proceedings to settle the details of his divorce, Harry collapses.
When he wakes up after a few days in a coma, Harry suffers from amnesia. The last 25 years seem to have been erased from his memory. He is now in the same hospital as the politician Adair, who has been undergoing treatment since fleeing from intrusive journalists and the associated fall from a bridge.
Although Harry's wife and children don't want to believe him and think the amnesia is a trick to delay the divorce, they take him back home. Using old photo albums, they try to refresh his memory. But on the advice of his doctors, they don't tell him about his career as a TV chef.
However, he is informed of this by his friend and lawyer. He also tells him that his wife wants to divorce him. Although Harry's full memory has yet to return, his recording director urges him to resume his cooking shows. During the first show, a spectator suddenly interrupts the proceedings. It's Walter Adair, dressed as a woman, pulling a gun and threatening Harry. The programme will then also be broadcast live on national channels. The now-cleansed cook is about to surrender to his destiny when Ruth suddenly appears. After she succeeds in disarming Adair, she promises to reconcile with Harry. However, she insists on divorce and urges him to reconsider his life. Only when he was absolutely sure that he wanted a future with her would he contact her again. Harry predicts that he will call her the same day and ends his cooking show by announcing the guests of the next show.
option_2_text:
Stroszek, a young German soldier, after being wounded in the war, found himself resting in a fort in Greece, in charge of a munitions depot. The idleness, the heat and the isolation gradually drove him into a kind of madness. Stroszek wants to set fire to the sea and the sun, threatens to blow up the powder magazine and becomes a real danger to those around him.
The screenplay is close to the story The Mad Invalid of Fort Ratonneau, written in 1818 by Achim Von Arnim. The director did not know the story but was inspired by the same historical anecdote as the writer: at the end of the 18th century, a mad soldier entrenches himself in the fort of Ratonneau, in Marseille, and declares himself king.
option_3_text:
In 1926, Joe Coughlin, an Irish-American World War I veteran and the prodigal son of Boston police captain Thomas Coughlin, falls in love with Emma Gould, the mistress of notorious gangster Albert White, the boss of the Irish Gang of Boston who Joe and his friends have been targeting in a series of robberies. Thomas objects to the relationship and advises Joe against his criminal activities, warning him that his wrongdoing will catch up with him eventually.
White's rival, Italian Mafia boss Maso Pescatore, finds out about their affair and blackmails Joe to kill White. Joe refuses, and instead he and Emma decide to flee to California. To fund the trip, Joe commits a bank heist with his partner Dion Bartolo and another man, during which three police officers are killed in an ensuing chase. When Joe goes to meet Emma, he discovers that she betrayed him to White. Joe is brutally beaten by White's men and nearly killed before Thomas and the police arrive and arrest Joe for the policemen's murders.
Thomas tells Joe that Emma drowned while being pursued by police. He also blackmails Chief Inspector Calvin Bondurant to ensure that Joe is indicted on a relatively minor charge rather than murder, and he is given only a three-year sentence. Two weeks before Joe's release, Thomas dies of a heart attack. Wanting revenge against White, Joe volunteers his services to Pescatore and is recruited as an enforcer for the latter's rum empire in Ybor City in Tampa, Florida, which is under attack by White. Joe brings Dion along and together they protect Pescatore's business in the area; the boss then sends orders for them to bring gambling and drugs into Tampa. Joe also develops a relationship with Graciela Corrales, the sister of a local Cuban businessman who supplies most of the rum, and they are soon married.
Joe befriends Sheriff Irving Figgis to get police protection for his bootlegging. Irving's daughter Loretta heads to Hollywood to become an actress but instead becomes a heroin-addicted prostitute. Irving's brother-in-law, R. D. Pruitt, a member of the local chapter of the Ku Klux Klan who blames Joe for bringing more non-white immigrants into Tampa, starts bombing Joe's businesses and killing his men. Joe promises Irving to help get Loretta off drugs and back to Ybor City in exchange for betraying Pruitt. Joe kills Pruitt personally and has his men hunt down and kill all of Tampa's KKK members in a string of brutal assassinations.
With Prohibition coming to an end, Pescatore orders Joe to switch to selling narcotics, which he disagrees with, instead planning to build a mob casino near Sarasota. He intends to persuade the state government to legalize gambling, but Loretta, who has become a devout Christian under her father's strict and punishing discipline, begins preaching that alcohol and gambling are against God's word. Her ministry is popular enough that the government decides not to legalize gambling. Joe recognizes that Pescatore will be enraged, particularly since Joe still refuses to invest in narcotics.
During a private meeting in a restaurant to settle their differences, Loretta confides to Joe that she does not truly believe in God and her sins cannot be forgiven. The next day, Joe is despondent to learn that Loretta committed suicide. While visiting his brother-in-law, an amateur photographer, Joe finds a recent picture of Emma, whom he believed to be dead. He decides to pursue her, but only after informing Graciela first, much to Dion's dismay.
Pescatore orders Joe to meet with him at a local hotel, where he reveals he has reconciled with White and given him the honor of killing Joe for his failures, planning to replace him with his son Digger. Anticipating Pescatore's betrayal, Joe distracts White by showing him Emma's picture, as White also believed her to be dead. Dion and his men ambush Pescatore's gang through a series of tunnels Joe had previously used to move rum into the hotel. In the ensuing gunfight, White, Pescatore and Digger are all killed, eliminating all of Joe's enemies in one stroke. He names Dion as his successor before locating Emma at the brothel she now works at. She relates how she faked her death to escape from White and enjoys her newfound freedom, and claims she never reciprocated Joe's love for her. Satisfied, Joe returns to Graciela.
Joe and Graciela move to Miami, where they have a son, Tommy, and devote their time to building houses for the impoverished. Driven insane by Loretta's death, Figgis tracks them down and shoots up their house, killing Graciela before being fatally shot by Joe. Joe arranges for Graciela to be buried in her homeland in Cuba and spends the rest of his days dedicated to charity and to raising Tommy, who soon voices his desire to become a police officer.
option_4_text: The successful young Swiss banker Roger Caviezel has been smuggling his German clients' black money across the border for some time. When he is stopped in his vehicle at a border checkpoint, he flees  as the police are chasing him  with the money bag into Lake Constance. This one, however, is populated by mystical beings. The banker bets a witch he can find his true love in three tries. When his flirtations with a shepherdess, a blonde seductress, and a waitress fail and he realizes that he cannot free himself from the clutches of the intrusive witch, he visits his allies home. There, on his grandmother's farm, he falls in love with a Turkish employee, which also does not last. After being able to parachute to safety from the witch, he is enchanted by another companion, the mermaid in Lara-Croft attire. She becomes his beloved Patricia, with whom Roger finds his new happiness as a beach bathing operator on Lake Geneva.

query_text:
The film is entirely in English and consists almost exclusively of historical documentary footage, with some graphic animation. It begins with the spoken rendering of an alleged Hitler quote in English, showing a stylized lattice mast similar to the Berlin radio tower on a globe. In front of the radio tower, a black swastika and white Japanese characters as symbols of National Socialism and Japanese imperialism and finally the head portrait of Adolf Hitler are displayed one after the other.
The alleged Hitler quote is:
The speaker now points out that the voices of the Nazis have been silenced, but the Big Lie lives on, in Josef Stalin and the Stalin Gang. It alternates with head portraits of Nazi functionaries and Communist leaders, beginning with Joseph Stalin, with the hammer and sickle and Chinese characters now displayed in place of the swastika as symbols of Communism. Other images show mass marches on the occasion of the Nuremberg Reich Party Day and Labor Day on Red Square in Moscow, with the indication that the parades have become longer and the marching music louder. Other similarities in parallel montages show scenes from National Socialist and Soviet forced labor camps, sham elections with predetermined election results in both political systems, show trials before the People's Court under Roland Freisler and in the USSR and marches of the Hitler Youth, Wehrmacht and SS against marches of the Pioneer Organization of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin and the Red Army. The series of comparisons ends with a stylized Iron Curtain drawn from above over the image of the marching Soviet soldiers, now dividing Europe into the free world and the world of slaves.
Against the backdrop of women workers huddled together in a textile factory and scenes from grocery stores, the speaker announces that this is the world of slaves. In broken English with a strong Russian accent, in stark contrast to the pictures, it is stated that communism does not mean poverty and scarcity, but the prohibition of poverty and scarcity.
An animated map of Europe shows Soviet annexations such as the Baltic states, Belarus, and Ukraine in black, and Soviet satellite states such as Poland, the GDR, Czechoslovakia, Mongolia, and North Korea in gray, depicting the Soviet Union's efforts to incorporate sovereign states or bring them into total dependence. Bulgaria, Poland, Romania, North Korea and Red China are cited as examples, with pictures and quotes from their heads of state, all of whom have fallen under the influence of the Kremlin and its Big Lie.
This is followed by mass scenes from various satellite states, each of which is introduced with the indication Sold out (sold) and supported by typical propaganda statements for the country. Poland, Romania, Hungary, China, North Korea and Czechoslovakia are shown like this. Below are pictures of the state funeral for Jan Masaryk in 1948. Masaryk died in unexplained circumstances shortly after the February Communist coup by a fall from the window of the Prague Foreign Ministry. Referring to the official account of the death as a suicide, the spokesman states that Masaryk could not live with the Big Lie. The coffin of Masaryk will be followed to his grave by the freedom of Czechoslovakia.
Only one nation refuses to die. No Communist politician was more convinced of the Big Lie than Yugoslavia's Marshal Tito. He had also followed the example of other Communist leaders and had made his pilgrimage to Moscow, but then had pushed back the Iron Curtain. He said that the special road to Yugoslavia had defeated the big lie that Yugoslav grain was now feeding Yugoslavia, and not Russians at the expense of starving Yugoslavia.
In the absence of content, the last 'communist lie', the 'lie of the pigeon', is attacked. Filmed footage of Communist armament factories and military parades is accompanied by Soviet propaganda statements about the desire for peace and disarmament. But these words are countered by other deeds, the (communist) Greek Civil War: The dove that goes BOOM. Similarly, three more sequences of images of peace conferences and arms production are attached, underpinned by peace propaganda with a strong Russian accent, images of the Indochina War, the Korean War and the Chinese Civil War: The dove that goes BOOM. The film closes with two warnings: fear the Big Lie, fear the pigeon that makes BOOM.
The slogan The dove that goes BOOM of the last section is the translation of the French title La colombe qui fait BOUM of a cartoon, which is also reproduced in the film. A dove of peace has transformed in such a way that its wings have become armor chains and its head represents the turret of a Soviet battle tank marked with a hammer and sickle. This symbol was published by the French anti-communist group Paix et Liberté as the first poster in a series, and 300,000 copies were printed and distributed. It was a caricature of the 1949 silhouette of a dove designed and lithographed by Pablo Picasso, which was chosen by Louis Aragon as the symbol of the 1949 World Peace Council Congress in Paris. For this work, Picasso received the International Peace Prize of the World Peace Council in 1955. Since then, Picasso's dove has become an internationally recognized symbol of peace and the peace movement.
option_0_text: In a Portland grocery store, a gay American falls madly in love with Johnny, an illegal immigrant from Mexico who doesn't speak a word of English and isn't even twenty years old.
option_1_text:
Natasha "Nat" O'Brien is a celebrity pastry chef, sent to London to collaborate on a state dinner hosted by Queen Elizabeth II and hosted by culinary critic Maximillian "Max" Vandeveer; Max is also the obese editor of the gourmet magazine Epicureo as well as the patron and patroness of several well-known European chefs, each of whom is known for his own dish.
When they meet, Max is looking forward to the latest issue of the magazine, whose article "The World's Most Fabulous Meal" highlights the masterpieces of his favorite chefs; however, Max's health has long been affected by his poor eating habits, due to the constant tasting of sophisticated and hard-to-digest foods.
Natasha's painful note is the presence of her ex-husband Robert Ross, aka Robby; while Nat deals with fancy dishes and refined palates, Robby is a fast food entrepreneur and focuses on the average consumer.
After finishing her meal at Buckingham Palace, Nat meets colleague Louis Kohner and has a one-night stand with him; the next morning Natasha finds Kohner dead in a 450° oven; she is interrogated by Inspector Blodgett, and then leaves with Robby for Venice. Here he meets another renowned chef, Fausto Zoppi, and they make an appointment in his kitchen; but on arrival Nat finds him drowned in a lobster tank. Interrogated again by the Venetian authorities, Natasha receives a phone call from Robby asking her to come to Paris to prevent the death of a French cook; in the capital they discuss the deaths of Kohner and Zoppi, in particular how they were killed. That same night Max calls them, and Natasha senses the common factor: both deaths appear on Max's article with their most famous dish. From this, the pastry chef deduces that the next victim will be Jean-Claude Moulineau, whose best dish is the Canard à la presse (pressed duck).
Robby suspects Max, because he chose the names that appear in the article, but Natasha suspects a person excluded from the list, Auguste Grandvilliers; trying to warn Moulineau, they are instead contacted by Grandvilliers who claims that someone is in his restaurant; Nat and Robby go to the place and find the chef in the refrigerator, hanging from a hook used to hold the meat but still alive.
In all this the two ex-spouses are getting close to the point of falling in love again; the next day Inspector Doyle informs them that Moulineau was killed by sticking his head in a duck press. Natasha has to return to London to participate in the program A Moveable Feast, and Robby follows her to protect her; but then they learn from Max that Inspector Blodgett called Ms. Beecham to inform Max of the end of the investigation: Grandvilliers has confessed to the murders. Relieved, Robby can leave for Brussels; but at the airport, while watching Natasha on TV, he notices that the cake used in the show is different: someone has replaced it with another one containing a bomb. Called Blodgett to find out more about Grandvilliers' confession, he discovers that there was no confession; suspecting Max again, Robby runs to the television studio and drives Nat away from the bomb cake, which explodes less than a minute later.
In reality, Max is innocent: the murderer was Mrs. Beecham, the critic's assistant hoped that, by killing her boss's favorite cooks, he would decide on a serious diet to improve his health. It's over, Natasha and Robby are getting remarried.
option_2_text:
As the Iron Curtain falls, the peoples of Eastern Europe, China and North Korea are "sold out" to Kremlin-controlled puppet regimes. In common with other American propaganda of the time, the People's Republic of China is described as a Soviet satellite state, although it never actually was. Footage of marching is shown for each of the satellite states to symbolize how these countries fell under the Soviet yoke. Only Yugoslavia under Josip Tito escapes the Kremlin's grasp and regains its independence.
The final part of the film attacks the Soviet-front World Peace Council, contrasting their rhetoric of peace – repeated to film footage of Soviet armaments factories and military parades in Red Square – with the realities of Communist warmongering in Greece, Indochina, Korea and China.
The film concludes with the exhortation to "Beware the Big Lie! Beware the Dove that goes BOOM", as Pablo Picasso's La Colombe ("The Dove", which the World Peace Council was using as its symbol) is replaced by the cartoon La colombe qui fait BOUM, originally produced by the French anti-communist group Paix et Liberté. In this cartoon the dove is metamorphosing into a Soviet tank – its wings have become tank treads, and its head is a tank turret.
option_3_text:
After the previous owner Andrew Marr dies, Edward Foster inherits his mansion. Despite attempts to scare him out of the house, that is rumoured to be haunted, he decides to renovate and inhabit it.
Unbeknownst to him, Marr’s former physician Dr Ian Mandeville and his sister Sarah compete with solicitor Prescott in trying to locate two suitcases of money rumoured to be hidden on the large estate, that he hopes to claim for himself.
Edward, later revealed to have been recently released from an asylum, soon starts hearing voices and begins to have flashbacks of the life of Andrew Marr, slowly witnessing the latter’s marriage to his mentally unstable wife Victoria fall apart. Andrew had planned to leave her for the younger and more attractive governess Alta. In desperation Victoria had encouraged the two equally psychotic children to murder the governess whilst she attempted to seduce Andrew in the bedroom. Hearing the children murder Alta, Andrew strangled his wife and killed the children with a sword before bricking all four corpses up behind a wall with the two cases of money.
Edward, driven mad by the constant flashbacks and unable to distinguish between himself and Andrew, accidentally strangles Sarah while experiencing the murder of Andrew’s wife. He kills Dr Mandeville with a pick axe and attempts to kill Prescott before being arrested and led away by police, who also seize the money.
option_4_text:
Set in an anonymous, desolate and isolated small town in Hungary during the Communist period, the film begins with János Valuska, a young newspaper delivery boy, conducting a dance with the drunken patrons of a bar. The dance represents a total eclipse of the sun, which disturbs and stuns the animals, and ends with the return of the warm sunlight. György, an old friend of János, is a composer and one of the intellectuals of the village: he observes the imperfection and compromise of the musical scale (as defined by Andreas Werckmeister) and proposes some modifications to the scale to make it more harmonious.
Meanwhile, a circus made up of only two attractions, a prince and a whale, makes its appearance. János, after philosophizing about God and the whale, goes to the post office, where the workers are shocked by the disturbing signs of the circus' arrival, memories of the cloud that settles over every city visited by the circus. The presence of the whale and the prince lifts the masses, and János feels the circus master losing control of his faceless prince. The prince, freed by the circus owner, inflames the masses and the people revolt. The rioters are brutal, but their inhumanity seems almost normal and natural.
After the rebellion, János returns the diary of a rioter, which highlights how the rioters themselves did not know what they were angry about, even recounting the horrific rape of two working-class post office girls. János leaves the city for his safety, but is intercepted by a helicopter; he will be locked up in an institution for the mentally ill. Meanwhile, intelligence is being replaced by political opportunism.
György informs János that if he is released from the mental institution they can live together in his hut, in the company of his piano. György also states that he has tuned the piano in such a way that it is now the same as all the others, highlighting a personal capitulation, the abandonment of hopes for reform. János just stares at him, and the film ends with György looking directly into the whale's eye, and then walking away looking at the sad, lacerated whale, destroyed by the rebels the night before. Its rotting carcass is slowly shrouded in mist, which becomes whiter and brighter, warmed by sunlight.

query_text:
In the year 984, the knight Bowen trains the young prince Einon in swordsmanship and teaches him the virtues of chivalry, which are formulated in the ancient oath. A short time later, Einon's father, the tyrannical King Freyne, leads a punitive expedition against a village of rebellious peasants and is ambushed when he himself sets fire to the peasants' houses. He is mortally wounded by the rebellious peasants; even before he dies, his son, who wanted to rush to his aid and watched the process from a hiding place, rips off the crown. A peasant girl collides with Einon, who falls into a pointed stake and suffers a life-threatening injury to his heart.
The mortally wounded young king is taken by his mother, Queen Aislinn, a devotee of the dragon cult, to a dragon cave, where a dragon saves Einon's life by giving him half of his heart. The dragon will not make this sacrifice until Bowen has assured him of his pupil's virtue. Einon himself has to take an oath.
However, against his sworn oath, Einon becomes an even more cruel tyrant than his father. He wants to be the first to rebuild a castle that was originally built by the Romans, and he wants to make it even more splendid than the original. But, as he is told, this will require a very large number of people. Einon then has the peasants of the defeated village do frontal work there to advance the construction. Bowen is leaving Einon in light of this development. Knowing the young king differently, he now firmly believes that the dragon has bewitched the boy and vows to kill him for it.
Years later, the monk Gilbert of Glockenspur travels the kingdom and meets Bowen, who earns his money as a dragon slayer. Gilbert, in search of material for a heroic epic, joins Bowen, in whom he believes he has found his protagonist, when he sees him slay a dragon.
However, the next dragon Bowen wants to kill turns out to be an equal opponent. A stalemate ensues when Bowen, trapped in the dragon's mouth, positions his sword in such a way that the dragon would kill itself if it bit him. After a long conversation, in which it turns out that they are the last living dragons, they agree to conclude a truce. The dragon sees little point in fighting, as if he won, he would soon have the next dragon slayer on his back, while Bowen, if he killed him, would be out of a job. Bowen "defeats" the dragon in show fights and collects the bounty for the "killed" dragon from the people or their landlord, but leaves him alive. Gilbert continues to work on his poem about Bowen and Draco  without knowing how the last fight, of which he could only observe the beginning, turned out, and without knowing anything about this agreement.
In the conversation between Bowen and the dragon, it becomes clear to the viewer through a parallel plot that the half-heart of the dragon connects Einon with this one, but the dragon does not recognize Bowen as the donor of the half-heart. Bowen also gives the dragon, whose real name no man can pronounce, the name Draco, after the Latin name of the constellation Draco.
After some time, Bowen meets Kara, the girl from the previous story, who has now grown into an attractive woman. Kara tries to persuade Bowen to start a rebellion against his former student, but Bowen flatly refuses. After a failed showdown, Draco flies to Avalon with Bowen, Kara, and Gilbert, who arrives during the showdown. In the rain, Bowen hears King Arthur's voice reciting the old oath, and he becomes aware of his ideals again. Draco reveals himself as the dragon who saved Einon's life. His motive was to renew the promise of the dragons to care for humans, to establish the alliance between humans and dragons, and through this good deed after his death to enter the constellation of the dragon, whose stars are the souls of dead dragons. However, because of Einon's wickedness, this is now denied him. After repeating the oath at Arthur's tomb, Bowen is ready to go to war against Einon, and begins to train peasants to become partisans back in Einon's kingdom, with Draco as a miracle weapon giving them psychological (and military) support and chasing the king out of the castle.
In the ensuing conflict, the rebels mortally wound Einon, but he pulls the arrow from the wound and lives on, while Draco falls from the sky severely wounded and is captured. Einon realizes that his life is linked to that of the dragon, and keeps it alive in captivity in order to be immortal. Queen Aislinn is captured and killed by Einon as she attempts to slay the dragon. Bowen can defeat Einon, but he can't kill him as long as Draco lives. Draco tries to convince Bowen to kill him so that Einon and the evil in him will also become mortal. The knight stubbornly refuses, only when Einon attacks is he ready. With the dragon, Einon will die.
Through his sacrifice, Draco's soul is taken up into the starry heavens before the eyes of Bowen, Kara and Gilbert. Gilbert of Glockenspur recounts that Bowen and Kara together ruled wisely and justly over the land, it was truly golden years, and when once there was a need, the constellation of the dragon shone especially brightly to the people.

Seventeen-year-old Veronica Clarke takes a pregnancy test at school and is interrupted by her former best friend Bailey Butler, who sees that the test is positive. At first, not knowing who it belongs to, Bailey offers to drive her to a clinic where she can have an abortion if she needs one. Then she assumes Veronica wants to keep the baby and discards the test.
Veronica decides to have an abortion, only to discover that it is illegal in Missouri without parental consent. She quickly makes a plan to get to Albuquerque, New Mexico, where clinics perform abortions without the involvement of the parents, but she lacks the money to make the trip. When she meets up with her boyfriend Kevin, she is shocked when he responds to the pregnancy news with a proposal. He also confesses that he noticed that the condom had burst. Veronica pretends to consider the proposal and takes the ring with her. She then goes to Bailey, who agrees to drive her to Albuquerque.
At their first stop, Veronica attempts to pawn her engagement ring, and is stopped by Kevin, who pursues her. When the pawnbroker learns that Veronica needs the money for an abortion, she agrees to buy her ring. Veronica and Bailey travel to Texas, though they argue about their former friendship, which Bailey fails to recognize because Bailey's father was ashamed of her as a child.
While making a stop at a diner, Bailey is startled by the arrival of the local sheriffs. She reveals that the car they're driving belongs to her mother's boyfriend. The girls are running away. Later, Jarrod takes her and introduces her to Matthews, a racing driver who offers to drop her off at the next bus stop. Turns out it's a woman Bailey finds attractive. Bailey then comes out as a lesbian and later has her first kiss with Matthews. Before Matthews can drive her to the bus station, a young couple who happen to want to go to Albuquerque offer to drive her all the way there.
Bailey and Veronica wake up in the morning at the couple's house, where they discover that the couple are actually radical pro-life and radical religious fundamentalists who are trying to stop Veronica from getting an abortion. They manage to escape the couple by stealing their GMC Yukon and faking their own deaths.
When they arrive at the next bus station, they find that there are no buses leaving, but there is a workshop next door run by the anti-government survivalist Bob. When he hears Veronica needs an abortion, he agrees to drive her to the clinic in an old limousine. While driving, Veronica's friends call her to say that the pregnancy test supposedly belongs to Bailey. To protect herself, Veronica agrees that Bailey is the most likely suspect. Bailey overhears the phone call, which triggers an argument between them and the breakup of their friendship. Bailey disappears while Veronica drives off in the limo. When Veronica realizes that Bailey wants to visit her father, she postpones her appointment at the clinic and follows Bailey. When Veronica arrives at a flower shop where Bailey's father works, she witnesses Bailey's unpleasant reunion with her father, helps Bailey and they reconcile.
At the clinic, Kevin surprises her again, threatening to tell everyone about the abortion unless Veronica stays with him, but she tells him to do it. After the abortion, they realize they have no money left, so they call their mothers, who get them plane tickets home. At home, Veronica's mother admits to being confused by her decision, but reaffirms her love for her daughter.
At school the next day, Veronica learns that Kevin never told her friends about her abortion, but she decides to tell them anyway. She also decides to continue her friendship with Bailey, and sits down with her for lunch.
Sometime later, the two take another road trip to Roswell.

Now 17, at the beginning of the school year, Lola is left by her boyfriend, who constantly insults her and insults her heavily and makes her life a living hell. She is comforted by her best friend Kyle, who has a very strong bond of friendship with the girl. But Ashley is obsessed with him. Emily, Lola's best friend, copulates in the boys' bathroom with a boy and, having the same bag as Ashley, Lola mistakes it for her and because of the misunderstanding she and Kyle argue, since Lola had fallen in love with him in the meantime.
Meanwhile, Kyle's father punishes his son by breaking his guitar (Kyle has a passion for music and competes with other bands in a competition) and confiscating his computer and cell phone. The only way left to talk to Lola is through friends. Only after Emily realizes that Lola is really sick does she tell her that she was the one making love in the bathroom and not Ashley and Kyle, but she doesn't tell her the name of the guy she was with. So Lola, sorry she got mad at Kyle, leaves him a bunch of texts, but he can't get back to her, so she gets mad. Kyle explains everything to her and they get engaged. On the trip to Paris Emily confesses to Lola breaking down the wall that had been created between the friends. At the end of the trip, Lola's mother, searching for her sweater, finds Lola's secret diary, discovering that her ex-husband insulted her heavily and that she smokes marijuana. After a while, in a fit of rage, he tells his daughter about the diary. Consequently, Lola goes to her father angry about the fact that her mother has read his diary, but returns immediately because without her mother she is ill and the latter regrets having read her diary.
Lola and Kyle officially become engaged while Emily loses interest in a young and charming professor and becomes interested in the boy she kissed in the bathroom and Lola's ex, Chad, gets involved with Ashley, who has become friends with the protagonist. Lola also realizes that she resembles her mother in character. Her mother, meanwhile, decides to get a divorce and finds another man.
option_2_text:
The film is set in a small town with the fictitious name of Châteauneuf. In the opening scene, we see about 15-year-old schoolgirl Catherine Roussel walking home from school crying. At the request of her parents, she explains that her teacher Jean Doucet sexually abused her. He vehemently denies the charge. However, when other students in the class are questioned, the girl's statement is confirmed, as two other students make similar accusations, including Helène Arnaud, the best in class and the daughter of a construction contractor. The mayor, wanting to avoid a scandal, advises Doucet to leave the place, but he refuses, as it would be tantamount to an admission of guilt. Eventually, he is arrested and sent to prison for further investigation. He faces life imprisonment in a penal colony.
Doucet's wife Suzanne, who is convinced of her husband's innocence and knows the inhabitants of the village well, now interrogates them in detail and discovers the true backgrounds and connections.
In the end, Jean Doucet is released, but declares that he no longer wants to live in the village. His wife, who had long wanted to leave the small town anyway, is delighted.
option_3_text:
In the year 984, during the bloody suppression of a rebellion, the tyrannical King Freyne is killed by a mob and his son, the young prince Einon, is accidentally wounded in the heart by a commoner who trips on him. The boy is immediately rescued by his mother Aislinn, and mentor Bowen, who lead him to a cave so that the dragon that lives there can save his life. The dragon agrees, as long as the prince swears to rule wisely and with mercy, following the dictates of The Ancient Code of the Knights of Camelot, and gives half of his heart to the boy, thus curing him of his mortal wound. As time passes, however, Einon proves even more ruthless than his father, and with his cruelty he brings the people of the kingdom to their knees. Bowen, believing that the boy's soul has been poisoned by the dragon's heart, sets out in search of the latter to kill him and take revenge.
Twelve years later Bowen has become a dragon slayer, while King Einon, now an adult, has consolidated his tyranny. One day, after encountering Brother Gilbert, a monk with poetic velleities who decides to follow him, Bowen finally manages to meet and confront the dragon (although he does not recognize him), who reveals to him that he is the last dragon left due to the continuous persecutions against his species. Dragon and knight fight for hours and hours until, both exhausted, they decide on a truce, during which they become friends. The two decide to form a partnership, staging plays where the dragon terrorizes the superstitious peasants into paying Bowen to eliminate the fake threat.
Although the ruse works, the dragon is not pleased with Bowen's move: the creature thinks it is a sneaky move as the peasants are reduced to their limits by King Einon's tyranny. Bowen is not interested in all of this, however, having now lost hope of seeing the world changed now that his pupil Einon has become even worse than his father.
One evening, intent on resting after the last con, the dragon observes Bowen's shield reinforced with the teeth of his fellows, and realizes that his friend hated dragons as much as he did. Bowen explains that he hunted dragons only to find and avenge the one who split his heart with Einon by corrupting his soul and making his former pupil a ruthless and cruel tyrant. Now good friends, Bowen decides to name the dragon after Draco, from the constellation of the Dragon. Draco claims to know that constellation very well, whose stars are, according to tradition, the souls of the most famous fallen dragons that have ascended to heaven.
Soon, however, the dragon, also convinced by the peasant Kara, the rebel who several years earlier had wounded Einon, begins to rebel against the King's tyranny, given the desperate situation in which the people find themselves. Bowen initially wants nothing to do with this, but by then he is joined by Einon, who was on Kara's trail to make her his, and is now overwhelmed by it. Bowen confronts his former pupil with a sword, asking him why he has become like this, and Einon explains that Bowen was just a tool for him and that he took what he wanted from him, considering the ancient code to be worthless and unimportant. Bowen is eventually wounded, but as Einon is about to give him the final blow, Draco opens his chest and shows him a luminous scar. In panic, Einon fled with his militia. Kara recognizes in Bowen that old knight who helped the peasants rebel years ago against Einon's father, and that his strength can once again help a people subjugated by a tyrant.
Following a scam gone wrong, Draco transports Bowen, Kara, and Bowen's friend Friar Gilbert to the island of Avalon. Here Draco explains that, in ancient times, the wisest of the dragons of his race gathered all the dragons, making them swear to watch over and protect humanity's new arrival on Earth. At the time of his death, the constellation of dragons was subsequently born. Draco had decided to share his heart with a dying boy, hoping to reunite man and dragon as they once did, thus earning himself a place in the dragon's paradise alongside his brothers, but the choice proved wrong, as the boy became a ruthless and evil king. Bowen thus understands that it was Draco who divided his heart with Einon: Draco confesses that already years before he was aware of the young man's temperament, but he hoped that half of his heart could purify him. Feeling responsible for all of this, Draco decides to go with Kara and Friar Gilbert to prepare to overthrow Einon. Bowen, left alone in the rain, has a vision of the great King Arthur, reminding him of the value and significance of his knighthood through the words of the Old Code. Bowen then repeats the oath, and at the end, Draco offers him shelter from the rain under his wing.
As Kara and Gilbert try to convince the peasants to rebel, Bowen appears along with Draco, ready to help the peasants by training them for the impending fight to free themselves from Einon's yoke. Despite the apparent victory in the battle against the forces of the realm, Bowen discovers that Einon cannot be killed directly: any mortal wound to his heart instead inflicts pain on the original owner, Draco; only if Draco is killed, Einon will also die. Realizing this, Einon has Draco captured by dragon hunters hired by his mother Aislinn, to keep him safe. Bowen, accompanied by Kara and her brother Gilbert, sneaks into the castle to rescue Draco.
Upon being discovered by the guards, they are promptly rescued by the peasants, who are also fond of Draco, who try to buy time to allow Bowen to save him while they open the castle gates. Realizing the vital bond that binds her son Einon to Draco, Aislinn, in the night, reaches Draco held in chains and declares remorse for having asked Draco that time to save her son, only realizing later how cruel and ruthless he was. Draco eventually asks her to end his life as the only way to stop Einon, but his attempt to kill Draco is stopped by Einon himself, who senses his mother's true intentions and the reasons why she had called the dragon slayers to the castle.
Although aware that she will soon be killed, Aislinn openly admits that she wanted to make up for the mistake of saving her son in the past. Having succeeded in entering the stronghold along with Kara, Bowen openly duels Einon and defeats him by causing him to fall from the top of the castle, finally rescuing his friend the dragon. Although Einon has been defeated, Draco is aware that his evil will not be destroyed as long as he lives, and the only way to stop him permanently is for Draco himself to die, so he finally asks him to give him the fatal blow. The rider is devastated by the news of killing his dragon friend and refuses, knowing that he is the last of the dragons left.
Einon reappears at that moment and attempts to kill Bowen, but Draco opens his chest revealing his heart: grief-stricken, Bowen delivers a fatal blow to his friend's heart, thus ending Einon's life as well. Bowen, who is joined by the peasants, witnesses Draco's final moments and asks him how they will do without him: while his body transforms into pure spirit of light, Draco answers serene that he always looks at the stars in the sky. Thanks to his heroic sacrifice, the last dragon ascends to the celestial vault and rejoins his brothers among the stars of the Dragon constellation, watching over his friends and their kingdom for years to come.
option_4_text:
In Victorian era Britain, Dr. John Dolittle is a Welsh veterinarian with the ability to communicate with animals. After his wife Lily dies at sea, Dolittle retreats from human society and only tends to animals at his sanctuary that Queen Victoria gifted him.
Years later, Tommy Stubbins, a young boy, accidentally wounds a red squirrel named Kevin while out with his hunter father. He finds himself led to Dolittle's home by his macaw Polynesia, who hopes his arrival will help Dolittle reconnect with humans.
At the same time, Queen Victoria dispatches her maid of honor, Lady Rose, to seek Dolittle's help when she falls seriously ill. After treating Kevin, Dolittle agrees to see Victoria, after Poly reveals he will lose his home to the Treasury if the queen dies.
At her palace, Dolittle finds Victoria being tended to by his lifelong rival, Dr. Blair Müdfly. Examining her himself in the presence of Müdfly and Lord Thomas Badgley, a member of the House of Lords, he discovers she was poisoned with nightshade and can only be cured with the magical fruit from the Eden Tree.
Dolittle mounts an expedition to handle this, leaving his lurcher Chip and a stick insect to keep an eye on the Queen while he is away. Although he takes along several animals for the journey, including Chee-Chee the gorilla, Yoshi the polar bear, and Poly, he refuses to take Tommy.
Poly, refusing to let Tommy be left behind, sends a giraffe and fox to collect him. He manages to reach the ship and helps out after beginning to learn how to talk to animals, especially when Müdfly begins pursuing Dolittle to impede his efforts.
To track down the fruit, Dolittle brings his expedition to Monteverde, ruled over by Lily's father King Rassouli, to recover her journal. He believes that it will help lead the way to the site where the fruit is found. However, Rassouli apprehends Dolittle when he tries to steal the journal and locks him in with a moody tiger.
While Tommy works to recover the journal, Dolittle stalls the tiger until Chee-Chee locates him and finds the courage to defeat it. Although the group acquire the journal, Müdfly steals it and destroys their ship. Rassouli, learning that Dolittle is trying to honour Lily's memory with his expedition and he also misses her, loans him a ship to chase after Müdfly.
Both parties eventually reach the island of the Eden Tree, only to find it is guarded by the dragon Ginko-Who-Soars. Although it attacks the groups, causing Müdfly to fall down a hole, it soon collapses from internal pain. Dolittle diagnoses and cures the dragon, causing Ginko to gratefully reward him access to the tree and its fruit.
Dolittle returns in time to cure Victoria, before revealing that Badgley had poisoned her to take the crown for himself. The queen has him sent to the Tower of London for treason, thanking Dolittle for saving her.
Returning home, Dolittle re-opens it to others, while taking on Tommy as his apprentice.
