Harvey Shine, an American musician who works as a jingle writer, arrives in London for his daughter's wedding the next day. However, the reunion is not as happy as he had hoped, Harvey feels alienated by Susan, who has not been attached to him for a long time. Then there is the bitter surprise that it will not be he who accompanies her to the altar, but the stepfather, who has replaced the father figure all too well. Harvey takes a hard hit and, pressured by work, decides to leave right after the religious ceremony.
When he arrives at the airport, he misses his plane and cannot make it back in time for a business meeting. For your boss, that's grounds for immediate dismissal. Harvey, between despair and resignation, stops at the airport coffee shop. There he meets Kate, a charming 40-year-old travel analyst. Kate had tried to interview him the day before, but Harvey had abruptly dismissed her. Harvey then tries to make up for what had been a gratuitous rudeness, and overcoming the woman's initial resistance, invites her to lunch. Kate is a pleasant, sociable, sensitive woman, but she hasn't found the right man yet, and she's stressed out by an anxious, nagging mother.
Kate begins to enjoy Harvey's company, so much so that instead of saying goodbye to him, she asks him to take her to a creative writing class. At the end of the lesson he is still there waiting for her and reveals the strange situation that led him to give up his daughter's wedding party. So Kate senses the importance of it, convinces him to go. Harvey agrees on the condition that you accompany him. Coldly welcomed, and not just because of their tardiness, Harvey and Kate settle in, arousing the curiosity of many. When the father of the bride is called to make a toast and his wife's companion takes the floor, Harvey interrupts him and with a beautiful speech full of affection and humanity, he wins back his daughter and touches Kate's heart as well.
The two continue to talk pleasantly throughout the night and, after just one tender kiss, make an appointment for the following day at noon. Unexpectedly, Harvey receives news from his company; the executives, aware that they have lost a person who is difficult to replace, offer him to return "as if nothing had happened", but Harvey refuses. His life is changing, and he is now seeing other prospects. The intense emotions and unusual physical activity lead to a sudden mild heart attack. Harvey is unable to go to the long-awaited date with Kate, who, in despair, thinks that she has once again deluded herself unnecessarily. As soon as he is discharged, however, Harvey joins her at the airport and, apologizing for what happened, gets a cautious but clear opening from her to a possible relationship.
For Harvey, this may be his last chance.
option_0_text: Charlie Bartlett (Anton Yelchin) is an optimistic and honest boy, from a very wealthy family, but who suffers from behavioral problems that cost him expulsion from several high schools, forcing his mother Marilyn to enroll him in a public high school. Charlie has a fantasy of being liked by everyone in his new, initially unfavorable environment, and he does everything in his power to fulfill his dream. Soon, and by performing illegal drug practices that he manages to get through all his psychologists, he becomes the most popular boy in high school, being a kind of therapist for his peers. What he doesn't know is that his innocent advice and dangerous prescriptions would change the lives of his colleagues, the director (Robert Downey Jr.) and even his own.
option_1_text:
Detective Philip Marlowe searches for compromising photos of Carmen, General Sternwood's youngest daughter, and soon falls in love with her sister, Vivian. Carmen seems to be the victim of blackmail while Vivian is mixed up with the local thugs. Marlowe will have to solve the case in the midst of thugs, killers and vampires.
The complex plot divides the film into two parts. In the first Marlowe searches for and finds the murderer of A. G. Geiger; in the second he discovers the reason why Vivian is being manipulated.
option_2_text:
A virus has spread around the world, turning those infected into a kind of zombie - they're just called "infected".
Young Ann, her husband, Jason, and their infant child drive to a rural, wooded area. That's where Jason grew up, knows the area well, and believes it's the safest place for both of them. He also teaches his wife some skills needed to survive in the wild, such as how to handle a rifle.
Since they cannot obtain sufficient food by gathering berries and mushrooms, they also rely on setting animal traps. They also visit nearby abandoned houses to collect leftover food. This is risky, however, since there are often infected people roaming around. However, over time, they discover that the infected react primarily to body odor and blood, and it's possible to fool them, for example, by covering oneself with mud.
Jason is eventually attacked and killed by one of the infected while trying to search for supplies. However, by accident, the blood of an infected person on her coat enters the child's mouth, where Ann eventually finds conspicuous circular rashes on the skin - a sure sign of infection. Knowing that there is no hope of a cure, she finally kills the child.
From now on, she fights alone for her survival. The car with the gas in it is just using it as a shelter from the rain. One day, as she wanders around, she encounters two figures on a street: young Olivia and her stepfather Chris, who is injured but not infected. She decides to take them to her camp. Chris is recovering quickly, and both are grateful for the help, which in these times is no longer taken for granted. They're coming from the south, and they're trying to push their way north. Unlike Ann, who has a fixed camp, Chris believes that staying in one place permanently is deadly. That's why they want to move again soon.
Ann and Chris are finally getting closer, sleeping together. Olivia, who has developed feelings for her stepfather and is now jealous, then attacks Ann at a shared food gathering in an abandoned house, tying her up and luring the infected. Back at the camp, she tells Chris that Ann didn't make it. However, she manages to break free and finds Chris and Olivia in the camp being attacked by infected people. With the rifle, she can fend them off, but she can't stop Chris from dying.
The end of the film shows Ann and Olivia sitting in the car together and driving on.
option_3_text:
Johnny Eager (Robert Taylor) masquerades as a taxi driver for his gullible parole officer, A. J. Verne (Henry O'Neill), but in reality, he is the ruthless head of a powerful gambling syndicate. Verne introduces him to socialite Lisbeth "Liz" Bard (Lana Turner), a sociology student. Johnny and Liz are attracted to each other, but then he discovers that she is the stepdaughter of his longtime nemesis, John Benson Farrell (Edward Arnold). As a crusading prosecutor, Farrell was responsible for sending Johnny to prison, and now as the district attorney, he has gotten an injunction preventing Johnny's expensive dog racing track from opening.
Johnny decides to use Liz as leverage against her stepfather. When she comes to see him, he has Julio (Paul Stewart), one of his underlings, burst in and pretend to try to kill him. During the faked struggle, Julio drops his gun. Lisbeth picks it up and shoots Julio when he seems to have the upper hand. Johnny then hustles her out of the room before she can realize that the gun is full of blanks and Julio's blood is actually ketchup. Later, Johnny threatens to expose her as a murderer unless Farrell removes the injunction. Farrell gives in.
Johnny is depicted as a man without a conscience. When childhood friend Lew Rankin (Barry Nelson) gets fed up with his subordinate role in the gang and starts plotting against him, Johnny murders him without the slightest qualm. He lies to his devoted girlfriend Garnet (Patricia Dane) to get her to go to Florida while he romances Liz. Mae (Glenda Farrell), a prior girlfriend, asks him to help get her incorruptible policeman husband transferred back to his old precinct because his long commute is straining their marriage. Johnny not only lies, claiming he no longer has any influence, he also hides the fact that he got the man transferred in the first place because he would not look the other way. When Jimmy Courtney (Robert Sterling), Liz's high society former boyfriend, becomes alarmed because Liz is going to pieces due to a guilty conscience, he offers Johnny all his money to leave the country and take Liz with him. Johnny cannot figure out his "angle", why he would do such a selfless thing. In fact, the only soft spot Johnny seems to have is for his intellectual, alcoholic right-hand man, Jeff Hartnett (Van Heflin), and even he is not sure why. Jeff has an insight, telling his boss that "even Johnny Eager has to have one friend."
However, when Johnny learns that Liz intends to turn herself in, he discovers the meaning of love for the first time in his life. He confesses to her that he staged the whole incident, but she does not believe him. To prove his claim, he decides to produce a live Julio, but Julio has defected to Johnny's dissatisfied partner, Bill Halligan (Cy Kendall). Johnny manages to bring Julio (at gunpoint) to Liz, but in the process he shoves Johnny and runs away. Johnny forces Liz and Courtney to flee to safety before the gunfight with Halligan and his men. Eager kills Halligan and Julio, but is spotted by a policeman as he attempts to flee and is shot down. Jeff arrives and embraces Johnny as he finally dies.
The policeman, in a twist of fate, turns out to be Mae's husband.
option_4_text:
Divorced American Harvey Shine writes television commercial jingles, despite being a jazz pianist and composer. As he departs for his daughter Susan's wedding in London his job is tenuous. Upon arrival at Heathrow, he encounters single Londoner Kate Walker who collects statistics from passengers as they pass through the terminals. Harvey brusquely dismisses her, as he is anxious to get to his hotel.
At the hotel, Harvey finds he is the only wedding guest booked there, as the house his ex-wife Jean rented is for all the US guests—except him. At the rehearsal dinner, Harvey is clearly an outsider to his daughter's life and excluded from Jean's new husband Brian's clan. Their insincere politeness makes him uncomfortable.
Harvey tells Susan he can attend the ceremony but not the reception, as he has to urgently return to the States. She replies that, as Brian has been more of a father to her recently than he, she prefers that Brian walk her down the aisle.
Meanwhile, Kate is on an unsuccessful blind date. After a call from her neurotic mother Maggie, she returns to the table to find her date has invited some of his friends to join them. Feeling excluded, she goes home.
The next morning, Harvey is slighted when he is seated at the back of the church rather than near his daughter. He leaves immediately after the ceremony for the airport, but heavy London traffic causes him to miss his flight. Calling his boss about the delay, he is fired. Drinking in the airport bar, he recognizes Kate from the day before. He apologizes for his rude behavior, and she initially resists his attention. Soon they are both glad to finally have an honest, genuine conversation.
Harvey does not want to stay in an airport hotel, so he follows Kate, joining her on the train to Paddington station. He walks with her to her writing class on the South Bank. Kate is pleased when he meets her afterwards. As they stroll along the River Thames, Harvey mentions he is missing the wedding reception, and Kate urges him to go.
Harvey relents, but only if Kate accompanies him. Insisting she is not properly dressed, Harvey buys her a dress. At the Grosvenor House Hotel, they are welcomed by Susan and placed at the children's table, the only seats still available. When the 'father of the bride' is called to make a toast, Brian starts to speak, but Harvey interrupts, as he is her biological father. His touching, eloquent speech redeems him with Susan and endears him to Kate.
After the couple's first dance as husband and wife, the groom calls Harvey to dance with Susan. He happily does so; then everyone joins them on the dance floor. As Harvey is enjoying himself, Kate is left alone at the children's table. Feeling out of place and seemingly forgotten, Kate quietly leaves, but Harvey realizes she has gone.
Harvey sees her at the elevator, then ducks into a nearby room and begins to softly play jazz. Hearing the music, Kate finds Harvey smiling and waiting for her. He asks her to return to the reception so he can "dance her socks off". She agrees and they have a great time.
Afterwards, they walk and talk through London until dawn. On parting they exchange a single, gentle kiss, agreeing to meet at noon that day. Back at his hotel, Harvey has serious heart palpitations after faulty lifts force him to use the stairs. In hospital, he is forced to stay for treatment and misses the appointment with Kate, who turns up and waits for him.
When Harvey is discharged the next day, his boss calls and asks him to return immediately, as they've been unable to handle an important account without him. He declines, preferring to stay and try to make amends with Kate.
He calls Kate at work to explain, but she refuses to take the call. He goes looking for her at the airport and finally tracks her down at her writing class. Explaining why he missed their rendezvous, he says he wants them to pursue a relationship. Fearing emotional pain, she resists, but finally agrees to try.
As they stroll along the South Bank, Harvey suggests she ask him the questions she originally had for him at the airport. When she asks him for his place of residence, he says it is "in transition".

France at the end of the 19th century. At the Larnay Institute, the nuns take care of some deaf girls who have been placed in their care. Among the nuns is Sister Marguerite, who suffers from lung disease, but who has so far been entrusted mainly with the work in the monastery garden.
A man drives his cart through the yard. Next to him is a young girl, tied to the carriage goat for her own safety, but apparently happy. Her hair is unkempt, she is barefoot, and she wears a dirty long-sleeved shirt instead of a dress. A closer look reveals that, unlike the other girls, she is not only deaf but even deaf-blind. The husband, her father, turns to the Mother Superior and explains that although his daughter is in desperate need of care, he does not want to send her to an insane asylum, as advised by a doctor.
Marie, unable to comprehend what should happen to her, takes refuge in the branches of a tree. Sister Marguerite tries to calm her down and get her down from the tree. In the process, she has strong feelings, about which her diary later reports: "Today I met a soul... " Finally, the Mother Superior tells the girl's father that her admission to the convent is out of the question, due to her double disability and obvious lack of social competence. Monsieur Martin has to take Marie back home.
Sister Marguerite, however, is outraged at the Superior for allowing her to take Marie back and try to teach her. After some back-and-forth, the Prioress finally relents, and Sister Marguerite sets off on foot. She also returns with Marie (on a short wrist strap) largely on foot. She notices on her walk that Marie reacts in a positive way particularly strongly to touch stimuli such as the warm fur on a cow or to phenomena such as the fast flowing water of a stream. Marie shows that she seeks to evaluate and judge other people through touch, such as sensitively touching their faces. And it makes it very clear that there is a chance to gain access to it. For the last part of the arduous journey, she pushes Marie in a wheelbarrow.
Mary's upbringing turns out to be a months-long, exhausting, and at times seemingly brutal struggle. It's practically impossible to get laid in a dorm room with the other girls. After all, Sister Marguerite manages to bathe her, put her in a dress, stockings, and shoes, and comb her hair and tie it into a braid. However, Marie continues to refuse to participate in the study. Sister Marguerite often doubts herself and turns to her diary in these situations, but she never gives up. Once again on the verge of despair, Marie makes her first usable gesture: a knife.
After some time, Mary's parents come to visit and meet their daughter in the presence of Sister Marguerite. They can hardly believe what they're seeing. Marie speaks to them in sign language and Sister Marguerite translates. Marie can even make her name out of wooden letters. Her parents are very touched.
Marguerite's lung disease is rapidly manifesting with a severe bout of weakness. Marguerite is advised that the only way out is quiet and mountain air. The Superior thinks she can spare Marie by concealing from her the absence and stay of Marguerite in a clinic in the mountains. This leads to a bad relapse. One cannot help but inform Marguerite, who immediately cancels her stay in the clinic. Marie is calming down. Sister Marguerite is now suffering a breakdown of her own. She doesn't recover from it, but gradually deteriorates more and more.
Marguerite doesn't want Marie to see her like this, so she locks her out of her room. Once again, Marie has a relapse, behaves like a lunatic, bangs on the door. Marguerite's good friend, the deaf sister Raphaëlle herself, who had previously mediated with setbacks, vainly persuades her to let Marie back into her life. Only the Prioress - previously sceptical and at times making Marguerite's work difficult - is able to change her mind by revealing her own rebellion against dying as the true motive. From then on, Marie lovingly helped with Marguerite's care. She understands that Marguerite must die and there will be no rescue, but she at least wants to accompany her on her final journey. Even after Sister Marguerite's death, Marie shows herself to be more mature. Sister Marguerite's unwavering commitment is crowned by Marie's arrival in life.

Scientists discover that a violent storm is heading toward New York City and begin the warning process throughout the city. They believe that something is wrong with the natural barometer patterns and that an unprecedented event is imminent. A sudden eclipse of the sun verifies their speculations, and it seems that global destruction is near. Telegraph messages from Rome and London explain days of unending earthquakes and state "The End of the World is at Hand". Tremendous earthquakes hit the Pacific Coast, killing millions, and it is reported that the entire west coast of the U.S. has been destroyed. The earthquakes have also caused major tsunamis in the world's oceans and disaster is just moments away.
Martin Webster and his wife Helen prepare for the oncoming disaster by gathering their children and some essentials and head for a high rock formation to escape the floods. Martin leaves Helen and goes back to the house to get more food and clothes, but the destruction of New York begins. Buildings crumble from earthquakes and large tsunami waters envelop the city. Martin returns to find his wife and daughters are nowhere to be found. In the aftermath, grief-stricken Martin builds a shelter and tries to survive on his own.
Surviving in a cabin on the outskirts of in another part of the New York City, two men, Jepson and Norwood, find Claire unconscious, washed up on the shore outside their cabin. As she recovers, the men start feuding  and become very possessive. When she is attacked, Claire flees across the water (she is a world-class swimmer), leaving the men angry and vengeful. Jepson kills Norwood and begins to search for her, vowing to bring her back.
Claire washes up on another shore, where Martin finds her. Martin and Claire become good friends and eventually fall in love. Meanwhile, in a nearby town, survivors have gathered together to start civilization again. Among the survivors is Martin's wife, Helen, and their two children. Tom, one of the townsmen, found Helen in the aftermath, and has been taking care of her ever since. He has also fallen in love with her, but Helen is convinced that her husband is still alive.
Jepson teams up with the Bellamy gang, who eventually find Claire and Martin, and trap them in a tunnel. The townspeople stumble upon this situation and save Martin and Claire and bring them back to their new city. Once they arrive, Martin finds his children and discovers that his wife is alive and well and goes to her. As a result, Claire and Tom are devastated.

Tarzan and Jane live in the jungle, along with their chimpanzee Cheeta. Harry Holt and his business partner Martin Arlington, leading a large party of locals, meet them on their way to take ivory from an elephant burial ground. Holt had visited the burial ground with Tarzan on an earlier trip, during which he had also met Jane. Holt had sought Tarzan out, as he was the only one who knew the way to the burial ground. On this trip, Holt tries to convince Jane to return with him to civilization by bringing her gifts such as clothing and modern gadgets. Jane tells him she would rather stay with Tarzan. She does agree to convince Tarzan to act as their guide.
When Tarzan calls an elephant, Arlington gets the idea that they can use elephants as pack animals, enabling them to haul much more ivory. When Jane tries to convince Tarzan to call more elephants, she explains to him about hauling the ivory away. Tarzan, thinking that taking the ivory is profaning the burial ground, refuses. In addition, he refuses to even lead them to the burial ground, now that he knows of their intent. Arlington and Holt have everything they own tied up in this venture and are frantic to continue on. Arlington asks Holt how they found the burial ground the first time, and Holt explains that they had followed a dying elephant. Seizing on that idea, Arlington shoots an elephant, mortally wounding it so that it will lead them to the burial ground.  Only Jane's intervention keeps Tarzan from murdering Arlington.
After being abandoned by Tarzan and Jane, Arlington and Holt lead their baggage carriers, led by Saidi, a friend of Jane and Tarzan's, to the burial ground, following the wounded elephant. Elephants, aware of the impending disgrace of their sacred ground, turn up in the hundreds, and threaten to exterminate Holt and Arlington's party. Tarzan and Jane arrive in time to save them, after which Arlington feigns repentance, promising to leave the next day without the ivory. Satisfied, Tarzan agrees to guide their departure, and sends the elephants away.
Early the next morning, Arlington ambushes Tarzan, shooting him out of a tree. Tarzan falls into the water, and Arlington thinks he has killed him. After Arlington leaves, a hippopotamus rescues a semi-conscious Tarzan and carries him to a group of chimpanzees, which tend to him. Tarzan has received a head wound, but the bullet only grazed him, though it has left him very weak. The head chimpanzee applies plant sap to staunch the bleeding.
Arlington returns to the group, claiming that he saw Tarzan being killed by an alligator. A distraught Jane agrees to return to civilization. Arlington and Holt have their baggage carriers each take a tusk from the burial ground, and they begin to head back. Cheeta leaves Jane and looks for Tarzan. Chased by a lion, Cheeta escapes and comes upon the chimpanzee group tending to Tarzan.
As Tarzan recuperates, the safari makes its way through the jungle. Cheeta returns and lets Jane know that Tarzan is alive. However, shortly after the safari is confronted by a hostile tribe of "lion men", who kill two of the bearers and intend to kill the entire safari. Under cover of gunfire, most of the safari makes it to some nearby caves, set into the face of a rocky cliff. The bearer who was carrying the ammunition crate is killed on the way. When Saidi makes an attempt to retrieve the crate, he is captured by the lion men. Cheeta escapes and runs off to tell Tarzan.
The safari watch in horror the next morning as Saidi is staked out to a tree, as the lion men intend to use him as bait to call lions to attack the safari. When Holt rushes out to save him, he is wounded by a thrown spear. Wounded, he begins to free Saidi when the lions show up and tear him and Saidi to pieces. Meanwhile, Cheeta has returned to Tarzan, who while still weak, sets off after Cheeta.
The lions attempt to get at the safari, but are held off by Jane and Arlington and one of the bearers. When the bearer goes down on a ledge, Arlington goes out to save him, and he is attacked by a lion. Arlington is killed, but Jane kills the charging lion. As the lions become more aggressive, Tarzan and the chimpanzees arrive. The chimpanzees begin to throw the lion men out of the trees, where they are set upon by the lions. Jane kills two lions before she runs out of ammunition. As she is about to be attacked by the last lion, Tarzan arrives and kills it with his knife. Shortly after, a large herd of elephants arrives, trampling the lions, killing several and running the remainder off.
With the lion men and the lions routed, the elephants, along with Tarzan, Jane, and Cheeta, return the ivory to the burial ground.

In Germany, American convict Laura (Karen Morley) is released from prison because she is pregnant.  Before leaving, she assures her boyfriend and fellow American convict Nicky (Ricardo Cortez), who does not know of her pregnancy, that they will reunite when he gets out.  Meanwhile, the German wrestler Polakai (Wallace Beery) has just won another bout in a string of victories on his way to a national championship, but he works for income at a local beer hall, hoisting large beer barrels on his shoulders to both entertain and serve the customers.
Laura arrives and orders a large meal but is unable to pay.  When Mr. Herman, the beer hall's owner (Jean Hersholt), is about to call the police, Polakai offers to pay for the meal himself.  Later that evening with nowhere to go, Laura accepts Polakai's offer to stay in his small apartment, which is also owned by Herman and his wife (Greta Meyer).  The stay turns out to be a lengthy one.  It is implied that Polakai and Laura sleep together, but even though he proposes to her several times, she turns him down.  Though she is touched by Polakai's simple but generous nature, Laura is still in love with Nick.  When Polakai catches her stealing his money to obtain Nick's release,  Laura confesses but claims that Nick is her brother.  Once again, the gullible wrestler comes to her aid.
Nick arrives and plays along with the ruse that he's Laura's brother.  When he learns that Laura is pregnant, though, he takes money that Polakai has given him and immediately heads back to America.  With Nick gone, Laura finally assents to Polakai's proposal and reveals her pregnancy, leaving him to believe that he will be the father.  On the night that the child is born, Polakai wins the German wrestling championship.  Laura still pines for Nick despite his having left her, but Polakai thinks that she's homesick for America.  The Hermans have already emigrated to the U.S., and Polakai decides that he and Laura should follow them, hoping that he can win a world wrestling championship there.
In America, Polakai and Laura are reunited with Nick, whom Laura has forgiven and who offers to be Polakai's manager, although he is actually in league with Willard (John Miljan), a crooked promoter. As Polakai learns how his matches are being rigged, he begins to drink.  Laura tries to sober him up and get him to win his championship match, which he is supposed to lose, but Nick begins to beat her.  Polakai, coming to, strangles Nick.  He goes on to the wrestling match anyway, which he wins, only to be arrested.  In the aftermath, the district attorney seems willing to go light on Polakai, and Laura promises to go away so that she will not hurt him anymore.  Polakai, however, holds her hand.

Cee, a teenage girl, and her father Damon descend in a land capsule from a transport spacecraft to the surface of a forest moon covered in poisonous spores to search for gemstones. During the descent, a technical malfunction disables the lander, and the two land some distance from their planned mining area. The duo make their way there on foot and stumble upon an abandoned excavation site. Damon and Cee retrieve a fleshy shell from the earth and dissect it to reveal a precious gem. Cee pleads with her father to take the gem and return to the lander, but Damon insists that they return to the original landing site.
The two set off again, and Damon is approached by Ezra and his companion, two rival Seekers. They plan to rob him, but Damon suggests they team up. Damon explains that he was contacted to help a group of mercenaries who stumbled upon the legendary "Queen's Cave", an excavation site of extraordinary value. Damon suggests that Ezra, his companion, and Damon work together and claim the entire excavation site for themselves instead of digging for the mercenaries.
Ezra agrees, but Cee, who has been in hiding for the entire encounter, ambushes the two enemy seekers with a rifle and allows Damon to snatch Ezra's weapon before taking him and his partner hostage. Damon tries to rob Ezra, but his partner attacks him, and the two shoot each other. Ezra's partner is killed and Damon is mortally wounded before being executed by Ezra himself.
Cee flees back to her damaged lander, which no longer takes off, and is found a few hours later by Ezra. When Ezra tries to enter, Cee wounds him in the arm with her rifle and takes him prisoner. Ezra suggests that they follow Damon's original plan and help the mercenaries in exchange for a crossing on the mercenary ship. Cee reluctantly agrees, and the two make their way to the Queen's hideout. Ezra's wound has become infected by the poisonous spores in the atmosphere, so the two approach a group of human villagers with the intention of trading medical treatment. Instead, the villagers offer a trade in gems in exchange for Cee. When Ezra asks for the details of the offer, Cee flees the village, escaping persecution by the villagers.
After wandering the planet alone, Cee meets Ezra again. His wound has worsened considerably, and Cee is helping him amputate his arm. The two set off again and soon reach the mercenary camp that surrounds the queen's hiding place. After negotiating a passage on the mercenary ship, Cee and Ezra attempt to fulfill their part of the contract and retrieve gems from the Queen's cave. Several extraction attempts fail, and when their mercenary guard turns around to report their failure, Ezra attacks him and kills him. The riot attracts the rest of the mercenaries, and a fight ensues. Several mercenaries are killed, and Ezra is badly wounded. Cee tends to Ezra's wound, and the two escape with the mercenary's ship into orbit.

In 1885, Marie Heurtin, the daughter of a humble artisan and his wife, is born deaf and blind and unable to communicate with the world around her. Desperate to find a connection with Marie and avoid sending her to an asylum, the Heurtins send her to the Larnay Institute in central France, where an order of Catholic nuns manage a school for deaf girls. There, the idealistic Sister Marguerite sees in Marie a unique potential and, despite her Mother Superior's skepticism, vows to bring the wild girl out of the darkness into which she was born.
# Background
Marie's Story is based on the true story of Marie Heurtin, who continued her education at the institute and lived there until her death at the age of 36.

When Limpinski tries to goad Marc about his relationship with Kay, Marc taunts him, leading Limpinski to assault him. Frank witnesses this and implies that Limpinski will be let go for this. Marc, unhappy, visits the gay bar alone, and though he seeks a sexual encounter with another man, he ends up rebuffing him. Back at the house, Marc and Bettina admit to each other that they can't see their relationship going on as before. The film concludes with Marc at the academy, on a jog with his peers as in the first scene of the film; he outpaces them and runs ahead, alone.

query_text: Johnny (Jane Birkin), a waitress at a truck bar in the middle of nowhere, leads a lonely and bored life. She falls in love with a dump truck driver, Krassky (Joe Dallesandro), despite warnings from her boss Boris (Reinhard Kolldehoff), who tells her that he is gay. Due to the young woman's androgynous appearance, Krassky is nevertheless also attracted to her. However, their romance is thwarted by the jealousy of Krassky's boyfriend, Padovan (Hugues Quester).

Sports reporter Jimmy Jones aspires to become a well-known crime reporter. While writing a story about a women's softball team, he discovers that the team's sponsor is a former gangster named Foy Harris, who pretends to want to put his criminal past behind him. Jimmy, however, is convinced that Harris still has dirt on him. As a result, he decides to take a closer look at him and the softball team. At the same time, he takes the opportunity to cast an eye on the beautiful player Ann Casey.

option_3_text: Overpowering a nurse and dressing in her clothes, a madman escapes from the Casa de la Loco Sanitarium. The Thief then goes on a crime spree that nets him a gun, a car, a fortune in stolen cash, and one dead loan office manager. As he escapes the murder scene, he comes upon a forbidden cemetery just as a burial is taking place, replete with bagpipe music and a bizarre ceremony employing tuning forks and strange icons. As the undertaker, the caretaker, and an odd assortment of mourners leave the service, The Thief peers into the coffin, thinking it is a good place to hide his briefcase full of ill-gotten gains. As he strikes the tuning fork that is buried with the robe-draped skeleton, bagpipe music fills the air and throws him into convulsions. The coffin lid slams shut, locking his money inside, and The Thief is thrown into an open grave, knocking himself unconscious. When he awakens, he sets off to track down everyone who had been present at the funeral in an attempt to find his missing cash, killing anyone who gets in his way.
option_4_text:
The clan of cowboys from the McQuown ranch is terrorizing the village of Warlock. After the cowboys drive out the sheriff, a citizen's committee decides to hire a prefect, a killer, who will be contracted to rid the city of the cowboys. One man, Clay Blaisedell, has made a name for himself in this field, receiving a pair of gold-backed pistols as gifts from admirers. He accepts the offer on the condition that he be accompanied by Tom Morgan, another gun ace.
Disgusted by the killings, Johnny Gannon leaves the McQuown gang and accepts the position of deputy sheriff with one goal, to enforce the law against any violence, whether it comes from the cowboy gang, or Blaisedell and Morgan.

option_2_text:
Alvaro Cosenza is a young partisan immigrant from the south, who, in Rome occupied by the Germans, takes up arms against them but, after the liberation, together with the members of his gang begins a series of illegal activities that give him the reputation of a dangerous bandit.
His main enemy during fascism is Commissioner Moretti, Nina's father, the woman he discovered to love after raping her and impregnating the official; he is then killed by Alvaro after the Commissioner, discovering the violence suffered by his daughter, tried to have him killed by his own comrades, establishing a collaboration with him.
Nina, discovered Alvaro's action, first aborted and then, left alone after the death of her father, is linked to Leandro, a former partisan, remained monk following the beating suffered by Moretti, who starts her in a prostitution activity but, after having met Alvaro again, discovers that she still loves him.
option_3_text: Four different women leave their rainy, gray surroundings to go on vacation to Italy. Mrs. Arbuthnot and Mrs. Wilkins, who belong to the same ladies' club but have never spoken, meet after reading an advertisement in the newspaper for a small medieval castle on the shores of the Mediterranean to be rented furnished for the month of April. They find some common ground as they both struggle to rescue their unhappy marriage. Having decided to look for other ladies to help share the expenses, they are reluctantly confronted by the elegant but annoying old Mrs. Fisher, and the impressive, distant and very wealthy Lady Caroline Dester. The four women meet at the castle and, after many unexpected twists and turns, find rejuvenation in the quiet beauty of their surroundings, rediscovering hope and love.
option_4_text:
Simon, a musician and punk rocker, not only takes drugs but also deals in them. Because the money still isn't enough, he donates his body to drug research. As a participant in a study, he should be compensated.
His drug dealings are just one of many reasons why the local police are looking for him. Simon narrowly escapes the cops, thanks in part to the intervention of Patty, an employee at a pet store. The young woman seems awkward in many ways. She invites Simon to her home, unimpressed by his strange hairstyle. Simon hides out in this suburb of Detroit until he realizes that Patty is a big fan of his alter ego John Q. Public, the masked and anonymous lead singer of the punk quartet Psyops.

query_text:
New York in the late 1950s. To escape the hustle and bustle of inner-city life, people head to the Coney Island amusement park off the coast of Brooklyn, where there is a Ferris wheel, carousels, and a swimming beach where Mickey Rubin looks to the right as a lifeguard. Humpty, who operates a merry-go-round, also makes a living with pleasure seekers. His wife, Ginny, works as a waitress at a nearby clam house, where clam dishes are served. She's got a little boy who's always lighting fires.
One day, the couple receives an unexpected visit from Humpty's daughter, with whom they haven't spoken in years. Carolina had married a gangster against her father's wishes, but broke up with him again and testified to the FBI. Now she's completely destitute, on the run from his people.
Mickey's studying literature and wants to write plays later. He and Ginny are having an affair, and Ginny is hoping for a better life with him, where she can resume her career as an actress. But also Carolina  watched jealously by Ginny  arouses Mickey's interest.
One night, Carolina and Mickey meet at a pizzeria. The gangsters are looking for Carolina again, and Ginny goes to the phone to warn Carolina. When she gets the restaurant on the line, she hangs up. At the restaurant, Mickey confesses his love for Carolina. The two of them say goodbye in front of the restaurant and you can see that the black limousine follows the gangster Carolina.
The next morning, Humpty asks Mickey if Carolina stayed with him. Mickey answers truthfully that they broke up in front of the restaurant. Mickey begins to investigate and then asks Ginny why she hung up on her call at the restaurant without warning Carolina. Ginny's been drinking and pretending not to understand. Mickey's leaving her.
Humpty's drinking again, too, because he's having a hard time dealing with the loss of his daughter. He begs Ginny not to leave him. They're both facing the wreckage of their lives.
option_0_text: Jenna works as a waitress at Joe's Diner, where she makes beautiful desserts with bizarre names. But Jenna's life isn't as sweet as the cakes she cooks, in fact she lives a gray, monotonous existence with her husband Earl, a manly, vulgar man. But Jenna's life takes a turn when she finds out she's unexpectedly pregnant, but doesn't know whether to be happy with who the father is, plus she falls in love with her charming, neurotic gynecologist, who has only one tiny "problem", he's married. In her own way, Jenna will be able to change her life and make a breakthrough that will finally see her fulfilled, happy and serene.
option_1_text:
Nejat Aksu, the son of Turkish immigrants, is a lecturer in German literature at the University of Hamburg. His father Ali, who lives in Bremen, was widowed when he was only six months old and therefore had to provide for his upbringing on his own. Now elderly, to fill his loneliness, he proposes to Yeter, a mature Kurdish prostitute, of whom he has been a "regular" client for several years, to go live with him.
One evening, Ali invites his son to dinner and introduces him to his new companion but, a few hours later, perhaps as a result of the abundant meal consumed, he is struck by a heart attack and has to be hospitalized in an intensive care unit. Returning home and still convalescing, in the grip of alcohol and jealousy over an unfounded suspicion of betrayal on the part of Yeter, he violently strikes the woman, involuntarily causing her death.
Nejat then decides to disown his father, who was sentenced to a prison term, and to go to Turkey. Nejat is searching for his origins but is also taken by a kind of guilt towards the murdered woman who, before dying, had confided to him that she had a twenty-seven-year-old daughter in Istanbul, whom she provided for her studies, but without ever revealing her activity. The young professor sets out to find this girl, Ayten Öztürk, who has not been heard from for months: asking for help from her Turkish relatives, printing leaflets and asking for information from the police, but he gets no results.
At the same time, Nejat matures the decision to stay permanently in Istanbul where he acquires a bookstore run by a German who wishes to return to Germany, thus giving up his chair in Hamburg and devoting himself passionately to the new activity.
In parallel we see the life of Ayten Öztürk, a student politically engaged in a clandestine organization that opposes the Turkish regime. Following his involvement in an episode of violence during a street demonstration, Ayten escapes from Turkey with a fake passport and travels to Hamburg, Germany, in search of his mother who he believes is employed as a clerk in a shoe store. Her fate touches that of Nejat when, exhausted from sleep, Ayten falls asleep in the classroom where he is giving a lecture. In a university cafeteria, Ayten meets Lotte, a language student, whom he asks for help and money. Susanne, Lotte's mother, tries to dissuade her daughter from offering hospitality to an illegal immigrant and advises Ayten to come out and ask for political asylum from the German government, but the two girls soon develop a romantic relationship.
After a quarrel between Susanne and Ayten, the two girls leave for Bremen to look for Ayten's mother but during the journey they are stopped by the police and Ayten is detained as "irregular". The German government refuses her request for political asylum and sends her back to Turkey, where she is forced to serve time in a women's prison. Despite an animated argument with her mother, Lotte decides to reach her companion in order to help, support and eventually try to free her. The case leads her to Nejat's bookstore where, in leaving a notice for the search for accommodation, she hears Nejat himself propose the rental of a room in his apartment. Lotte manages to visit Ayten, who is still in prison, and she reveals to her partner the hiding place of the gun used for the attack in the square that cost her and her group the prison. But a few hours after recovering the weapon, following a trivial pickpocketing by some kids, Lotte is killed in an alley.
Informed of her daughter's sudden death, Susanne travels to Turkey to try to reconstruct the last hours of Lotte's life and retrieve her personal belongings from Nejat's home. She also visits Ayten in prison and offers her forgiveness and help: Ayten, defying the contempt of her fellow fighters, decides to cooperate with justice and negotiate her release.
Meanwhile, the old Ali, expelled from Germany, returns to Turkey, settling near Trebizond where he intends to spend the last years of his life. The news reaches Nejat, who decides to entrust the management of the library to Susanne for a few days so that she can drive to Trebizond and finally reconcile with her father.
option_2_text:
It was the '50s, Coney Island. Ginny is a thirty-nine-year-old former actress who works as a waitress at a modest restaurant, located in a playground near the coast. She has a difficult relationship with both her husband Humpty, who becomes violent when he drinks, and her son from her first marriage, who is a pyromaniac. She is also frustrated by a life without prospects and by the memory of the failure of her first marriage, for which she feels guilty. She becomes infatuated with Mickey, a younger lifeguard who aspires to be a playwright. Their relationship is disturbed by Humpty's daughter, Carolina, whom Mickey casually meets: orphaned by her mother, the young woman, on the run from a failed marriage to a gangster, knows many of her husband's secrets, and in order to escape his henchmen, decides to hide from her father, who had disowned her for years. Humpty is initially furious to have her back home, but later reconciles with her and begins to spoil her, even at the expense of caring for his wife and stepson.
After receiving a visit from two of the boss' men, the father initially warns of danger. Ginny is furious at Carolina's presence because, after learning of Mickey's attraction to the girl, she became jealous. Mickey, wracked with remorse, decides to break up with Ginny, but without telling her the whole truth, just as she gives him a watch for his birthday, stealing Humpty's savings. Disappointed, Ginny drinks again and drags Humpty back with her.
Mickey invites Carolina to dinner, who announces the news to the family as well. Ginny, who initially wants to chase after her to catch her in the act, notices on the street the presence of the same two henchmen, who have found Carolina and know where she will go to dinner. Alarmed, she calls the pizzeria, but at the last moment she hangs up the receiver, effectively handing her stepdaughter over to her tormentors. After dinner with Mickey, Carolina walks away on her own while the two hit men chase after her. The next day, all trace of her will be lost. The next day again Mickey reveals to Ginny that he has eaten the leaf, providing overwhelming evidence for something else rather easy to spot and goes to visit her at home to find her drunk in a stage dress. Mickey before leaving her forever openly accuses her, while she loses herself in theatrical quotes, without confessing but not even denying the accusations. Meanwhile, Humpty returns home, desperate for his daughter's futile searches, and aware of the tragic end he risks encountering, asks Ginny to start over, but Ginny prefers to continue with her unhappy and erratic lifestyle.
option_3_text:
British sound engineer Gilderoy (Toby Jones) arrives at the Berber film studio in Italy to work on what he believes is a film about horses. During a surreal meeting with Francesco (Cosimo Fusco), the film's producer, Gilderoy is surprised to discover that the film is actually an Italian giallo film, titled The Equestrian Vortex.[3] Thus, he begins working in the studio doing the room effect, using vegetables to create sound effects for the torture sequences, which are increasingly bloody in the film, and mixing the voices of Silvia (Fatma Mohamed) and Claudia (Eugenia Caruso), the film's lead actresses.
As time passes, Gilderoy begins to miss his mother, whom he left home alone in the UK. His colleagues begin to be increasingly rude, and the horror sequences become even more shocking, but Santini (Antonio Mancino), the director, refuses to admit that they are working on a horror film. After a long and bureaucratic process that Gilderoy had to go through for the studio to reimburse him for his plane ticket with which he arrived in Italy, it finally could not be done because it did not exist.
The plot, from here on, becomes increasingly erratic. Gilderoy hears and sees things at night. He discovers that Silvia, the voice actress, was harassed by Santini. She runs away, destroying much of his work, forcing Gilderoy to re-record the dialogue with a new actress, Elisa (Chiara D'Anna). As Silvia's recording sequences are revisited, and tension grows between Gilderoy and the others, the boundaries between the blood-soaked yellow thriller and real life begin to blur. Gilderoy imagines himself in a movie about his life. Suddenly, he's fluent in Italian and increasingly distant and vicious. After he and Francesco torture Elisa during a recording session, she leaves, letting history repeat itself once more, and Gilderoy ends up contemplating the monster he has become.
option_4_text:
In 1988, Danny Maccabee, a 22-year-old man, leaves his marriage shortly before the ceremony begins, after discovering that his fiancée is cheating on him and that she only wanted to marry him because he would become a cardiologist; he goes for a drink at a bar, where he meets a woman who notices Danny's wedding ring and asks him about his wife, he explains to her how he recently left her for another, and the woman at the bar ends up sleeping with him. This scenario is repeated even in later years, and the technique of using faith will be constantly centered on Danny.
Twenty-three years later, Danny is a successful plastic surgeon in Los Angeles who invents stories of unhappy marriages to seduce women and avoid romantic commitments. The only one who knows of his plans is his assistant and best friend Katherine Murphy, a divorced mother of two. At a party, Danny meets Palmer, a young math teacher, with no wedding ring on, and they spend the night together. The next morning, Palmer finds the ring assuming Danny is married and refuses to continue dating him because his parents have divorced due to an adultery.
Instead of telling her the truth, Danny tells her he's divorcing a woman named Devlin because she cheated on him with a man named "Dolph Lundgren". When Palmer insists on meeting Devlin, Danny asks Katherine to pretend to be "Devlin". Katherine then meets Danny and Palmer and gives them her blessing. However, after overhearing Katherine talking to her children on the phone, Palmer believes they are also Danny's. Danny then meets Katherine's children, Maggie and Michael, to convince them to stay in the game and gives them the pseudonyms of "Kiki Dee" and "Bart" respectively. When Palmer meets the kids, Michael blackmails Danny in front of Palmer to take them all to Hawaii.
At the airport, Danny's cousin Eddie shows up, pretending to be Dolph Lundgren by adopting a disguise and an Austrian accent, and to avoid being discovered by Palmer, Danny and Katherine are forced to take him with them.
At the hotel in Hawaii, Danny tells Eddie that he's thinking of asking Palmer to marry him. Katherine and Danny also run into Devlin Adams and her husband Ian Maxtone-Jones. Due to the long-standing rivalry between Katherine and Devlin, Katherine introduces Danny as her husband rather than admitting to being a single mother.
Katherine meets Devlin again, who invites her and Danny to dinner. Eddie agrees to take Palmer out to dinner so Danny can go with Katherine. Since he pretends to be a sheep seller, his cover is nearly blown when he is forced to save the life of a sheep who was choking on a toy. At dinner, Devlin asks Danny and Katherine to tell each other what they admire most about each other, and as Danny and Katherine talk, they begin to feel a connection. Later, when Palmer and Eddie return to the hotel, the former asks Danny to marry her. In fact, Eddie, drunk, had told her about the man's intention to marry her. Danny and Katherine are both surprised by the proposal, but Danny accepts. Danny later calls Katherine, but she says she wants to take a job in New York so she can start her life over.
The next day, Palmer asks Katherine if Danny is still in love with her, which Katherine denies.
Katherine then meets Devlin in a bar and admits she was never married to Danny. Devlin confesses that she is divorcing her husband because he is gay and also that he did not invent the iPod, but made his money by suing the Los Angeles Dodgers after being hit by a baseball. Katherine confides to Devlin that she's in love with Danny, but then Danny shows up behind her, saying that he didn't marry Palmer because he's in love with her. Meanwhile, on the return trip, Palmer meets a professional tennis player who shares his interests. Some time later, Danny and Katherine get married.

Zazie, a ten-year-old girl with delusional manners and trivial language, arrives from the provinces, eager to experience the Paris subway. Her uncle Gabriel waits for her at the station and, to her great disappointment, throws her directly into a taxi driven by her friend Charles and drops her off at the café Turandot. There, she meets Mado P'tits Pieds, a big-hearted waitress, her aunt Albertine, a model housewife, and other sultry figures.
Zazie escapes to finally take a ride on the subway, but when she realizes that it's closed because of a strike, she starts crying. From now on, we'll just go about our business. The uncle disguises himself as a Spanish dancer in a café-concert, Charles declares his flame to Mado while Zazie discovers the flea market in the company of Pédro-Surplus, who will transform into agent Trouscaillon, then into Aroun-Arachide.
After two days of Parisian madness, Zazie finally takes the subway to the station and back. But Zazie, asleep in her aunt's arms, doesn't realize she's using the famous object of her curiosity... When she is promptly dropped off on the train by her aunt, Zazie awakens. When her mother asks her what she did during her stay, the little girl replies that she has aged.

Violette, a 40-year-old Parisian workaholic with a career in the fashion industry, falls in love with a computer enthusiast from the countryside of Biarritz, Jean-René, while on vacation in a spa with her best friend, the promiscuous Ariane. Jean-René moves to Paris to be with Violette and meets her young adult son, Eloi, who still bears the childhood name Lolo. Lolo is a self-taught artist and his mother supports him completely. Lolo seems to embrace his mother's new love, but he moves cunningly to wreak havoc on their relationship.
Lolo, a parasite who wants his mother's universe to be centered around him, begins his game when nothing seems to disturb the couple's relationship. He plants a virus in Jean's newly coded software for a bank; the execution of the software on the buyer's system infects the entire network and Jean-René is arrested.
Jean-René warns Violette that all these accidents are caused by Lolo and that he has found evidence of this in Lolo's diary. Later, at Lolo's gruesome art exhibition, Ariane's daughter reveals to her mother Lolo's series of efforts to sabotage Violette's love life, and Ariane reports it to Violette. Jean-René restores his reputation by solving the problem to the bank's computer system and gets an appointment in the company.
Violette confronts Lolo with the facts she has learned, but Lolo tries to blackmail her emotionally. In the end, Violette cuts the emotional cord with Lolo and moves in with Jean-René. Lolo struggles to adjust to his new life without his mother's presence. Violette later realizes that Jean-René may also be facing problems with his daughter Sabine, as Violette herself with her son.

option_2_text:
Don Carlos, the heir to the throne of Spain, is in love with Elizabeth of Valois, the woman promised to his father Philip. The latter tries to prevent this marriage by having the young woman watched.
His motives are anything but noble. Nevertheless, Elizabeth sees Carlos and wants to marry him. They're making a plan to escape. But the plot is discovered, and Philip delivers his son to the Inquisition. The father refuses mercy, Carlos is executed. Philip's triumph was short-lived. Elizabeth can't stand the pain and she kills herself. The despotic monarch becomes a broken man.
option_3_text:
At a Paris railway terminus, Gabriel greets his sister Jeanne, who leaves her ten-year-old daughter Zazie with him and goes off with her latest lover. Gabriel takes the child out to the taxi of his friend Charles, to Zazie's dismay: she wants to go on the Métro but it is on strike. They arrive at Turandot's café, above which Gabriel lodges, and he hands the child over to his wife Albertine, who puts her to bed. Gabriel gets himself ready to go to work, on the way out getting into a dispute with Turandot, who is appalled by Zazie's precocity and filthy language.
In the morning, Zazie sneaks out alone but Turandot spots her and follows her. When he tries to take her home, she accuses him of paedophilia and a crowd gathers. Turandot is obliged to slink away and, when Gabriel returns from work, over several glasses tells him what has happened. After talking to Gridoux, the cobbler next door, instead of searching, Gabriel decides to go to bed. Zazie meanwhile is happily exploring Paris, trying every Métro station but all are shut. An elegant man picks her up and takes her to the flea market, where he buys her a pair of jeans and treats her to a dish of mussels. To reward his curiosity about her, she tells him how her mother killed her father gruesomely with an axe but was acquitted. She then describes life with her mother's lover, who got too interested in her, so she has been passed on to her uncle.
Sensing that the stranger also is getting too interested in her, she picks up her jeans and leaves. He accuses her of theft and a crowd gathers. He pretends to be a plain-clothes policemen and escorts Zazie back to her uncle's apartment, where a surprised Gabriel submits to the fake cop's interrogation. After a suggestion that Gabriel is prostituting the forward little girl, he is forced to reveal what his night job is: a drag act in a club. After the alleged cop then accuses Gabriel of homosexuality, he is thrown out of the flat and retreats to the bar below. Meanwhile, the café waitress, Mado, takes lunch to Gridoux next door, who is concerned over the nosy stranger. She however wants to talk about the cabbie Charles, who she hopes will marry her. When she goes back to her work, the stranger tries to pump the intractable Gridoux.
Gabriel and Charles now set off to show Zazie the sights of Paris. Various adventures and misunderstandings follow, particularly at the top of the Eiffel Tower. Zazie keeps annoying both men by trying to find out if her uncle is really homosexual. He however is a hit with a group of good-looking German girls, who think he is cute. As he walks along with Zazie, still pestering him over his sexuality, the two attract the attention of the overdressed widow Moaque. When the German girls descend on Gabriel and drag him onto their tour bus as their mascot, she finds a policeman to report this kidnapping. The cop, called Trouscaillon and identical to the man who earlier accused Gabriel of pimping and illegal sex, immediately becomes the object of Mouaque's desire.
After various adventures and misunderstandings, the three eventually find Gabriel, who has invited the German girls to see his show that night. He then invites Moaque and Trouscaillon to eat with him and Zazie at a restaurant. Seeking attention, Zazie does not behave well. Ringing the bar below his flat, Gabriel asks the waitress Mado to ask his wife Albertine to bring his costume to the club, as he is busy entertaining his friends. Mado tells him that the cabbie Charles has at last proposed, so Gabriel asks the two to join his swelling party. At the club, Gabriel orders champagne for his friends and waits anxiously for his costume. Albertine has however fallen asleep, to be woken by the fake cop from the morning who starts another of his bizarre interrogations. When he moves from words to attempted rape, she jumps out of the window. After his drag act, for which Albertine brought him a dress just in time, he takes everybody off to a bar. What starts with a couple slapping each other turns into a massive saloon brawl, which wrecks the place and brings on an army of cops. The group are rescued by Albertine who shows them a way into the Métro tunnels, through which they can walk in safety as the system is still on strike.
In the morning, Albertine carries the sleeping child to the railway station, where her mother Jeanne regrets that she will have to find a better-performing lover. Waking up, Zazie says her experiences have made her a bit more grown-up. Outside, all the escalators of the Métro start up because the strike is over.
option_4_text:
The gray everyday life of the old pawnbroker Josua Webmann and his apprentice Klaas Henning offers little special. For example, there is the chubby and always candy-sucking Elise Feuerhake. Klaas doesn't like them. Elise's mother would love to have him as a son-in-law. Suddenly, Klaas Henning and Joshua Webmann are witnessing a small miracle. A truly supernaturally lovely girl, who has come to town on holiday and lost her money, enters the shop and wants to borrow a large golden harp. When the charming creature is also interested in Webmann's collection of music boxes, the pawnbroker agrees and lends the instrument for 250 marks.
In the evening, Klaas visits the Youth Club for Education and Knowledge, which is actually a dance club. Klaas, who had previously played a rather inconspicuous role, unexpectedly becomes the hero of the day. The charming harp girl has accepted his invitation to the club and is dancing with him. From then on, the attractive Lissy also takes an interest in him. However, the evening threatens to come to a sad end when police station chief Haverkamp, Lissy's father, shows up to evict the club for disturbing the peace. Klaas can avert misfortune with a clever excuse. At the same time, Josua Webmann and his friend Hinrich Prigge, a recently retired ship's cook, argue about the mysterious girl with the harp in the inn "Zum Goldenen Lamm". While Prigge is convinced that this is an angel, Webmann fears for the loan he advanced in his ecstasy. There they are approached by a certain Mr. Parker. The stranger deals in musical instruments and, to Webmann's relief, also expresses an interest in the harp. Hinrich Prigg's attention, meanwhile, is on the hostess, Gerda Petersen. The two of them are very fond of each other. A genuine rapprochement, however, fails because of Hinrich's refusal to settle permanently.
The instrument dealer Parker shows up the next morning at the pawnshop and notices that the harp is of high value. If Webmann could buy the instrument for 2,000 marks, Parker would buy it from him for 2,700 marks. Webmann is enthusiastic about the planned deal and contacts the official appraiser Liebesam for security. In the evening, other miracles happen: Klaas goes out with Lissy Haverkamp and kisses her. In the pawnshop, the angel appears to charm Joshua Webmann and Hinrich Prigge with his harp playing.
But the next day the angel disappeared with the harp. Just as Webman alerts District Superintendent Haverkamp to initiate a manhunt for the fraudster, the mysterious creature reappears and pays back the loan. Webmann's offer to buy the harp for 2,000 marks, however, the girl doesn't want to hear about. In this way, the official appraiser will no longer be able to inspect the instrument. Parker, too, is disappointed by the collapse of the deal, since it is obviously a particularly valuable harp worth 10,000 marks. Meanwhile, a rift develops between Klaas and Lissy, because Klaas still has not gotten rid of his overly worried mother and her bosom friend Mrs. Feuerhake. Shortly thereafter, the angel appears to District Superintendent Haverkamp and asks him to take charge of the harp for a few days.
In the middle of the night, a burglar breaks into the pawn shop. Webmann, Prigge and Klaas are struck down by the unknown and end up in the hospital. What you don't know is that this gangster is an instrument dealer named Parker. In the hospital, the three wounded dream one after another of the magical angel, who reminds them of their previously missed goals in life. In fact, everyone is gaining more clarity about themselves and is now taking a much bolder stance. Klaas is finally telling his mother and Mrs. Feuerhake what he thinks. In the evening there is both the reconciliation between Klaas and Lissy and the engagement between Hinrich Prigge and Gerda Petersen. Finally, the angel reappears in the pawnshop. This time Webmann manages to buy the harp for 2,000 marks. Webmann's joy, however, is soon shattered by Schätzer's affection. The instrument is only worth 800 marks. On the other hand, a toy watch is worth more than 1,000 marks, so his loss is less. Whether the supposed angel is real or not is up to the viewer.

An old widow with a bad temper had two daughters. The eldest, Fanny, was unpleasant and proud, but behaved like her mother and resembled her, and was therefore the favorite of the matriarch; the youngest, Rose, was sweet, gentle and beautiful, but resembled her father. So the jealous and resentful widow mistreated the girl.
One day, as Rose was drawing water from the well, an elderly woman approached her and asked for some water to quench her thirst. The young woman kindly offered it to her, and afterward she discovered that the old woman was actually a fairy, who had taken that appearance to test the girl. Because she had been so kind and compassionate, the fairy blessed her: whenever she spoke, a precious metal, a jewel, or a beautiful flower would fall from her lips.
Upon returning home and explaining to her mother why she had taken so long to return, the widow was fascinated by the vision of that blessing. So, wishing his favorite daughter, Fanny, to have it too, he forced her to go to the well and feign kindness when an old woman approached. Fanny sat by the well but this time the fairy appeared to her transformed into a princess and again asked the young woman for some water. Fanny, however, spoke rudely and insulted her. The fairy then decided that as punishment for her contemptible attitude, a frog or a snake would come out of her lips every time she spoke.
When Fanny returned home and told her mother what had happened, with every word she uttered, frogs and snakes began to come out of her mouth. The widow, enraged, threw her younger daughter out of the house. In the forest, Rose met the son of a king, who fell in love with her and married her. In time, even the widow became disgusted with her favorite daughter. He threw her out of his house and she finally died alone and miserable in the woods.
option_0_text: Henry Roth is a marine veterinarian in Hawaii who has a habit of not getting attached and changing partners very often, giving them all sorts of excuses and using tricks. Between him and Diana and Chin, it's a dangerous game of cat and mouse.

In 1878, Colton Briggs, a gunfighter in the Montana Territory, is part of an out-of-court squad sent to arrest and hang the brother of notorious outlaw Walter McAllister. Walter and his men attempt to prevent the public execution, resulting in a shootout in which Colton and the younger McAllister are the only survivors. Colton informs Walter's brother that he should not be killed; his execution was just a ruse to lure his brother out of hiding. Furious, the younger McAllister tries to shoot Colton in the back. Without hesitation, Colton shoots him and rides off quietly while Walter's young nephew James watches.
Twenty years later, Colton has become a different and peaceful man. Under the influence of his wife, Ruth, he has become a respectable, decent businessman who owns a general store, a small farm, and a 12-year-old daughter named Brooke. To Colton's dismay, Brooke is defiant and reluctant; he finds that she is also emotionally withdrawn and unable to behave like "normal people" - qualities that remind him of his former life. One day, four men ride to Colton's farm; their leader identifies himself as James McAllister. His gang kills Ruth before she can paint a mocking message on the wall with her blood and move on.
Colton and Brooke return to the farm, where they encounter Franklin Jarrett, the U.S. Marshal and several deputies pursuing the McAllister gang. As Colton buries his wife Ruth, Jarrett reveals to Brooke that he and Colton were once close friends and that he is proud that Colton gave up his violent ways to start a family. Before he leaves, he admonishes his old friend Colton not to pursue his desire for revenge against James. Colton decides to do this anyway and tells Brooke that she will accompany him. In his old gunfighter clothes and armed with his old pistols, Colton burns down his farm and his house before leaving with Brooke.
The two eventually catch up with Jarret after ambushing a wounded deputy for his horse; James had set a trap for his pursuers in which three of them died and the others were too injured to continue. Colton and Brooke are disarming the survivors and threatening to torture them if Jarret doesn't talk. He finally admits that James is on his way to Santa Rosa, a town in southern Colorado, to retrieve a buried chest of money filled with Mexican pesos and flee across the border. Colton informs Jarret that he will take a horse with him, and warns him not to interfere with his quest for revenge, as he will kill him.
Arriving in Santa Rosa, Colton instructs Brooke to visit a local store and ask about James' whereabouts while he waits outside the city. James is not fooled and arrests Brooke when she tries to leave. In anticipation of further ambushes, Colton eventually manages to kill five members of the McAllister gang before the last remaining member comes at him with a shotgun aimed at Brooke. James informs Colton that he has two options: either he kills him, with Brooke dying, or he can save himself.
Given his situation, Colton decides to kill the second man while James shoots him in the chest. While James celebrates his victory, Brooke takes her father's gun (she learned to shoot on her travels) and avenges him by killing James.
Later, Jarret rides over and makes a deal with Brooke to tell everyone that Colton Briggs died a hero's death in the capture of the criminals and in return would keep the McAllister gang's cash box. What Jarret doesn't know, however, is that most of the money is in a pair of saddlebags that Brooke rides home with at the end of the film.

After a prologue that shows the trial of Soghomon Tehlirian who murdered in 1921 in Berlin Talaat Pacha, one of the main responsible for the Armenian Genocide, the film tells the story of the arrival of an Armenian family in Marseille, fleeing repression.
The story unfolds over 20 years following the memories of 6-year-old Azad, punctuated by voice-over commentary and flashbacks to the genocide period.
Azad tells us about his difficulties of integration in a France hostile to immigrants, including neighbors who do not want to let them use the communal oven; the landlord who accuses his tenants of having brought the bugs from their country; high-class classmates who make fun of Azad for his precarious living conditions and for his unusual religion, which they do not know is Christian, etc.

Set a few years after the Civil War, the film begins with a stagecoach crossing the windswept plains of Wyoming one winter during a snowstorm. The passengers, bounty hunter John Ruth (Kurt Russell) and his fugitive Daisy Domergue (Jennifer Jason Leigh), travel to the town of Red Rock as the only passengers on the stagecoach, where John Ruth, known in those lands as The Hangman, will bring Domergue to justice to be hanged and collect the bounty.
On the way they meet two strangers: Major Marquis Warren (Samuel L. Jackson), a black former Union soldier turned bounty hunter who has three dead fugitives lying in the snow; and then, in the middle of a forest, with Chris Mannix (Walton Goggins), a southern renegade who calls himself the town's new sheriff and says he needs to travel to Red Rock in order to receive the sheriff's appointment. Both of you get on the stage.
Threatened by a blizzard that advances forcefully behind them, John Ruth, Marquis Warren, Chris Mannix and the captive Daisy Domergue, seek shelter midway at Minnie's Shelter, an old country house in the middle of the road to Red Rock that could receive them and by which all stagecoaches must pass on their way to the village, which could keep them safe from the storm and keep the horses in a stable, so that after the storm they could continue their way to Red Rock and try to collect the reward for the capture of Daisy Domergue.
Upon arrival they meet Bob (Demian Bichir), a Mexican who says he is taking over the business temporarily while Minnie looks after her mother; Oswaldo Mobray (Tim Roth), an executioner who also travels to Red Rock; cowboy Joe Gage (Michael Madsen) and Confederate General Sandford Smithers (Bruce Dern). As the storm takes over the mountain and surrounds the shelter, our eight travelers will discover that they may not make it to Red Rock after all.[1]
While keeping the horses in the stable, Marquis Warren begins to suspect that something strange is going on in the shelter and decides to investigate the mystery on his own. John Ruth is also suspicious and decides to converse with the other inhabitants of the shelter to learn more about their lives. He disarms cowboy Joe Gage with the help of Marquis Warren, who puts a knife to his neck and warns them not to try to do anything against him because his group has more guns than they do.
As the group eats, Chris Mannix assumes that the Abraham Lincoln letter that Marquis Warren has is a forgery. Warren admits this, saying the letter gives him room to maneuver in front of the whites, outraging bounty hunter John Ruth. Shortly after, Marquis Warren places a gun next to Confederate Sandford Smithers and urges him to reach for it by telling him that he tortured his son by forcing him to walk naked in the snow, and then killed him. When Smithers picks up the gun, Warren shoots him in retaliation for Smithers' executions of black soldiers at the Battle of Baton Rouge.
At the same time, someone poisoned the coffee. Ruth and OB drink it, which kills OB while poisoned Ruth attacks Domergue, who then kills him with her own gun. Warren disarms Domergue, leaving Ruth in chains, and holds the others at gunpoint. He's joined by Mannix, whom Warren trusts because he almost drank the coffee.
Upon discovering that the chair Sweet Dave usually occupies is stained with blood and revealing that Minnie hated Mexicans and would never leave the grocery store in the care of one, Warren deduces that Bob killed the owners and executes him immediately. When Warren threatens to execute Domergue, Gage admits he poisoned the coffee. Jody (Channing Tatum), hiding in the basement below, shoots upward through the floorboards, hitting Warren in the groin. Mobray shoots Mannix, who fires back, wounding Mobray.
Hours before, Bob, Mobray, Gage and Domergue's brother Jody arrive at the shelter. They kill Minnie and five other people, leaving Smithers alone. Jody tells him they plan to rescue Domergue and they'll forgive him if he keeps quiet. They're disposing of the bodies and hiding the evidence. When Ruth's stage arrives, Jody hides in the basement.
In the present, Mannix and Warren, both badly wounded, hold Domergue, Gage and Mobray at gunpoint. When they threaten to kill her, Jody surrenders and is executed by Warren. She claims that her brother's men are waiting in Red Rock to kill Mannix; if Mannix kills Warren and allows him to escape, the gang will forgive him.
Warren shoots Domergue and Mobray, killing Mobray himself. Gage pulls out a revolver, but Mannix and Warren shoot him dead. Warren tries to shoot Domergue, but he doesn't have any bullets. Mannix rejects his offer, but faints from blood loss. Domergue cuts off Ruth's handcuffed arm and breaks free. Mannix regains consciousness and shoots him. Warren convinces him to hang Domergue from the rafters in honor of Ruth. As they agonise, Mannix reads aloud Lincoln's letter from Warren.

The film begins with an overview of the career stages of Jake "the Snake" Roberts. Mention is made, among other things, of his appearance at WrestleMania III in front of 90,000 spectators. Also speaking are some of his fellow wrestlers, including Steve Austin and Edge. Also addressed are his decades-long alcohol addiction and his infamous appearance in the documentary Beyond the Mat, which depicts him as a broken man. The last low point is an appearance at an independent wrestling show in 2008 in front of almost 700 people, where he appears heavily intoxicated and completely disoriented.
The film jumps to the year 2012. Diamond Dallas Page (DDP), who has previously described Jake Roberts as a mentor, visits Jake Roberts at his home in Gainesville, Texas and tries to convince him of his newly developed yoga program. Roberts has taken a hard fall, suffering both from his alcoholism and from severe pain after his last surgery. He also reveals that he smoked crack a month ago.
Jake moves into DDP's house, which he renames "The Accountability Crib" for the purpose, and begins an extensive rehabilitation program consisting of yoga, various conversations, training, and shared activities. There are several relapses, but over the course of the program, Robert's health begins to improve and he begins to deal with his family, from whom he has become very distant. His goal is to compete in the WWE Royal Rumble as a celebrity guest. After a few months, he needs surgery on his shoulder. Since he doesn't have health insurance, the money will be raised through a crowdfunding campaign on Indiegogo. After 15 weeks, a second colleague joins DDP's program along with equally stranded Scott Hall.
It also documents how Jake Roberts continues to be active in the wrestling business. He attends fantasy meetings, podcasts and other events. On the road to recovery, he's also being honored by the Cauliflower Alley Club. In the end, he is first invited to an "Old School" episode of WWE Raw. The highlight of the film is his induction into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2014. There it is introduced by DDP. On the same night, Scott Hall will also be honored. The film ends with Page, Hall, and Roberts discussing their lives.
